title: Colts Week 7 Snap Count Analysis: 3 Takeaways From Vikings Loss
full_text:
A box score can only tell you so much about an NFL game. Snap counts offer another perspective, showing which players coaches trusted most , who saw their role change and where opportunities opened up.
The Indianapolis Colts ' 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings provided plenty to examine beneath the surface. With seven games in the books, the latest snap counts offer a closer look at how the roster is taking shape as the team tries to salvage its season .
The Colts' search for consistency at linebacker continues. Sunday's loss to the Vikings offered another example of how unsettled the rotation remains.
Only Akeem Davis-Gaither has solidified his place as the unit's every-down MIKE linebacker. The WILL spot has been a revolving door.
Davis-Gaither played 57 of 59 defensive snaps against Minnesota, but three different linebackers split time next to him: Jaylon Carlies played 23 snaps, Germaine Pratt played 20 and Austin Ajiake saw 18.
The circumstances explain some of the rotation. Rookies CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher were inactive with injuries, Carlies was returning from a two-game absence, and Pratt had just been elevated from the practice squad after joining the team earlier in the week. Still, the Colts have struggled to establish a consistent pecking order at the position through the first seven weeks of the season.
Carlies opened the year as a starter but has missed time with injuries. Boettcher had been part of the rotation before his latest setback, while Ajiake has really only played when options have been thin. Pratt's arrival added another name to the mix without necessarily providing a long-term answer.
Davis-Gaither has earned his workload, but the same cannot be said of anyone competing to play alongside him. With Indianapolis sitting at 2-5, the team is running out of time to establish continuity. Allen's eventual return could give the Colts another opportunity to evaluate their options, although he has primarily played the MIKE.
For now, the rotation remains a question mark. Injuries have complicated the situation, but the Colts really need someone to seize the opportunity and give the defense some much-needed stability.
The Colts' wide receiver rotation has become difficult to understand.
Keenan Allen saw his playing time drop significantly against Minnesota despite leading Indianapolis in receptions, while Laquon Treadwell continued to play a major role in an offense that desperately needs more production through the air.
Josh Downs led the receivers with 52 snaps, followed by Treadwell with 45 and Allen with just 30. Allen played 49% of the offensive snaps after seeing 71% against Tennessee, a notable decline for a veteran who caught all three of his targets for 31 yards against the Vikings. He led the Colts in both receptions and receiving yards.
For context, the run-heavy game plan likely played a role in Allen's reduced workload. Still, that explanation only goes so far. Allen's experience and size should make him a useful option in a game plan that requires receivers to block on the perimeter, particularly when Downs, a smaller player, is one of the primary alternatives.
Treadwell's continued involvement is also worth questioning. He played 45 snaps but managed just two catches for 19 yards. This season, Treadwell has logged just 15 catches on 358 snaps.
Downs wasn't much more productive, finishing with two receptions for 18 yards on four targets. With Alec Pierce unavailable, Indianapolis was already short on proven receiving options, yet Deion Burks played just seven snaps and Ashton Dulin saw only one in his return from a hamstring injury.
There may be legitimate reasons for the distribution, including the specific packages Indianapolis wanted to use and the need to manage players returning from injury. But the results were hardly encouraging. The Colts scored just 10 points, and no receiver managed more than 31 yards. No Colts wide out has caught a touchdown since the team's last win, a 19-17 victory over Houston.
Indianapolis needs to find ways to keep its most reliable receiving options involved, particularly as the offense struggles to move the ball.
Tyler Warren's absence created an opportunity for the Colts' other tight ends to step up, but the distribution of playing time against Minnesota raised some questions about how Indianapolis views the position.
Mo Alie-Cox led the group with 39 offensive snaps, playing 64% of the team's offensive plays. That was a significant increase from the 31 snaps he recorded against Tennessee.
Will Mallory went in the opposite direction. After playing 43 snaps against the Titans, Mallory saw his workload fall to 21 against Minnesota, a notable shift considering Warren's absence had created an opportunity for Mallory to establish himself as a reliable option.
The results didn't exactly justify the rotation, either. Mallory was targeted three times but failed to record a catch, while Alie-Cox was targeted twice without a reception. Drew Ogletree was the lone Colts tight end to catch a pass, finishing with two receptions for 12 yards.
Warren's eventual return should restore some order to the position, but Indianapolis still needs to figure out what it wants from the players behind him.
Alie-Cox has experience as a blocker, while Mallory offers a different skill set. With the offense struggling to produce points, the Colts need to make better use of their available personnel rather than simply cycling through options without much production to show for it.

title: Colts Week 7 Position Grades: Offense Falls Flat Against Vikings
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts finally got a respectable performance from their defense Sunday. Unfortunately, the offense completely fell apart against Minnesota's relentless pressure.
Minnesota walked away with a 16-10 win, dropping Indianapolis to 2-5, and Brian Flores' defense was the story.
Flores is a mad scientist, and watching his pressure packages connect is like watching a piece of art come together in real time. The Vikings blitzed on an NFL-record 85.2% of Colts dropbacks in the Next Gen Stats era, and a one-dimensional Indianapolis offense had absolutely no answer.
A Colts fan could only wish. Here are my position grades from Week 7.
Daniel Jones finished 13-of-22 for 108 yards, zero touchdowns and one late interception, earning a 53.2 offensive grade and 46.5 passing grade from PFF.
Jones faced pressure 16 times and took four sacks. He completed 9-of-11 passes for 83 yards from a clean pocket, but his completion percentage dropped to just 36.4% when under pressure.
Whether Jones had nowhere to go with the ball or Minnesota's pressure simply got there too quickly, he looked like the old Giants version of Daniel Jones again.
Jonathan Taylor was basically the entire offense, rushing 18 times for 95 yards and a touchdown while gaining 64 yards after contact.
Seth McGowan also had a strong afternoon with 46 yards on 11 carries and provided a major spark in the return game.
No Colts receiver finished with more than Keenan Allen's 31 yards, and the entire room combined for only 10 targets and 79 yards.
Jones did not always have time, but this group still made almost no impact. Indianapolis desperately needs some explosiveness back in this receiver room.
Drew Ogletree caught two passes, while the rest of the tight end room went without a catch on five targets.
This offense badly needs Tyler Warren back. The pass blocking was also rough, including a 30.4 PFF pass-blocking grade from Mo Alie-Cox.
Bernhard Raimann and Quenton Nelson held up well in pass protection, but the rest of the line struggled against Minnesota's constant pressure.
Indianapolis allowed four sacks on 16 pressures, while Tanner Bortolini, Nelson and Matt Goncalves averaged just a 45.8 run-blocking grade.
For once, this defense gave Indianapolis enough to win.
Minnesota finished with 136 rushing yards but no rushing touchdowns, while the Colts' defensive line generated 11 pressures and two sacks. The defensive ends played particularly well, although DeForest Buckner had a quiet afternoon.
Akeem Davis-Gaither showed real improvement in coverage with a 70.2 grade, but the rest of the linebacker room averaged just 43.9.
Run defense also left plenty to be desired outside of Jaylon Carlies, but limiting Minnesota's overall production was still a step in the right direction.
Justin Walley had his breakout game with a 94.2 PFF coverage grade, while Kenneth Harris also played well.
Charvarius Ward struggled, but the group missed zero tackles and held Minnesota to only 150 passing yards and one touchdown without Sauce Gardner. This was a good showing for this group.
Defending the run wasn't the issue for this unit. Pass coverage was a completely different story.
The unit averaged a 44.5 coverage grade and allowed a reception on every target, while Cam Bynum and A.J. Haulcy surrendered passer ratings of 118.8 and 152.1 when targeted.
Spencer Shrader missed two field goals for the first time in his career, from 56 and 48 yards.
The expectations are high because Shrader has been so reliable, so those misses hurt in a six-point loss. I still have zero concern about him going forward.
For most of this season, the defense has been the problem in Indianapolis.
Sunday was the exact opposite, and until this offense becomes more than Jonathan Taylor and hope, performances like this are going to keep happening.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts' Season Is Spiraling. These 5 Quotes Tell the Story
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have hit a wall. Three straight losses have dropped them to 2-5 and put their season in serious jeopardy.
Sunday's 16-10 defeat to the Minnesota Vikings left Indianapolis with plenty of questions to answer. In the aftermath, several members of the organization offered revealing comments that provide a closer look at where the Colts stand following another disappointing loss.
Steichen Remains Committed to Daniel Jones
Head coach Shane Steichen has no plans to make a change at quarterback, despite having every reason to.
Following Sunday's 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, Steichen was asked whether he had considered benching Daniel Jones. His answer?
"I have a ton of faith in Daniel."
As the season progresses and Jones shows few signs of improvement, that faith is beginning to become unwarranted. Jones completed just 13 of 22 passes for 108 yards against Minnesota, took four sacks and threw an interception on Indianapolis' final possession to seal the defeat. He has now thrown seven interceptions against just four touchdowns through seven games.
"I got a ton of faith in Daniel (Jones)." #Colts head coach Shane Steichen said he has not thought about a quarterback change. pic.twitter.com/VF5j10SKaE
Steichen pointed to the game plan's emphasis on running the football, but the passing attack's continued struggles have become difficult to ignore. With Indianapolis sitting at 2-5, sticking with Jones is a significant gamble for a coaching staff that needs results. Anthony Richardson Sr. remains an alternative, though he has yet to play this season and Steichen has consistently dismissed him as a possible option.
Even if it's borderline delusional, Steichen's confidence in Jones is obvious. For a guy coaching for his job the rest of the way, it's easy to see that if Steichen is going to bow out, he's doing it on his terms.
DeForest Buckner has been very forthcoming regarding his frustration with the Colts. After yet another loss, the veteran defensive tackle had little patience for questions about a team that continues to fall short.
When asked if he's frustrated, Buckner kept things blunt. "I don't know. How about you guess. Yeah, I'm frustrated. Same thing, we lost," he said.
Asked where the Colts go from here and what was missing from the team, Buckner offered little optimism, responding, "(I) couldn't tell you" and "I don't know."
It's a troubling place for Indianapolis to be. The Colts have no clear answers for how to reverse their slide. Buckner has been through years of disappointment with the franchise, and his comments reflect the frustration of a veteran who has yet to see the sustained success the organization has been chasing.
If I spent my prime years playing for a consistently mediocre team, I'd be seething too.
If there's a silver lining for Buckner, it's that the loss puts the Colts one step closer to a full roster clean out before the Nov. 10 deadline, which is expected to include the 32-year-old.
Jonathan Taylor's Future in Indianapolis Is Uncertain
Jonathan Taylor is trying to tune out the noise surrounding his future with the Indianapolis Colts, but the trade speculation isn't going away.
Taylor's wife, Ayanna, fueled the conversation over the weekend by discussing the possibility of her husband being traded on social media. Following Sunday's loss to the Minnesota Vikings, Taylor was asked about her comments and largely brushed them aside.
"It's been out there already, so I think her adding (to it) doesn't really change anything. You know everybody's on TikTok these days. So, you just gotta … stay focused," Taylor said.
Part 2 from #Colts RB Jonathan Taylor’s wife, Ayanna, on his trade rumors: “How are they gonna get new leadership to come in when they really have no options? …” “That’s what brings us back to my husband. Do they keep him? … Or do they just cut their losses and trade him?” https://t.co/hs5S81hKLS pic.twitter.com/WQJrBC435R
Given how the past few weeks have gone in Indianapolis, it's easy to understand why the speculation has intensified. With the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaching, the Colts face major questions about their direction and whether moving veteran players could help them rebuild.
Still, Taylor has remained indifferent to a trade. He signed a two-year, $44 million extension in August that keeps him under contract through 2028, making a trade a significant decision for the franchise. But his wife's comments have put his future in the spotlight at a time when little appears settled in Indianapolis.
Interestingly, reports from ESPN's Adam Schefter indicate that Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon is inclined to retain Taylor. "Irsay-Gordon views Taylor as a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," he writes, adding the Colts would have to receive a near-too-good-to-be-true compensation package to move their superstar running back.
Quenton Nelson Is Still Holding Out Hope
Offensive guard Quenton Nelson is urging the Colts to keep believing they can turn their season around.
"Everyone needs to believe that we can do it. That we can get a win," he said postgame. "All it takes is one to go on a run."
It's an understandable message from one of Indianapolis' veteran leaders, but the Colts need more than just belief to change their trajectory. Their recent stretch of defeats that has raised serious questions about the team's direction, and Sunday's defeat marked another missed opportunity to get back on track.
Nelson is right that one win can change the tone around a struggling team. But with the Colts running out of time, results need to come quickly.
Anthony Richardson's Comments Raise Questions About His Judgment
Anthony Richardson has yet to see the field for the Indianapolis Colts this season, and his latest comments aren't likely to help his chances of earning another opportunity.
Richardson was asked Sunday about his recent misdemeanor marijuana possession charge, which stems from an October traffic stop. He declined to discuss the ongoing legal matter in detail but offered an answer when asked whether he regretted the incident.
"I enjoy life. I don't really regret a lot of things I do. I appreciate my life. I appreciate God waking me up every morning," Richardson said.
Richardson is entitled to let the legal process play out without commenting on the specifics of the case. But his broader response raises larger questions about his judgment at a time when his NFL future is in the balance.
The former No. 4 pick is in his fourth season and has made just two appearances since the start of 2025. With Daniel Jones struggling and the Colts falling to 2-5, Richardson could theoretically have an opportunity to get back into the quarterback conversation. Instead, this is just another example of how he can't seem to get out of his own way.
Richardson's comments don't establish whether he regrets the specific incident, and it would be unfair to treat them as an admission that he doesn't. Still, with his career at a crossroads, he needs to give the organization confidence that he's prepared to make the decisions required to earn another chance.
Right now, they don't seem keen on giving him one.

title: Shane Steichen Doubles Down on Daniel Jones Despite Poor Results
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have lost three straight games, fallen to 2-5, and watched their season spiral out of control. Yet head coach Shane Steichen apparently has no interest in reconsidering his quarterback situation.
Following Sunday's 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, Steichen reaffirmed his confidence in Daniel Jones, saying he has a “ton of faith” in the veteran quarterback.
At this point, that faith is unjustifiable . Jones has struggled all year and is a shell of the player the Colts had for 10 games a season ago.
Jones has thrown just four touchdowns to seven interceptions through seven games this season. Sunday's performance was another low point: he finished with 108 passing yards, no touchdowns, and an interception on the Colts' final drive.
The contrast with last season is stark. In 13 starts in 2025, Jones threw for 3,101 yards and 19 touchdowns against eight interceptions while completing 68% of his passes, giving the Colts a reason to believe he could be their answer at quarterback.
The current version of Jones has done little to warrant Steichen’s dogged commitment.
Despite those struggles, Steichen is digging his heels in, determined to do anything but entertain the possibility of benching Jones. When asked after Sunday's loss whether he had considered a quarterback change, Steichen said he had not, reiterating his confidence in the veteran.
Here’s the problem. Everyone can see that Jones isn’t producing the results necessary. That is, everyone but Steichen.
Steichen’s response is difficult to defend. Coaches should stand behind their players, but that support cannot come at the expense of making necessary decisions. Jones has had seven games to affirm last year wasn't a fluke, but he's done next to nothing to inspire confidence.
At 2-5, the Colts have reached a point where continuing to roll Jones out there with the starters week in and week out borders on malpractice.
The bigger question is what Steichen's refusal to consider a change says about Anthony Richardson. If Jones' struggles haven't been enough to prompt a serious evaluation of the alternatives, it raises questions about how the coaching staff views the former fourth overall pick and whether he has any realistic path back into the starting lineup.
Richardson hasn't exactly made his own case easier .
In addition to swinging and missing at his first chance as the starter, Richardson’s recent marijuana-related charge and subsequent comments expressing no regret have added another complication to an already uncertain situation.
Still, those issues shouldn't eliminate the possibility of giving him another chance. If Steichen no longer believes Richardson can be a viable option, the organization needs to confront that reality. If he does, it's difficult to understand why the Colts wouldn't at least explore a change with their season slipping away.
Richardson doesn't need to be the long-term answer to justify giving him another opportunity. With the season slipping away, there is little to no downside to finding out whether he can offer something Jones hasn't.
Even if Richardson fails to capitalize, Indianapolis would have a clearer picture of its quarterback situation heading into the offseason.
Ultimately, Steichen's unwavering support for Jones says as much about the coach as it does the quarterback. At 2-5, Steichen has every reason to reevaluate his approach. Instead, he appears determined to stick with his guy regardless of the results.
If Steichen is going down with the ship, he's making it clear that he'll do so on his own terms.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From Colts' Loss to Vikings: Who Stood Out Most?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts fell to 2-5 in the 2026 regular season after losing 16-10 to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings on the road.
While this season is all but over, there are still some positives to pull from, at least from an individual performance standpoint.
The current-look Colts are dead in the water , but not all is lost with their future outlook, regardless of how bleak it may seem.
With that being said, I'm taking the opportunity to break down who stood out most in the Colts' most recent showing.
Follow along as I break down the Colts' biggest winners and losers from their Week 7 loss to the Minnesota Vikings.
We've been watching Adetomiwa Adebawore's career with great interest, and it's slowly but surely paid off.
The Colts drafted Adebawore in the fourth round of the 2023 NFL Draft (110th overall), betting on his absurd athletic profile and intriguing pass-rush tools.
The fourth-year interior defensive lineman was always envisioned to become the ideal complement piece to veteran DT DeForest Buckner, and that vision is quickly coming into shape.
Adebawore improved upon his career-best performance from earlier this season, a 1.5-sack showing against the Houston Texans, with a legitimate arrival against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 7.
Against the Vikings, Adebawore was all over the place:
5 tackles, 2.0 sacks, 2 tackles for loss, 1 pass broken up, and 2 QB Hits.
Adebawore notched career-highs in sacks and tackles for loss, and now sits with a career-best four sacks after just seven games.
Even though Adetomiwa Adebawore is breaking out right at the worst time for the Colts, aka doing so on an expiring deal when the franchise is staring down a full-blown rebuild, the belief the organization has shown in him throughout the years may grant them a solid building block for the future once free agency comes around.
Shocker: Jonathan Taylor is still a superstar running back.
Taylor had one of his best performances of the 2026 regular season against the Minnesota Vikings, totaling 95 rushing yards and one score on 18 carries.
Taylor's 5.3 yards-per-carry is his best single-game performance of the season so far, and although he failed to reach 100 yards rushing for the first time this season, it's still impressive considering the Colts' opponents have been regularly stacking the box and/or blitzing to disrupt Daniel Jones and Co.
More than anything else, Taylor's performance improved his personal stock.
As the NFL trade deadline nears (11/10 at 4 PM EST), teams will be calling the Colts as they embark upon a cleaned house, and Jonathan Taylor is the top trade candidate to call about.
Colts Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon views Taylor as "a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," according to ESPN Insiders Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter .
This makes sense given his fresh extension and consistent production, but the Colts can't value loyalty over the future if the right price comes calling.
Any legitimate Super Bowl contender will be interested in Jonathan Taylor's services, especially those without a bona fide RB1, so while it'd be ideal to keep him around for the looming rebuild, the Colts can't turn down worthwhile trade compensation.
The Colts' second pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, safety A.J. Haulcy, is finding his footing as an NFL starter.
Haulcy has had some up-and-down showings to kick off his NFL career, but against the Minnesota Vikings, he appeared to have an "I get it now" moment.
The Colts' third-round pick (78th overall) led the team in total tackles (9) and solo tackles (5) in their Week 7 matchup against the Vikings.
Haulcy did have a miscommunication in coverage that led to the Vikings' lone touchdown of the day, but I'm willing to chalk it up to rookie growing pains.
Outside of his lone blip in coverage, Haulcy was lights out.
The rookie defensive back was flying around the ball and looked to be the ideal Nick Cross replacement at strong safety that the Colts envisioned he could become.
Although the future is bleak, at least some of the Colts' recent draft picks are looking like solid foundational pieces to build on.
The Indianapolis Colts know what the quarterback carousel looks like after a near-decade of Chris Ballard roster construction, and Daniel Jones's recent installment looks no different.
Jones had arguably his worst showing of the season in Week 7 , which is saying something, considering he's had a handful of stinkers to choose from, and was fresh off his poorest performance of the year against the then-winless Tennessee Titans.
Against the Minnesota Vikings, Jones had similarly poor showing:
13-22 (59% completion) for 108 passing yards (4.9 yards per completion), one interception, and was sacked four times for a 52.8 passer rating
According to Next Gen Stats, Flores' Vikings defense blitzed Jones and Co. on 85.2% of dropbacks, the highest blitz rate by a defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). Minnesota generated pressure on 60.9% of those blitzes, with all four of its sacks coming when blitzing.
The Vikings knew exactly how to stop Jones and Co., and the Colts did nothing to stop it.
Jones is just one of two starting quarterbacks in the NFL who have thrown more interceptions (7) than touchdowns (4) through seven weeks of play, joining Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert.
The Colts may have financially tied themselves to Daniel Jones for the foreseeable future, but there's an out in his contract that would allow Indianapolis to save ~$38 million if they make him a post-June 1st cut designation.
Regardless of what the Colts decide when it comes to Jones's future in Indianapolis, we've been given no reason to believe that he'll magically become the brief version of himself that helped the Colts jump out to an unforeseen start in 2025.
There's simply no justification as to why Daniel Jones should remain the Colts' starting quarterback moving forward , despite whatever belief head coach Shane Steichen says he has in him.
Aside from his first kick attempt of the new season, a missed extra point attempt, Spencer Shrader was perfect entering Week 7's matchup against the Minnesota Vikings.
Shrader was a perfect 19-for-19 on field goal attempts entering Week 7, including an impressive 6-for-6 on 50+ yard attempts.
However, when the Colts' anemic offense needed him most, Shrader vanished.
Shrader went 1-for-3 on field goal attempts against the Vikings, his second miss being a 48-yard attempt that would've tied the game 13-13 with a little over four minutes remaining in the fourth quarter.
To be fair, Shrader had been the team's MVP through six weeks of play, but as Ross Tucker said during the broadcast, "it's like every week, somebody for the Colts takes turns not doing their job."
I wouldn't be too concerned with Spencer Shrader moving forward, as the worst thing we learned about him from his uncharacteristically poor performance is that he's indeed human after all.
Shane Steichen's Colts offense looked to have found a groove against the Minnesota Vikings, as they went 8-15 on third-down conversions and successfully converted their lone fourth-down attempt; it wasn't enough to suggest that they'll perform any better down the stretch.
The Colts entered Week 7 with the worst turnover margin (-8) in the NFL, having gone 11 consecutive games without winning the turnover margin — the longest active streak in the league and the longest for Indianapolis since a 13-game stretch in 1998-99, according to Next Gen Stats — and that streak continued as the Colts lost the turnover battle (-1) against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 7.
Neither Steichen nor defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo is doing enough to get the job done.
Although longtime general manager Chris Ballard's midseason firing and the ongoing pressure from ownership suggest they would be coaching elsewhere come next season, the coaching staff's collective seat is getting hotter by the week.
Steichen has had his shortcomings as a head…

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly From the Colts’ Loss in Minnesota
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts suffered another frustrating defeat on Sunday, falling 16-10 to the Minnesota Vikings on the road. What began as a promising afternoon ended in another missed opportunity for a team desperately searching for something to build on.
Indianapolis has now lost three consecutive games and dropped to 2-5 on the season. With the losing streak growing and the season slipping further off course, the pressure is mounting on a franchise that needs to find a way to turn things around.
Here's a look at the good, the bad, and the ugly from Sunday's loss.
Indianapolis leaned heavily into their run game against a Vikings defense that caused chaos for Daniel Jones through the air.
The Colts recorded 154 rushing yards as a team, with Jonathan Taylor accounting for 95 by himself. Taylor also had the lone Colts’ touchdown, a 38-yard scamper in the first quarter.
Seth McGowan was the most impressive, however. He saw the most run of his young career up to this point, knowing the Colts needed to keep Taylor fresh if they were to continue leaning into the run game.
McGowan had 46 yards on 11 carries, both career-highs. If Indianapolis does have a true fire sale ahead of the trade deadline and move on from Taylor, McGowan will have a chance to audition for a larger role in the seasons to come.
It’s safe to say Adetomiwa Adebawore has finally arrived.
The fourth-year defensive tackle was easily the best player for a Colts defense which played with the most energy and effort we’ve seen from them this season. Adebawore logged two sacks, his second multi-sack game of the season, tying his career-high for sacks in a season (4).
Adebawore is a pending free agent at the end of the season. If Colts interim general manager Ed Dodds signs him to a contract extension, I don’t think there would be many complaints.
With the DeForest Buckner era all but over, Indianapolis may already be looking at their 3-tech of the future.
The Vikings defense entered Week 7 leading the league in third-down defense, allowing a conversion just 22% of the time. Yet, the Colts found a way to have success.
Indianapolis finished 8-for-15 on third down (53%), with several conversions coming on the ground. For a unit that came into the game moving the chains just 37.3% of the time, that’s a noteworthy improvement.
Unfortunately, that didn't translate to more points.
The Colts offensive line knew they’d be blitzed, and blitzed, and blitzed again by Brian Flores’ defense. But even knowing what was coming, they couldn’t handle the pass rush.
Minnesota got to Daniel Jones for a sack four times, picking on the Colts running backs in pass protection most of the time. It’s the second week in a row the Colts have surrendered at least that many and the fifth time this season they’ve given up multiple in a game.
While Jones isn’t blameless himself, the Colts offensive line, which was supposedly one of Indy’s biggest strengths, has been all over the place through seven games. A lot to clean up moving forward.
Shane Steichen is far from devoid of blame for this loss.
Steichen's offense continues to look increasingly dysfunctional. Indianapolis managed just 10 points despite winning the time of possession battle. While the Vikings have one of the league's best defenses, Steichen couldn't find a way to consistently generate offense when the passing game stalled.
The Colts leaned heavily, maybe too heavily, on Jonathan Taylor and the running game, but that wasn't enough to compensate for the lack of a passing attack.
Steichen deserves criticism for failing to find answers against Brian Flores' aggressive defensive scheme as well as continuing to stick with Daniel Jones at quarterback, especially with the season slipping away.
Daniel Jones didn't make enough plays in the passing game, but it’s not all on him.
Indianapolis' receivers did little to help Jones against Minnesota's aggressive defense. Josh Downs managed just two catches for 18 yards, while no Colts receiver finished with more than 31 receiving yards.
The offensive line and Jones deserve plenty of blame, but the pass catchers didn't do their job, either.
Shane Steichen has continued to vehemently defend Daniel Jones to the media despite continued poor play. Sunday, Jones did nothing to back his head coach’s claims up.
Jones managed just 108 passing yards and threw an interception on the game’s final drive, ending any chance the Colts had at a late comeback.
Steichen can continue to stand behind his quarterback publicly, but at some point, the results have to justify that confidence. Jones has done little to warrant the unwavering support, and Sunday's performance only strengthened the case that Indianapolis needs to reconsider its options under center.
With the season already a wash at this point, the Colts truly have nothing to lose by giving Anthony Richardson Sr. a shot. Your move, Shane.
Indianapolis' pass rush was once again a major disappointment.
Adetomiwa Adebawore came to play, but the rest of the defensive front did not, struggling to consistently pressure Kyler Murray or disrupt Minnesota's passing game. The rest of the defense covered for their pass rush and found ways to get off the field, but that can only take a defense so far.
For a team that entered the season with questions about its ability to rush the passer, Sunday was yet another reminder that the problem remains unresolved.
DeForest Buckner can only do so much (and may be on the way out), and Indianapolis needs more players capable of making an impact up front. With the Colts now 2-5, addressing that weakness should be a priority as the organization evaluates its roster moving forward .
Spencer Shrader has been one of the most consistent players on the Colts this season, but Sunday was his worst performance of the season so far.
Shrader picked a bad day to have a bad day, missing two field goals, from 56 and 48 yards each. Given the Colts lost by six, those misses ultimately made the difference.
Definitely a day to forget for the 27-year-old, who can only hope a day like Sunday is just a fluke.

title: It's Time For Colts to Accept Their Fate: Loss to Vikings Confirms Rebuild is Imminent
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts fall to 2-5 in the 2026 season after losing 16-10 on the road to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings.
The new look (same old?) Colts lose their first game since firing longtime general manager Chris Ballard, proving that the roster he built is simply not good enough.
The Colts actually looked like a competitive team for most of the game, as most post-firing squads appear, but at the end of the day, this is the same roster that got Ballard fired after six weeks.
Indianapolis' season is over, and now the Colts need to put all of their focus and resources into kicking off their rebuild.
Colts' head coach Shane Steichen has put his undying faith in quarterback Daniel Jones , and this loyalty has resulted in an unsustainable offense through seven games of the 2026 regular season.
The Colts' offense looks nothing like it did in the early stages of the 2025 season, the very version Steichen has clung to for far too long.
A worse offensive roster and lingering side effects from Jones's infamous torn Achilles have given us peak Daniel Jones (derogatory), and Steichen's continued belief in his starting quarterback has become unwarranted.
Entering the Colts' Week 7 road matchup against the Vikings, Daniel Jones was just one of three starting quarterbacks with more interceptions (6) than touchdowns (4), and that trend only continued in Minnesota.
This was always set to be a brutal matchup for Daniel Jones and Co., but man, did it bring out the worst in the Colts' starting quarterback.
Jones has struggled immensely against pressure this season, specifically against the blitz.
Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is known for his blitz-heavy scheme, and he took advantage of the matchup in question.
According to Next Gen Stats, Flores' Vikings defense blitzed Jones and Co. on 85.2% of dropbacks, the highest blitz rate by a defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). Minnesota generated pressure on 60.9% of those blitzes, with all four of its sacks coming when blitzing.
As a result, Jones put up the following numbers against Flores and Co.:
13-22 (59% completion) for 108 passing yards (4.9 yards per completion), one interception, and was sacked four times for a 52.8 passer rating.
Following the loss, head coach Shane Steichen said that he has not considered a change at quarterback because he has "a ton of faith in Daniel [Jones]."
But through seven weeks of play, there's no reason to think this offense led by Daniel Jones is so much better than one led by Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard that Indianapolis needs to ride this train until the wheels fall off.
Steichen is wrong to be so confident in this version of Daniel Jones , and such loyalty may be his ultimate undoing as the Indianapolis Colts' head coach.
The Indianapolis Colts wanted to give Shane Steichen one last fair shake after longtime general manager Chris Ballard was let go, but that's already looking like a mistake.
The Colts aimed to treat their next two games against the undefeated Minnesota Vikings and the division-leading Jacksonville Jaguars as final tests for how this roster will look once the regular season ends, seeing if there's enough to warrant keeping top trade pieces around for a playoff push.
The season was already over entering this two-game stretch, as evidenced by the roster, but this showing against the Vikings proved that this version of the Colts is not good enough.
After longtime assistant manager Ed Dodds took over as the Colts' interim general manager earlier this week , it was revealed that head coach Shane Steichen and all non-personnel staff will report directly to ownership for the remainder of the season.
The Colts are at a point where trading off as many assets as possible for the future is most important, but they can still muster a miracle out of their current roster, but Steichen has refused to give them that hypothetical look.
There have already been numerous instances this season where Steichen could turn to Anthony Richardson, whether that be as a pure rushing threat in the red zone or as a last-resort Hail Mary thrower.
Steichen has been out on Anthony Richardson since the young quarterback's sophomore season showcased a brutal example of the 'terrible twos,' but with his seat hotter than ever, you'd expect him to make any move that could save his job.
Richardson's recent charge for marijuana possession provided Steichen with more reason not to turn to him , but there's simply no reason not to turn to any quarterback not named Daniel Jones at this point.
Steichen's unwarranted belief in starting quarterback Daniel Jones is at the forefront of such coaching malpractice, and this decision to roll with Jones may just be his own final nail in his coffin.
The Indianapolis Colts have become the hot topic of the NFL trade deadline for the second consecutive season - but not because they're unforeseen buyers, but because they've become sellers.
No player is expected to be off-limits if the Colts indeed decide to begin wholesale changes to their roster, but there are a couple of players they'd prefer to keep around for the new era.
Star running back Jonathan Taylor is still viewed as a cornerstone player.
Colts Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon views Taylor as "a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," according to ESPN Insiders Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter .
This makes sense given his fresh extension and consistent production, but the Colts can't value loyalty over the future if the right price comes calling.
A high second-round pick remains the starting point in negotiations, but if a contender wants to trade away a late first-round selection for Taylor's services, you simply cannot say no.
Taylor is no doubt a superstar that you can lean on, but with the Colts' immediate future looking bleak without a first-round pick at their disposal, you have to take that opportunity.
Taylor will help the 2027 Colts stay afloat, but he'll be 29 years old entering his first season alongside Indianapolis' quarterback of the future, if they choose to do so in the 2028 NFL Draft.
Furthermore, the Colts would likely also like to re-sign future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson to kick off the rebuild, but his expiring contract makes convincing almost impossible.
Nelson has stuck around for multiple rebuilds, and given that he's reached his thirties, a fresh start elsewhere feels most likely.
Finally, the Colts are in such a brutal position when it comes to draft capital due to their blockbuster trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner at the 2025 trade deadline, which included two first-round picks in compensation.
Indianapolis would likely jump at any opportunity to recoup any lost capital from said trade, but given that Gardner has played in just 10 games since joining the Colts, it's likely they won't receive even a fraction of what it cost to obtain him.
Ideally, the Colts start their rebuild with a franchise pillar on each side of the ball (Nelson, Gardner), but if enough compensation comes calling, tearing down the franchise to its studs could be on the table.
Outside of those three players, as well as wide receiver Alec Pierce and any players still on their rookie contracts, the Colts are shopping their entire roster.
The only thing that would hold them back from making such a drastic move is the state of the AFC South. The Colts remain second in the division despite their 2-5 record, but the Jaguars aren't too far behind at 4-2.
However, the lowly AFC South shouldn't determine how the Colts operate moving forward. The season is over, and the future is now.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts Could Make Entire Roster Available Ahead of Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts could be approaching a significant turning point in their season. After firing general manager Chris Ballard, the franchise now faces a decision that could reshape its roster heading into 2027.
With Indianapolis sitting at 2-4 and the NFL trade deadline approaching on Nov. 10, the next few weeks will determine whether the organization remains committed to trying to win with its current roster or begins getting ahead of the rebuild that's on the horizon.
According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero, the Colts have received strong trade interest in offensive guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. Pelissero also reported that no player is expected to be off-limits if Indianapolis decides to sell before the deadline.
Despite the team's recent struggles, Indianapolis wants to see whether head coach Shane Steichen can get the season back on track before making any major decisions about the roster.
NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport explained the team's approach during an appearance on The Pat McAfee Show , saying, "They want to give Shane Steichen the opportunity to see if he can win games."
Rapoport added that the next couple of games may determine whether the Colts commit to contending for a playoff spot or begin to get the ball rolling on their inevitable roster retooling.
"If they win two, it's like okay, we're in the mix, it's still out there, we'll see what happens," Rapoport said. "If they lose two then it's like, alright, we probably know which way the season is going, let's capitalize on some of these really good assets."
The bad news for the Colts is that the schedule offers little room for error. Indianapolis faces the undefeated Minnesota Vikings before traveling to Jacksonville to take on the 4-2 Jaguars, a place they haven't won since 2014. So the path forward is far from encouraging.
If the team fails to respond, the organization will shift its attention toward preparing for the future. With Ballard already gone, the next few weeks could determine the direction taken by the next permanent general manager.
Nelson and Buckner are the most prominent potential trade candidates after Pelissero reported that both have drawn strong interest. The veteran offensive guard and defensive tackle are in the final year of their current contracts, making them attractive options for contenders seeking immediate help.
Nelson has been a cornerstone of Indianapolis' offensive line since being selected sixth overall in the 2018 NFL Draft. Trading him would leave a significant hole up front, but it could also allow the Colts to acquire valuable draft capital before he's a free agent. That way, they get something in return.
Buckner could provide a contender with an immediate boost to its defensive front. Green Bay has reportedly explored the possibility of acquiring the veteran, with Packer Report's Easton Butler identifying a second or third-round pick as Indianapolis' reported asking price.
The Packers have called the Colts about DTs Grover Stewart and DeForest Buckner, per source. The asking price for Bucker is a 2nd/3rd, while Stewart is a 4th. pic.twitter.com/dYGXGIWwWR
Butler also reported that the Packers had inquired about defensive tackle Grover Stewart, with a fourth-round pick representing the reported asking price. Those figures are only potential starting asking prices and any deal would also need to account for the financial implications of acquiring either player.
The most consequential possibility could involve running back Jonathan Taylor. Multiple teams have reportedly expressed interest in the star, and Butler's reported asking price is a first-round pick plus additional compensation, though that feels steep for a running back, even a star.
The Colts are opening to trading some key players, following the firing of GM Chris Ballard. One of the players is RB Jonathan Taylor, but the price wont be cheap. Per sources, the Colts are looking for a 1st + more for the star RB. pic.twitter.com/KmdAGOHXWM
Taylor signed an extension in August and remains under contract beyond this season, making a potential trade a much larger commitment to a rebuild than moving veterans approaching free agency. Still, if a team is willing to meet Indy's high asking price, then Taylor may be onto a new chapter.
Although Indianapolis could make much of its roster available, it would be foolish for the organization to blindly accept whatever offers come its way.
The reported asking prices suggest the Colts want meaningful compensation for their established players. Taylor's reported price is particularly notable, while the potential returns for Buckner and Stewart could give Indianapolis additional selections to work with in future drafts.
The team's draft situation adds another layer of complexity to those decisions. Indianapolis lost its own 2027 first-round pick in  the trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline, making the possibility of recouping premium capital especially relevant if the franchise ultimately decides to rebuild.
Of course, asking prices are mere speculations of what the Colts may receive. The market for each player will depend on competing offers, contract considerations and how aggressively other teams pursue reinforcements before the deadline.
For now, Indianapolis appears willing to give Steichen and the current roster another opportunity to respond. But if the next few games go poorly, the organization could quickly shift its priorities toward the future.
And no player will be off-limits in that scenario.

title: Colts 5 Best Bets to Cash in Week 7 Against Undefeated Vikings
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are 2-4, their general manager is gone, and trade rumors are swirling around some of the biggest names on the roster.
Some think this team is ready to roll over. I think there are plenty of players with a fire lit under them, and despite Minnesota entering undefeated and favored by 6.5 points, I believe Indianapolis can stay inside the number.
Through six weeks, we're 13-3 on Colts-specific props and 15-13 overall. Even if this team keeps making Sundays painful, hopefully we can keep making them profitable.
Here are my best bets for Week 7.
Brian Flores is intimidating and his defense's unprecedented pressure rate is exactly why I like this play.
Minnesota has blitzed on 77.8% of its defensive snaps this season, meaning Jones will likely be forced to move around against one of the league's most aggressive defenses.
Jones rushed for 30 yards against Tennessee last week, his highest total of the season, and cleared this line in his last regular-season matchup against Minnesota.
As he continues working back from his Achilles injury, it's about time Jones starts getting after it with his legs again.
At this point, Taylor is one of the few things keeping this Colts offense afloat.
He has seven rushing touchdowns through six games and has found the end zone nine times over his last nine games.
With Indianapolis' passing attack struggling, Minnesota will undoubtedly focus on slowing Taylor down. But sometimes it's simply good-on-good, and I'm trusting the Colts' best offensive player to find the end zone again.
We have ridden this bet all year, it has cashed in five straight games, and Shrader is a perfect 18-for-18 on field goals this season.
Flores' defense has been immaculate, and I can easily see Indianapolis moving the ball enough to create scoring opportunities without consistently finishing drives.
Shrader has cleared this line in eight of his last 10 games and 11 of his 14 healthy career starts with Indianapolis.
Until this bet stops printing money, I'm going to continue to put it on the card.
Addison is developing chemistry with Kyler Murray, hauling in five receptions against Tampa Bay and four against Miami in his last two games played.
He also caught five passes the last time he faced Indianapolis, and with Sauce Gardner ruled out, this secondary could have its hands full.
I expect Murray to look Addison's way plenty on Sunday.
Murray has completed 27 and 24 passes in his last two starts, and this line has hit in seven of his last 10 games. Indianapolis' coverage unit ranks 29th in the league via PFF, and with all the turmoil surrounding this franchise, the defense has plenty to prove.
Unfortunately, I expect Murray to do what just about every quarterback has done against this Colts secondary: carve it up.
The Colts might surprise people with their effort Sunday, but that doesn't mean their defensive problems will suddenly disappear.
The approach is straightforward this week. Trust Taylor, keep riding Shrader, and take advantage of the matchups Minnesota presents. Good luck and bet responsibly.

title: Colts Stars Respond to Trade Rumors as Deadline Approaches
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have already made one massive change this week, and with the Nov. 10 trade deadline getting closer, the speculation is not slowing down.
Since firing general manager Chris Ballard on Monday, Indianapolis has become one of the NFL's most intriguing teams to watch as the trade deadline approaches. At 2-4, names like DeForest Buckner, Jonathan Taylor and Quenton Nelson have naturally been pulled into trade conversations.
I still don't believe the Colts should tear this roster down. There are too many cornerstone players worth keeping around for whoever takes over this front office next.
But the players themselves are hearing the noise, and this week, several of the biggest names in Indianapolis addressed their futures.
Buckner is probably the easiest name to connect to trade speculation because he is 32 years old and playing on an expiring contract.
When asked directly whether he wants to remain with the Colts, though, Buckner wouldn't entertain the conversation.
“Yeah, right now I'm just focused on the Vikings,” Buckner said.
He acknowledged that he knows how the business works, but called the speculation a distraction. His focus remains preparing to help Indianapolis beat Minnesota on Sunday.
Buckner also spoke highly of Ballard, saying the two had a “great relationship” and that he has “nothing but love for him and his family.”
Like the rest of the locker room, Buckner's approach to a chaotic week has been simple: move forward and focus on the task at hand.
Taylor was much more emotional when discussing Ballard, the general manager who drafted him in 2020.
“Just lost for words,” Taylor said. “Definitely upset because at some point, it's on the team as a collective, coaches and players, in order to prove the GM right.”
Taylor said Ballard meant “a ton” to his career, pointing to their Wisconsin connection and the belief the organization showed in him coming out of the draft.
As for the possibility of being traded, Taylor wants no part of that conversation right now.
“I haven't given it any thought,” Taylor said. “That'd be crazy right now.”
He called looking ahead to what could happen a disservice to his teammates and the organization with an undefeated Minnesota team waiting Sunday.
Taylor also made it clear why he wanted to remain in Indianapolis when he signed his recent extension. He praised the way the organization treats its players and staff, calling the Colts “a special place.”
Nelson took a similar approach when asked whether Ballard's departure created questions about his own future.
“No, I have no questions,” Nelson said. “I leave that up to God.”
His focus is on getting better and being at his best this week, and Nelson called facing an undefeated Vikings team a “great opportunity” for Indianapolis to start turning things around.
But when asked if Indianapolis is somewhere he would like to continue playing long term, Nelson left little doubt.
“I love it here,” Nelson said. “Met my wife here. Really appreciate and love this organization.”
Nelson also expressed appreciation for Ballard, recalling the accountability his former general manager showed him as early as his rookie season.
For now, Buckner, Taylor and Nelson are all saying essentially the same thing: ignore the noise and prepare for Minnesota.
The trade rumors aren't going away before Nov. 10, especially after a front-office shakeup. But at least publicly, three of the Colts' biggest names are more concerned with saving this season than worrying about where they might be playing next.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Jaguars Know The Magic Number in the AFC South, and Now They Can Make Their Run
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ready to make their run.
The bye week turned everything around for the Jaguars a year ago, and the comparisons to this year can certainly be drawn. Jacksonville was 4-3 and coming off a tough loss in London at last year's bye week, and this year the Jaguars were 4-2 entering their bye and coming off an emotional last-second loss to the Houston Texans in London.
Adding Jakobi Meyers at the trade deadline certainly helped, but overall the Jaguars were a different team post-bye last season. Jacksonville went 9-1 after last year's bye week to set themselves up with a 13-4 record, an AFC South title, and a home playoff game.
Now, they will need to make the same thing happen now that they know what the magic number in the AFC South is : 13 wins.
The math is simple. If the Jaguars go 9-2 over the next 11 weeks, they will win the AFC South. With the Houston Texans and Indianapolis Colts sitting at 2-5 after Week 7 , the Jaguars can ensure an AFC South title with 13 wins ... a number the Colts and Texans can not reach. Now, winning 9-of-11 games is difficult and something most teams do not do over the second-half of a season, but the Jaguars will be coming out of their Week 7 bye hoping to not be like most teams.
It helps that the Jaguars got quite a bit of help from the AFC South in Week 7. The AFC South went 0-3 on Sunday, and the Jaguars' three rivals have just five wins combined this season. The Texans have made runs before, and nothing is ever secured, but the Jaguars' chances of winning the south increased on a Sunday where the Jaguars were at home.
“It helps. It definitely helps. I did keep some eye on some of the opponents that we will be seeing in the future. To see the type of game style that they play and how they're doing," Jaguars cornerback Jourdan Lewis said Monday. "The AFC South helped us. We’re still number one in the division and just trying to make sure that we don't have any skids to where we let anybody get any opportunity to take that from us.”
To ensure the Jaguars avoid those skids and make a run, the Jaguars have a few clear areas to improve. Head coach Liam Coen noted some of these areas Monday, pointing out red-zone penalties on offense, explosive plays allowed through the air on defense, and kickoff and punt coverage units.
Each of these aspects of their team came up big in their lone two losses, especially in the Week 6 loss to the Texans. That is where the Jaguars' bye week comes into play. Last year, the bye week was about improving Trevor Lawrence and the passing game, and the Jaguars did exactly that. Now, their focus moving into Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts and beyond is clear.
"Anytime you get a little bit of an opportunity to reset, gather your thoughts, also get away from it a little bit. Sometimes absence makes the heart grow fonder in ways, and no different in football. I couldn't sleep last night," Coen said Monday.
"Excited about getting back in the building and getting back with these guys and attacking these next 11 games together and really getting after it. It also came a little earlier this year than last, if you will, right, in terms of the way it played out and how many games we've played. But six weeks in and you see all the stuff that happens on any given Sunday, specifically within our division, it should only allow you to have a mindset and mentality to come in here and attack this thing with a division game up this week.”
The Jaguars have one of the NFL's easier schedules over the next 11 weeks, facing the Colts and Titans twice, the 2-5 Texans once more, the Washington Commanders, and some other very winnable games against the Dallas Cowboys, Baltimore Ravens, New York Giants, and the Pittsburgh Steelers. The toughest game left looks to be the Chicago Bears in Week 13.
But the Jaguars, more than anything, need to avoid those skids that Lewis mentioned. They can't take anything for granted, and they are still facing their own injury questions and pre-trade deadline chatter. It is, however, clear what it will take for the Jaguars to reach their goals.
Nine more wins, and the Jaguars will play a playoff football game in Jacksonville. It is time for the Jaguars to make their run.

title: The Colts Have Already Given the Jaguars the Perfect Week 8 Blueprint
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a big game coming up in Week 8, and they may have been given some early help in the form of the Minnesota Vikings.
The Jaguars are set to host their AFC South rival Indianapolis Colts in Week 8 as Jacksonville comes off their bye week, and they will be getting a Colts team that is fresh off a 16-10 loss to the Vikings. But beyond the fact the Jaguars are getting a slumping Colts team at the right time, the Jaguars also got a boost from the Vikings via a blueprint for disrupting the Colts, Shane Steichen, and Daniel Jones.
No team in football is blitzing more than the Vikings, who are led by defensive guru Brian Flores. Flores is going to send the house every single week, and he made sure to really turn up the pressure against the Colts and Jones. The plan clearly worked, with Jones going 11-of-18 for 101 yards and an interception against the blitz: giving him a passer rating of 53.2 and just 5.6 yards per attempt. Jones was one of the worst quarterbacks in the NFL this week against the blitz by most metrics, numbers that track with season-long averages.
The Vikings defense blitzed on 85.2% of Daniel Jones' dropbacks, the highest blitz rate by a defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). Minnesota generated pressure on 60.9% of those blitzes, with all four its sacks coming when blitzing. #INDvsMIN | #Skol
This season, Jones ranks No. 21 out of 33 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA/Dropback against the blitz, No. 26 in passer rating, No. 33 in sacks, No. 27 in pressure rate, and No. 29 in air yards per attempt. In short, he gets sacked a ton against the blitz and, when he does throw it, he isn't exactly pushing the ball downfield. Jones is not accurate enough or a quick enough processor to consistently win as a quick-game passer, and Flores was able to get after this flaw on Sunday.
Simply put, the blueprint has been out on Jones for some time. But the performance he put together against the Vikings, combined with the fact that the Colts have the NFL's slowest receiver room with Alec Pierce injured, makes it clear that to secure a win on Sunday, Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile should take a page out of his former bosses' playbook.
Campanile has worked for a number of top defensive minds, including Flores, Vic Fangio, and Jeff Hafley. While there is no coach quite like Flores, he has certainly made an impact on how Campanile sees the game and structures his defense, which means it might not be overly difficult for Campanile to attempt to replicate some of the things the Vikings did against the Colts.
“I think a lot of people had a huge influence on me. I'd say recently, obviously working with Jeff Hafley, I thought we had a very similar belief system and style. We see things very similarly and then Vic Fangio is probably a guy who—he had a tremendous impact on me, just in seeing certain things in the game and how you call the game," Campanile said last year. "And even in terms of how you practice things, so he's been somebody that has been a great resource for me, was a huge help to me. And he definitely had a big effect on me as well. Jeff's one of those guys and Flo [Vikings Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores] too. Coach Flores had a huge impact on me. And you can probably see a lot of the things that we do,  they may show up  for some of those teams as well.”
There are different factors to work in, of course. The Jaguars have an elite shutdown cornerback in Travis Hunter who can impact the math when it comes to blitzing and the defensive approach. The Jaguars have also not blitzed anywhere near as much as the Vikings, with Minnesota blitzing on 68.9% of passing plays (No. 1 in the NFL) compared to 30.5% from the Jaguars (No. 14). The highest rate of blitzing the Jaguars have done in a game this season was 45.2% against the Denver Broncos in Week 2, which would still fall below the Vikings' lowest blitz rate of the season (54.35).
But the blueprint is there, and the Jaguars can spin things in their own way to get home. Against the Colts a year ago, the Jaguars blitzed Jones twice on seven drop backs in his limited time on the field. Expect that number to go up after the success that Flores and the Vikings had, because it is clear that Jones and the Colts' offense as a whole simply can not handle it.

title: 4 Realistic IDL Trade Targets for the Jaguars Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- For the last several years, it feels like there has been a common trade deadline theme for the Jacksonville Jaguars: defensive tackle help.
The Jaguars' defensive tackle room has been productive in some facets this season, with Jacksonville's interior defensive line playing a large role in the unit being one of the NFL's best against the run. But there are other aspects of the unit that have disappointed, such as the lack of a consistent interior pass-rush.
So, if the Jaguars opt to use the trade deadline to improve the middle of their defensive front, who would make the most sense? We break it down below.
We have talked up Moro Ojomo as a logical fit for the Jaguars for a few weeks now, and it is easy to see why. Ojomo is only 25-years-old, his cap hit is $1.84 million, he is a productive interior rusher, the Eagles are trending towards a firesale, it is highly unlikely the Eagles would extend him since they have two big-money defensive tackles ... do I need to keep going? He has one of the most clear trade cases in the entire NFL, and he would serve as a nice boost to the Jaguars' interior pass-rush potential.
Adding a player like Ojomo would give the Jaguars a rental for the next 11 games to pair inside with Arik Armstead, Travon Walker, and Josh Hines-Allen on third-downs, while also giving the Jaguars some options for the future. If Ojomo impresses with Hamilton and Armstead in contract years, the Jaguars could re-sign him and make him a pillar of the defensive line moving forward. If they have other plans, they could see him walk in free agency and likely nab a high compensatory pick depending on the size of the deal he signs in free agency.
It remains to be seen i f the Jaguars could actually afford to trade for Daron Payne . He would cost about $9 million to add to the roster, and the Jaguars would need to create some space to do that. With that said, Payne is still uber-talented at 29-years-old and he is right up there for Ojomo in terms of the ability to be an X-Factor and actually change the trajectory of the Jaguars' interior defensive line moving forward.
Payne is in the last year of his deal, so the compensatory pick formula game would once again apply. He is having a solid year as both a pass-rusher and a run-defender and would give the Jaguars quite the formidable talent inside their defense for what would likely amount to an all-in on a rental veteran before he hits free agency for the first time.
A player who has a few connections to members of the Jaguars' defensive staff, Zach Sieler would make sense for a lot of reasons. He may not be at the level of Payne or Ojomo in terms of impact, especially as a pass-rusher, but he would give the Jaguars improved depth at defensive tackle from both a run-defense and pass-rush perspective. It would also make a ton of sense for the Dolphins to move him, even after their first win against the New York Jets on Sunday.
Simply put, the Dolphins are clearly still all-in on building toward the future in terms of draft picks and flipping veterans for the right price. They have hung onto a few young playmakers, but otherwise they look like they are open for business. Unlike the opther players on this list, he is still under contract for a few years and would have $10 million be guranteed next year, so he would have to be seen as a long-term option.
The Los Angeles Chargers have other appealing trade candidates on their roster, especially along the edge defender spots on the depth chart. With that said, Tomlinson is an experienced veteran who is an immediate impact as a run-defender, and he could quickly help boost the depth chart for a team with an open window like the Jaguars. He would give the Jaguars a better run defender at the backup spot than Matt Dickerson has provided this year, and he would come cheap.
With that said, Tomlinson is the worst pass-rusher on this list by a healthy mile and it is clear the Jaguars would still have the issue of an interior pass-rush moving into the future. But this is about winning games no matter what it looks like, and Tomlinson would make the Jaguars a slightly better team at a cheap cost.

title: 2 Jaguars Players Who Make Sense to Surprisingly Be Traded Before the Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL Trade Deadline is quickly approaching, and the Jacksonville Jaguars have the ability to make quite a few moves.
Most of the trade deadline chatter when it comes to the Jaguars is going to focus on wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., or whether the Jaguars will add needed depth pieces on the defensive side of the ball. But what if the Jaguars are also looking to unload a few players?
With the Jaguars the clear favorites in the AFC South and a legit contender in a wide-open AFC, it stands to reason the Jaguars shouldn't want to move many, or any, of their non-Thomas Jr. contributors. With that said, what if it could help the Jaguars land ammo for a trade for a defensive lineman or defensive back? That is at least worth consdiering.
With that in mind, here are two players who I think could qualify as surprise trades from the roster who could help the Jaguars accomplish exactly that ahead of the trade deadline.
Trading away a starting offensive lineman right after losing left tackle Anton Harrison for the year would be odd, which, of course, is why it qualifies as a surprise option. I do think there is a scenario that even with the loss of Harrison that the Jaguars could see Cleveland as expendable as he enters his final 11 regular-season games under contract with the team, in part due to the contract situation and in part due to the other linemen on the roster.
Cleveland has never really been seen as an extension candidate after this season, so trading him for value now instead of hoping to potentially get a compensatory pick for him after next year's free agency would make long-term sense. In the short-term, the Jaguars have multiple other options they could slot in at right guard and likely get similar production as they have gotten from Cleveland this season.
Wyatt Milum, the current swing tackle, is more of a guard than a tackle. Same goes for backup lineman Daniel Faalele. Add in the impending return of Patrick Mekari from injured reserve, and the Jaguars can still have solid offensive line depth without Cleveland, who could fill in for a more offensive line-needy teams. This would also give the Jaguars a chance to package picks for defensive depth or an actual swing tackle option.
Jourdan Lewis has been a good soldier for the Jaguars since he signed with the team in free agency last March, but there is reason to believe the Jaguars could benefit by looking to move him at the deadline. Teams are always needing cornerbacks at the deadline, and Lewis is a productive and experienced veteran who has made a lot of plays in this league. The flip side, and why this would be a surprise, is the fact the Jaguars are one of those teams that needs cornerback help as well.
The difference here is that Lewis is a nickel cornerback, and the Jaguars could sustain losing his spot on the depth chart if it means improving the other outside cornerback spot across from Travis Hunter. Jarrian Jones has been more productive from the slot than on the outside, and he would give the Jaguars more speed at nickel than Lewis is able to give them right now. They would need Montaric Brown to return to form on the outside or need to add another outside cornerback to make it work, but it makes sense.
It is a bit tough to see Lewis on the roster beyond this season so, like Cleveland, it could be a short-term move to benefit in the long-term. It would be tough to trade a leader and a captain, but it is worth considering under the right circumstances.

title: Jaguars Get the Perfect Week 7 Outcome Thanks to AFC South Rivals
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- As far as bye week Sundays go, this one could not have gone much better for the Jacksonville Jaguars.
The Jaguars had some clear games they needed to see go their way in Week 7 as they enjoyed their bye week after a 4-2 start, and that is exactly what they got. Of course, they got some welcomed help from their AFC South rivals in the process.
The AFC South went 0-3 during the early afternoon slate of games on Sunday, with the Houston Texans losing at home in overtime to the New York Giants, the Tennessee Titans losing on a walk-off field goal against the Cleveland Browns, and the Indianpolis Colts losing yet another game, this time against the Minnesota Vikings.
The Jaguars were always going to remain in firm control of first-place in the AFC South regardless of Sunday's results, but their position was made even stronger by the fact that every single other team dropping their Week 7 game. As a result, the Jaguars gained a bit of a cushion against the rest of their rivals, with the space between them and the Texans as the highlight.
The AFC South through 7 weeks: pic.twitter.com/ltUY5NJ9BT
The Jaguars will get another chance to take a big step in the AFC South over the next few weeks, starting with Week 8's game against the Indianapolis Colts. With the Colts now at 2-5 and offseveral brutal losses, it certainly stands to reason the Colts could shop some of their key veterans and look very different a week from now as their season continues to slip out of control.
The Colts are already a cursed team when it comes to playing games in Jacksonville, but they could reasonably trade any of Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, or DeForest Buckner over the next week as they prepare for next year's rebuild. If the Colts are without any of those players, a scenario that was made more possible by Sunday's loss, then they are an even easier target for the Jaguars to hit next week.
As for the Texans, they are on a bye next week. This means a Jaguars win over the Colts in Week 8 would bring the Jaguars back to being three games ahead of Houston in the AFC South, which was the exact spot the Jaguars were in before they lost to Houston in Week 6. Few teams start 2-5 and win their divison. Even if the Texans are still far from done, they took a big hit this week.
The Jaguars play three AFC South games in their next five weeks, with next week's game against the Colts and then two games against the lowly Titans in the next four games after that. In part due to today's results, the Jaguars can make things look very, very good for their playoff chances by December.
Outside of this week's news about left tackle Anton Harrison being ruled out for the rest of the season , the bye week went about as good as the Jaguars could have hoped. Consider this a winning weekend for Duval and Liam Coen's squad.

title: 4 Players the Jaguars Desperately Need to Step Up After the Bye Week
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' bye week is almost over, and it is nearly time for the Jaguars to turn their focus to the rest of the 2026 season.
The Jaguars are in a good place as they enter the final day of their bye week, but things can always get better, can't they? The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 right now and in first-place of the AFC South, but they will need a team effort to continue their winning ways over the next few months.
For the Jaguars to keep taking strides after the bye week, though, they will need to see a few players take some big steps to pave the way. Here are those players they will need to seize the moment the most:
Walker Little is set to be the Jaguars' starting left tackle after Anton Harrison's season-ending injury , and the Jaguars will need him in a big way. Little played very well against the Houston Texans in the Week 6 loss in Houston against the NFL's best pass-rush duo, and he has a long history of being a productive blindside protector. When comparing their careers, it doesn't look like the numbers indicate there is much of a drop-off from Harrison to Little, if one at all.
Still, the Jaguars will need Little to step up and be at his best down the stretch. They still have to play the Texans and some other fierce pass-rushes this season, and Little will be an important piece of Liam Coen's offense as they look to continue set up Trevor Lawrence for an MVP-caliber season like the one he has had to this point.
The Jaguars' secondary has plenty of questions entering Week 8, and one of the biggest questions might be Jourdan Lewis -- especially when the Jaguars get Montaric Brown back from his hamstring injury. Lewis has done some good things for the Jaguars in the run game and he has recorded two interceptions as their primary nickel cornerback this season, but he has also given up some big plays in the process in the Jaguars' only two losses.
With the amount of attention teams clearly have on Travis Hunter, who they have been avoiding in coverage for the most part, more and more passes are going to come Lewis' way. The Jaguars will need Lewis to become more consistent and cut-down the explosive plays allowed in coverage if they are to fix their secondary issues.
If the Jaguars' pass-rush is going to get home more often over the second-half of the season, it will likely hinge on the interior pass-rush. Defensive ends Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen are consistent pass-rushers who bring plenty of pressure off the edge, but it is easier for quarterbacks and offenses to negate their impact when the Jaguars are not getting much of a pass-rush from the interior group.
Armstead has had some games where he has absolutely taken over, and other games where he has been just marginally productive. If the Jaguars are going to start ramping up their pass-rush production as the stakes increase each week, they will need Armstead to help lead that charge in a big way.
If the Jaguars trade Brian Thomas Jr. , it is clear that they will need Josh Cameron to step up in a big way. Even if the Jaguars do not trade him, they still likely need to see Cameron be ready to step into a larger role than the limited, but impressive, role he played for the Jaguars during the first six weeks of the season. Cameron has stepped up each time the Jaguars have gone his way, and he needs to continue this trend moving forward.
Cameron very easily could be the Jaguars' WR3 after the bye week, depending on how they view Thomas and his place in the offense. That would mean more on his plate than his duties over the first six weeks of the season, and the Jaguars will have to ensure that their sixth-round rookie wide receiver is ready for the moment if it comes to that.
