title: What the Jaguars Can Realistically Afford at the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The 2026 NFL Trade deadline is just a few weeks away, and the Jacksonville Jaguars could certainly be a big factor.
Most of the trade talk around the Jaguars understandably centers around third-year wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. , but what if the Jaguars are buyers at the deadline?
The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 and in first-place in the AFC South during their bye week , and they could reasonably look to add a potential difference-maker or depth piece at a number of positions before the trade deadline hits.
But what can the Jaguars afford when it comes to the deadline , both in terms of cap space and draft picks?
As things stand today, the Jaguars are set to have nine picks in the 2027 NFL Draft: six of their own original selections and three picks via the compensatory draft pick system after they saw Devin Lloyd, Travis Etienne, and Greg Newsome depart in free agency. The Jaguars have used the draft compensatory formula to give themselves more at bats in the draft, as well as give themselves more chances to trade for depth pieces such as Tim Patrick last season and Daniel Faalele this season.
"I think that's something in the spring we highlighted quite a bit about the idea of going down the compensatory picks approach and not signing immediately some of the street free agents. Really where we were going to turn our attention to was during training camp and the regular season, knowing that we had a larger stock of future draft picks to utilize to answer any questions that we might need to in those moments," Jaguars general manager James Gladstone said at the conclusion of training camp this summer.
"Yeah, that gives us more flexibility to pursue those paths and those options. I think that that's an ever-evolving strategy as to whether or not you're going to deploy that one year after the next. It was where we found ourselves this past cycle, and I think that's why you probably saw some willingness there, not to say that we weren't unwilling a year ago, because we were. I think the equivalent of that was probably [WR] Tim Patrick and using a sixth-round pick to get him from Detroit. We still have avenues for pursuing those into the regular season."
Compensatory Pick (Devin Lloyd)
Compensatory Pick (Travis Etienne)
Compensatory Pick (Greg Newsome)
When it comes to cap space, things are a bit tighter. The Jaguars can always work to create more room, but a lack of cap space now means that players on hefty deals, such as Daron Payne, may be tougher to trade for than players on their rookie deals still like Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo.
The Jaguars did some work to create cap space with restructures ahead of Week 1, and Spotrac has the Jaguars currently at $4,659,858 in available cap space, which ranks No. 25 in the NFL.
"I think that's a move to make so that we're not forced to do anything should we pursue an avenue. We want to make sure we have the flexibility we need to keep things on the table as the season progresses," Gladstone said before the season began.
"In the same breath, we're always going to do our part to consider all options, and through that lens not all those are going to come to the table or to the public's understanding. I think the understanding that we are always going to turn over every stone is certainly going to be the case."
In short, the Jaguars have plenty of flexibility before the deadline to be aggressive from a draft pick standpoint. From a cap space standpoint, a player either on their rookie deal or a cheaper contract makes the most sense.

title: Jaguars' Travis Hunter Becomes Latest to Be Hit Big By NFL's Fine Policy
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL has been quite fine-heavy this season, and Jacksonville Jaguars star Travis Hunter is the latest to be hit with one.
Hunter was fined $14,926 by the NFL this week for removing his helmet on the field against the Houston Texans in last week's 34-31 loss, which happened after Hunter picked off C.J. Stroud in the end-zone in the fourth-quarter for arguably the biggest moment in the game from the Jacksonville side.
Travis Hunter just making impact plays on both sides of the ball. HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/2iCxZBs80j
While this seems like quite the expensive fine for Hunter merely celebrating an exceptional play at a pivotal moment of the game, it does follow the letter of the NFL's rules, and the Jaguars are lucky that they were not hit with an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty for 15 yards, which Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1 of the NFL's rules state is the penalty for "Removal of his helmet by a player in the field of play or the end zone during a celebration or demonstration, or during a confrontation with a game official or any other player."
A bit silly? Yes, but it is the NFL's rules, and Hunter will now see the amount taken out of his next game check unless he appeals the decision and wins it, which seems unlikely since Hunter did clearly and plainly take his helmet off.
With that said, the Jaguars would likely welcome any future fines (but no penalties in close games) if Hunter keeps looking like one of the best players on the field and, arguably, the most versatile player in the game if he continues to produce on both sides of the ball. It seems like the Jaguars have found the right balance for Hunter, letting him play every snap on defense as their full-time CB1 and then stepping in on offense in certain packages.
Hunter clearly doesn't need a large snap count on offense to make an impact, either. He played just nine offensive snaps against the Texans last week but still produced four catches for 59 yards and a touchdown, racking up two explosive plays to set up two different scoring drives for the Jaguars. He did all of this while shadowing Nico Collins and more than held his own in that regard as well.
"That was part of the plan, getting him a little bit more involved early, made some critical plays for us on both sides of the football, obviously. Had the interception late, that gave us a chance to win the game. Proud of the way he completed, made some plays for us on offense and got to keep building off it," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said about Hunter after Week 6.
Hunter has looked like an elite cornerback over the past month, and now the production is starting to see an uptick on offense. As long as Hunter keeps making plays, and remembers to keep his helmet on, the Jaguars are going to continue to see their 2025 draft gamble pay off in a big way.

title: Ranking the 8 Best Fits for Jaguars, Brian Thomas Jr. Ahead of Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- With the NFL Trade deadline quickly approaching, it is clear where the majority of the focus is set to be for the Jacksonville Jaguars: Brian Thomas Jr.
Perhaps the Jaguars continue to be reluctant to deal the talented former first-round pick and 1,000-yard receiver before the deadline in a few weeks, but all signs (and reports) indicate that there is a better chance than not of him being moved sometime soon.
So if the Jaguars do trade Thomas, which teams make the most sense as trade partners? We identified eight below, ranking them from best to worst.
The Washington Commanders have always made sense for Thomas due to his connection and relationship with Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, who was his college quarterback. We have already seen that kind of connection play a factor in a receiver trade earlier this season with Marvin Harrison Jr. and the Houston Texans and CJ Stroud, and this would be a similar fit. Even with Dan Quinn on the hot seat, this move would make sense in the short- and long-term for Commanders general manager Adam Peters.
The Commanders badly need receiver help now due to the season-ending injury to Terry McLaurin. Even before McLaurin was injured, the Commanders were seen as a team that badly needed to retool its receiver room entering the season. They signed Stefon Diggs, who has been fine, but they need a new future No. 1, and Thomas could be that,
If the Jaguars were to trade Thomas to a fellow AFC team, the one that makes the most sense is clearly the Las Vegas Raiders. The Raiders make a ton of sense as a long-term landing spot for Thomas since they have a hopeful franchise quarterback waiting in the wings in Fernando Mendoza, and their need for a receiver moving forward is clear. Even with the Raiders slipping over the last few weeks, they could also see it as a short-term move.
The Raiders are getting nothing from the receiver room right now outside of Tre Tucker, who is talented but not a WR1. Brock Bowers is elite and Michael Mayer is a nice secondary option, so adding a player with actual WR1 potential (and past WR1 production) like Thomas would make sense. The Raiders are also the type of franchise that could be willing to pay a premium price, too.
Davante Adams and Puka Nacua combine to make up over 40% of the Rams' targets, and each is dealing with injuries: Nacua has a calf injury and his skill-set and play-style makes him a bit of an injury prone player, while Adams will miss most of the rest of the season with a 6-to-10 week injury he sustained earlier this season. The Rams receivers after them are Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, and Jordan Whittington, which, yeah...
The Rams are in serious trouble of missing the playoffs, and Sean McVay and Les Snead need to find some playmakers quickly. The Jaguars and Rams are very close as franchises due to Liam Coen's and James Gladstone's connections with the franchise, which could potentially make a deal even smoother if the Rams are willing to live with Thomas' flaws as a pass-catcher,.
The Falcons have one of the best skill player trios in the NFL with Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts, but they are really lacking in pass-catchers after them. The Falcons' No. 2 receiver right now is Jahan Dotson, and their backup receivers Olamide Zaccheaus and Zachariah Branch have a combined 21 targets through six games. Thomas could be the perfect foil for London and his ability to win across the middle.
The Falcons are in one of the NFL's most winnable divisions and Thomas' skillset could fit well with Michael Penix's trebuchet downfield throwing style. This would also put Thomas far away from having to face off against the Jaguars anytime soon, which would be another welcomed aspect of a deal with the Falcons.
The Steelers were mentoned by ESPN's Jeremy Fowler as one team that could be looking for receiver help, and I think they make more sense for the Jaguars to do a deal with than most other AFC teams that currently look like a potential playoff team. The Steelers swinging a deal for an explosive field-stretcher with their current offensive ecosystem would be a bit odd but, hey, the Steelers do odd things.
The Steelers' leading target-eaters at wide receiver are a middling DK Metcalf and rookie receiver Germie Bernard. Michael Pittman Jr. has been injured and Roman Wilson is getting fewer looks than Jaylen Warren and Pat Freiermuth, which means a big-play option like Thomas could make a lot of sense for the pass-happy team/
The San Francisco 49ers seem to lose a wide receiver to injury every week or so, and right now it looks like they could be eagerly awaiting the return of Christian Kirk from injury to provide a boost. The 49ers look like one of the best teams in football and have Brock Purdy playing at an MVP-level, so they should not hesistate to add an explosive outside option like Thomas if given the chance to be aggressive with an open window.
The fact that Thomas has struggled with drops and in-breaking routes could prove to be problematic in the 49ers' scheme, but Kyle Shanahan is an elite offensive mind and would likely find a way to fit Thomas in somehow. With that said, Liam Coen is also an elite offensive mind, and he hasn't been able to help the Jaguars find a way to make things work with Thomas.
We have noted the Seahawks as a team to watch in the past, even if the fit feels a bit more unlikely than the others. The Seahawks are 3-3 at the time of the writing and could be south of .500 by the trade deadline and could need to add an explosive piece to put their struggling offense over the top to gear up for a playoff run. They also lack a strong No. 2 option next to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, with Rashid Shaheed and Cooper Kupp not exactly scaring anyone. Teams keep rotating all their coverage to JSN, and Thomas could benefit from it in a big way with a big-armed quarterback like Sam Darnold.
If we were ranking the teams that needed Thomas the most, the Chiefs would probably be at the very top of the list. The same logic applies for if we were ranking the teams where Thomas would fit the best skill-set wise. But if you are the Jaguars, are you exactly rushing to give the Chiefs a talented weapon like Thomas? They are the only team on this list who is a true AFC contender, and the Jaguars should be rooting against the Chiefs most weeks , not trying to give them a potential game-changing weapon who they might have to defend in the playoffs.
Kansas City makes a ton of sense as a team who could be interested in Thomas, thus it is impossible to leave them off this list. With that said, the Jaguars would be better off not doing business with the Chiefs right now, for the same reason the Jaguars shouldn't want to send a talented player to a team like the Buffalo Bills.

title: Jaguars Week 7 Rooting Guide: How the Bye Week Can Help Liam Coen's Squad
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars might not be suiting up in Week 7, but that doesn't mean they can't still get a boost from the week's results.
The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 entering their Week 7 bye and they are still in first-place in the AFC South despite a recent surge from the Houston Texans. With the right results in Week 7, the Jaguars' spot in the AFC South's very early playoff race could be made even better.
So, what results should the Jaguars root for in Week 7 as they take Sunday off for their bye week ? We break it down below.
This one does not need much explanation at all. The Texans are the only real theat in the AFC South when it comes to the Jaguars' top spot, and the Jaguars can benefit from any potential hurdle that gets thrown up in the Texans' way along the rest of the season. A Texans win would put them close to the Jaguars in the AFC South standings, so the Jaguars have the almost unwinnable position of rooting for J.J. McCarthy. Good luck, but it is what it is.
AFC seeding is the focus here. The Jaguars and Broncos each sit at 4-2 but the Broncos have the tiebreaker over the Jaguars after the Week 2 result in Denver. As a result, the Jaguars should hope the Broncos find a few more losses to ensure the Jaguars can have a higher playoff seeding and prevent any chance of having to go into Mile High in January. The Jaguars need to do their part, of course, but they could use sme help starting this week with the Cardinals.
Rooting Interest: Cardinals
This one is clear. The Chiefs and Buffalo Bills are the only two AFC teams with a better record right now than the Jaguars, but the Bills are on a bye week. The Chiefs are the team to chase in the AFC right now due to their undefeated record, and the Jaguars should be rooting for them to slip weekly. A matchup in primetime against the Seattle Seahawks would give them the chance to make that slip, even if the Chiefs look like the most likely winners.
Rooting Interest: Seahawks
Like the other games mentioned above, this one is about future AFC seeding. The Browns are nowhere near as impressive as their 4-2 record says, but the Jaguars need to root against every team that is competing for a playoff spot in the AFC. Somehow, someway, that is the Browns this season. It feels unlikely that this will be the Titans' second win of the season, but it would go a long way for the Jaguars down the road.
The Jaguars are set to play a wounded Colts team in Week 8, which is a critical battle for Jacksonville after their loss to the Texans. The Colts are already quiet quitting on the season, as evidenced by their decision to fire Chris Ballard after six games, so I do not think the Jaguars need the Vikings to win for an AFC South reason. I do think that a bad loss to the Vikings could push the Colts to start getting serious about trading some of their few difference-makers, starting with DeForest Buckner and Jonathan Taylor. Imagine this Colts team coming into Jacksonville without one of those players? Imagine them without both?

title: What Matters (and What Doesn't) from the Chiefs' Brutal Loss in Seattle
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' Sunday Night Football loss to the Seattle Seahawks was a drubbing in all three phases, leaving plenty of questions unanswered about how the Chiefs can recalibrate for the next act of their season.
However, not all of the Chiefs' issues that were exposed in Seattle are worth worrying about. Following a loss that thorough, let's take a look at some issues that do matter and some that don't—at least until further notice.
For the fourth time in six games, the Chiefs' defense failed to record a sack of the opposing quarterback. Even though some of the underlying metrics have supported the KC pass rush due to better performances in statistics like pressure rate , they've allowed opposing quarterbacks to be too comfortable, too often. With Sam Darnold as the target on Sunday night, the Chiefs just needed enough pressure to rattle Darnold, forcing him to start making characteristic mistakes. Instead, he threw and ran for several long third-down conversions.
Meanwhile, the Chiefs' only sacks since Week 1 came against a completely battered Los Angeles Chargers O-line last week.
Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane had a couple of "welcome to the NFL" moments against Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but nothing about Delane's losses indicate that he's anything other than an excellent young player who got beaten by a superstar.
JSN WHAT A CATCH FOR A TOUCHDOWN KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bN6IT22fM4
Similarly to the long completion Delane allowed last week to Chargers wide receiver Quentin Johnston, the rookie was in excellent position, had his hand between the ball and the receiver's hands, and just couldn't land the final fingernail to break up the pass. Delane would love to have those plays back, I'm sure, but even elite cornerbacks lose to the best receivers at times. Delane looked like a near-peer to Smith-Njigba, not like a rookie out of his depth.
If you would have told me before the game that rookie Cyrus Allen would lead the Chiefs' wide receivers in receiving yards, I would have been thrilled. Allen has seen very limited work to begin his first year in the pros, and a chance to break out through a heavily injured Chiefs WR room would have been well-timed.
Well, he did lead Chiefs wideouts in receiving yards, but he only had one catch for 18 yards—reeled in on the second play of the game.
With Rashee Rice (hamstring) sidelined again and Tyquan Thornton (ankle) remaining on IR through at least the vast majority of the regular season , the Chiefs needed someone to step up. Tight ends and running backs led the receiving box score with paltry stats, while Allen's 18 yards narrowly outpaced Xavier Worthy's three catches for 11 yards, Justin Watson's one for seven, Andrew Armstrong's one for three and Jalen Royals' zero for zero.
The Seahawks' defense is excellent, but those are not the stat lines of a functional unit.
Rice is the Chiefs' most reliable wide receiver, while Thornton was the most explosive. Worthy's role is murky, as his blazing 40-yard dash speed doesn't quite seem to translate to game speed, and much of his potential remains theoretical. Royals and Armstrong may have roles as "dirty work" receivers, but the Chiefs still need to find significantly more firepower in the passing game.
As disappointing as Kenneth Walker's 14-carry, 36-yard performance was, there's no reason for his underwhelming stat line to overshadow his impact on the Chiefs' offense or what can be expected of him going forward.
With O-line uncertainty and the aforementioned woes in the passing game, the Seahawks knew what we all knew: the Chiefs' best chance for offensive success (and explosive plays) came with Walker, so the Seattle D played accordingly. While the star running back has shown that he can jump-start the Chiefs' offense against middling opponents, it's too much to ask for him (or any individual player) to thrive as the focal point of an otherwise-struggling unit against an excellent defense.

title: After Flopping vs. Seahawks, Patrick Mahomes Knows Chiefs' Offense Must Bounce Back
full_text:
No matter how you slice it or what you chalk it up to, there's absolutely no denying that the Kansas City Chiefs' offense did nothing short of flop against the Seattle Seahawks.
Add in that KC came into Week 7 with an undefeated record and had a chance to extend that streak on Sunday Night Football , and you get an even bigger disappointment in terms of performance.
From opening kickoff until the final whistle, head coach Mike MacDonald and his Seahawks defense completely bottled up a Chiefs offense that rolled into the evening as one of football's best per-play, per-drive and per-game units. There's tons of blame to go around, although it's no surprise that the team's best player spent the first moments after the 20-3 loss reflecting.
Quarterback Patrick Mahomes didn't sugarcoat Sunday's shortcoming, but he knows it's time to get right back to work and right some wrongs.
"You got your tail kicked," Mahomes said. "Didn't execute offensively, especially around that midfield area. Kept us away from a lot of points, or at least enough points to be competitive. But it's stuff you've got to learn from. That's obviously a really good defense, and we didn't execute at a high enough level to have success."
By Mahomes' normal standards, he delivered a terrible showing at Lumen Field. On 38 plays, per RBSDM , he averaged -0.13 EPA and had a -9.8% completion rate over expected. Over his last three contests, No. 15 has completed just 61.3% of his passes with an 81.0 passer rating, two touchdowns, two interceptions and an average of 220.7 passing yards each week.
It didn't really matter what the situation was, either. On early-down passes, Mahomes led Kansas City to -0.08 EPA/play (25th percentile) compared to -0.21 (37th percentile) on late-down passing plays. Ahead of Monday's Week 7 finale between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles, the two-time MVP is 14th among all quarterbacks in adjusted EPA/play (0.139) but is just 25th out of 35 players with 50-plus plays in the same metric (0.023) in Weeks 4-7.
The Chiefs are the only NFL team in the Super Bowl era to have a game with: no 10+ yard rushes no 20+ yard passes no red-zone drives no touchdowns multiple missed field goals
Has pressure factored into Mahomes' lackluster play? Outsiders would argue yes; he thinks on Sunday it was more so him not setting the right tone from the start.
"Obviously a little bit, but I thought especially early in the game, I thought my feet were kind of getting me into trouble where I could have maybe sat in the pocket and made some of the throws down the field," Mahomes said. "I got better a little bit later in the game. But at the same time, when you play a team like that, you can't let them get ahead and get into a game they want to play. Obviously they've had a lot of success doing that, and so [we've] got to be better starting faster — especially with me — and then try to do better throughout the entire game."
According to TruMedia , Kansas City has allowed the sixth-lowest pressure rate on the year at 31.4%. In Weeks 4-7, though, that's 19th at 37.6%. The club is actually being blitzed at a lower per-dropback share (22.8% versus 24.2%) in that sample, so it's a reflection of poor tackle play through and through. Jaylon Moore missing Week 7 and Josh Simmons missing all season hasn't helped.
As currently constructed, the Chiefs' passing attack simply isn't dynamic enough. It owns football's third-lowest average in yards to the sticks on throws (-2.6), and that's down to -4.5 yards in the last two weeks. Injuries can again be at least partially credited here, as Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ) is on injured reserve and Rashee Rice ( hamstring ) hasn't played in weeks.
At the end of the day, not everything falls on Mahomes. He can only put his Superman cape on so frequently, and it's impossible to do others' jobs for them. With that said, he undoubtedly could be playing better, which might just in turn raise the floor of a suddenly struggling offense.
Whether he can do so, fair or unfair, will determine whether Sunday was a blip on the radar or a reason to slam the panic button.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From the Chiefs’ 20-3 Loss to the Seattle Seahawks
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night in Seattle, and it wasn't close.
The 20-3 final score told the story of a night when the Chiefs struggled in all three phases against a Seahawks team that reminded the country exactly why they held the Lombardi Trophy eight months ago.
Seattle came in at 3-3 and struggled on offense, but their play felt much more dominant and urgent than Kansas City's. The Chiefs were outplayed from start to finish, and the winners column is notably short this week.
Here is the full breakdown.
If there was one moment Sunday night when it felt like the Chiefs might have something going, it came with seconds left in the first half. Seattle led 10-0 and lined up on a second-and-goal from the three, with the ball set to return to them to open the third quarter. A 17-0 halftime deficit would almost certainly have been insurmountable.
Instead, Sam Darnold targeted Rashid Shaheed, and Nohl Williams jumped the route, picked it off, and took it 65 yards the other way. His only mistake was not finding the end zone, which loomed large when Butker missed the ensuing field goal as time expired.
It was Williams's first career interception, notable for a corner known as a ball-hawk coming out of California. He finished the night as the Chiefs’ best defender by a wide margin, recording double-digit tackles, including a tackle for loss, and allowing just two catches for 22 yards on three targets, according to PFF’s preliminary grades. In a game short on positives, Williams stood out.
With tight end Travis Kelce dropping two passes and Patrick Mahomes missing him badly on the opening drive, his backup led the Chiefs in receiving. Noah Gray caught all three of his targets for 44 yards, including a 19-yard reception, continuing what has quietly become a bounce-back season for the six-year veteran.
He is now just nine catches and 20 yards away from surpassing his 2025 season totals, and he has caught 12 of his 14 targets this year, making him one of Mahomes’ most reliable options in a season where reliability has been hard to come by at receiver. On a night with little to celebrate, Gray’s consistency was a welcome constant.
The Chiefs generated just nine pressures on Darnold all evening, and Karlaftis accounted for five of them. That he was the lone bright spot along the defensive line says more about how poor the rest of the group was than it does about how good he was, though he was good.
He hit Darnold twice, batted down a pass, and recorded a tackle for loss, becoming the only Chiefs pass rusher to register a quarterback hit all night. Former All-Pro Chris Jones had zero pressures on 24 pass-rush snaps, according to PFF’s preliminary grades.
The other four pressures belonged to rookie R Mason Thomas, leaving a goose egg for the rest of the group. Karlaftis has been this defense's more consistent performer all season, and Sunday was no exception, even if the unit around him was subpar.
The matchup was billed as strength-on-strength, and Seattle won it in a landslide. Kenneth Walker , who had rushed for 665 yards in his first five games and topped 100 yards in four of them, was held to 36 yards on 14 carries, both season lows by a wide margin.
He averaged just 2.6 yards per carry and forced only one missed tackle, compared to nearly double digits in every previous game this season. The Seahawks bottled him up all night, and without the run game generating momentum, the play-action attack never materialized. Mahomes finished with just 165 passing yards, his lowest output of the season.
To make the optics worse, Seahawks running back Emanuel Wilson ran for 100 yards and a touchdown on the other side of the ball, flipping the entire pre-game narrative on its head. The Chiefs will learn from this, but it was a humbling night for the NFL’s No. 1 offense.
The kicking situation has moved from a concern to legitimate alarm territory. Harrison Butker now sits at just 69 percent on field goals this season after missing two more Sunday night. The first was a 45-yarder, the shortest miss of his season, that went wide right. The second was a 58-yarder at the end of the first half that he hit straight down the middle but left short of the uprights.
The latter is the more troubling miss because it raises questions about leg strength, not just accuracy. The Chiefs never reached the red zone all night, so two made kicks likely wouldn't have changed the outcome, but 13-9 midway through the fourth quarter rather than 13-3 with two missed kicks makes the game look entirely different.
Dave Toub and the Chiefs need to determine quickly whether this is a physical issue, a mental one, or both. For a three-time Super Bowl champion and one of the most decorated kickers in NFL history, the decline has been sudden and significant.
It is hard to single out one defender on a night when Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught nine passes for 150 yards, and the Chiefs allowed 11-of-16 third-down conversions, many on third-and-medium or longer. But cornerback L’Jarius Sneed stood out for the wrong reasons, and Spagnuolo clearly noticed.
Sneed allowed all five of his targets to be caught for 83 yards in just 14 defensive snaps before being benched for Chris Roland-Wallace in the second half, when the defense performed considerably better. Smith-Njigba piled up 129 yards in the first half, with Sneed on the field for much of it.
Sneed surrendered four first downs, three of them to Smith-Njigba and one to Cooper Kupp. The fact that Darnold was actively targeting whoever Sneed was covering in a game that was never particularly close suggests the league has begun to view him as a liability in coverage, and that Roland-Wallace may need to be the answer moving forward.

title: Andy Reid Defends Chiefs Kicker Harrison Butker After Rough Night: ‘He’s Off a Bit’
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks during Sunday Night Football can hardly be attributed to one player's mistakes. It was a putrid showing in all facets of the game for KC, and Mike Macdonald's squad came out dominant from the get-go.
With that said, kicker Harrison Butker's shortcomings continued to loom large on special teams. It's become a consistent theme for the 31-year-old, who has slipped significantly from his prime and endured several rough seasons in a row. Butker's first field-goal attempt of the evening came from 58 yards out. He wasn't able to connect. There's nothing dishonorable about missing a near-60 yarder, but the kick would have split the uprights had it traveled the distance.
That raises real questions about Butker and what has been causing this prolonged slump. He's only two months removed from drilling a record-shattering 69-yard kick in the NFL Preseason that had fans believing he was back to his elite self. Is there a lapse in focus with his kicks, a mechanical issue, or even an underlying injury?
He partially redeemed himself in the third quarter, hitting his second field goal from 50+ yards this season. However, he squandered that momentum by missing a 45-yard attempt wide right with more than eight minutes remaining in the final quarter. The kick would've cut the Chiefs' deficit to seven points and given them a chance to get back into the contest, but Butker couldn't capitalize on the opportunity.
In his postgame press conference, head coach Andy Reid acknowledged that Butker hasn't been himself lately but maintained that he remains confident in his longtime placekicker. "Listen, he's been one of the most consistent kickers in football," Reid said. "He's off a bit. So, we've got to fix that."
The numbers don't necessarily back Butker's reputation as one of football's most "consistent kickers," though. As noted by Associated Press writer Josh Dubow , his 15 missed kicks since the start of the 2025 campaign lead the NFL. That many failed attempts in that span is a far cry from the consistency Reid described.
Harrison Butker's 2026 field goal percentage and ranks via @TruMediaSports : Overall: 71.4 (29th) FG40%: 100% (T-1st) FG50%: 20% (28th) XP%: 93.3% (T-24th) @KCSportsNetwork pic.twitter.com/U9Gbiy1YNg
Dating back to the 2024 season, Butker has converted exactly 50% (9-of-18) of his field-goal attempts from 50 yards or deeper. While raw leg strength has long been his trademark, the fact that he's falling multiple yards short on long-distance tries now indicates that his value is no longer what it once was.
Reid has consistently defended Butker through his recent struggles, and there was a point when it was reasonable to believe the veteran could return to form. However, he's getting closer to the point of no return, having statistically performed like a bottom-tier kicker in recent years despite his penchant for coming through in clutch moments. Kansas City isn't exactly in a position to simply cut ties with the Georgia Tech graduate, who is signed through 2028 and ranks as the NFL's fourth-highest-paid kicker. Regardless, his current production is no better than what the Chiefs could get from the average practice squad kicker. If he continues costing the team games, a serious conversation about his future will have to be had.

title: Andy Reid Clears Air on Reported Spat With Josh Simmons in Team Meeting
full_text:
In the aftermath of their most embarrassing performance of the 2026 season by an insanely wide margin, the Kansas City Chiefs have bigger fish to fry than engaging in hypotheticals regarding those who aren't even on the active 53-man roster.
Given the lack of consistency or clarity with one particular player, however, it was only a matter of time before head coach Andy Reid was asked about left tackle Josh Simmons once again.
Just days removed from Kansas City placing the 2025 first-round pick on IR , a national report from ESPN revealed that Simmons had a back-and-forth with Reid on Wednesday and was asked by him to leave a team meeting. Did that incident have anything to do with the transaction the following day?
Speaking to the media after a 20-3 loss on Sunday Night Football to the Seattle Seahawks, Reid shot down any correlation between the two.
"Listen, Sam (McDowell), I've said so much on him," Reid said of Simmons. "Rick (Burkholder) has talked about him, this and that. Things happen. That's no reason that he was put on IR. He's got a bad back. He's got to get that worked out, and that's the main thing. I'll leave it at that, and that's where we're at with it."
According to the aforementioned report, Simmons was called out for having his feet up while sitting during the meeting and told Reid it was because of an aching back and hips. Upon being directed to seek treatment if he was indeed in pain, the former Ohio State star allegedly "disrupted the meeting" and even led to quarterback Patrick Mahomes to urge Simmons to step out as well.
Burkholder, vice president of sports medicine and performance, provided a statement to lead off Thursday's media availability and described Simmons' Wednesday absence from practice as something that allowed him to "get with his people" and decide next injury-related steps. After all, the second-year man is attempting to recover from a bulging disc in his back that's bothered him since mid-August.
With the Seattle game in the books, Simmons will miss at least the club's next three contests against the Denver Broncos, New York Jets and Atlanta Falcons. Mike Garafolo of NFL Network reports that the team holds out hope for Simmons eventually hitting the ground running again with the "right attitude and healthy, ready to go" for the stretch run of the season.
Reid appears to share that same end goal. Even if it's been an awkward week on the Simmons front, the leader of the team reiterates that the focus remains solely on the back injury and subsequent recovery.

title: 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs' Ugly Week 7 Loss to Seahawks
full_text:
Before the Kansas City Chiefs even took the field in Seattle to battle the Seahawks, most figured it would be a trying night for one of football's last undefeated teams. That certainly proved to be the case in Week 7, as head coach Andy Reid's crew got throttled in prime time.
The hosts came out firing on the Sunday Night Football stage, taking advantage of the visitors' shorthanded offense and also making the most of favorable matchups on the other side of the ball. Kansas City did attempt to snap out of its funk in the second half of play, yet it never got close and wound up dropping a brutal game by a final score of 20-3.
Here are 10 instant observations and Chiefs takeaways from Week 7.
It feels like forever ago that fifth-round rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen was dazzling during the summer and becoming a fan-favorite player, but in reality, it's only been a few months. Given the injuries to wideouts Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ) and Rashee Rice ( hamstring ), the door was opened for the Cincinnati product to make an impact. After logging a pair of catches for 27 yards in Week 6, he stood out from the jump on Sunday.
On just the second play from scrimmage for Kansas City, Allen hauled in a pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes down the left sideline and gained 18 yards. It was a dead silent half for him the rest of the way, however, which raises questions about his true involvement in the offense. Is Allen a scripted player or a difference-maker?
Look, it was glaringly obvious that finding a way to slow down someone who came into Week 7 with 49 catches for 717 yards and seven touchdowns would be super difficult. Flat-out stopping the reigning Offensive Player of the Year? Forget about it... which the Chiefs seemed to do at first whistle.
Receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba wasn't fair in the opening half of play, routinely burning cornerback L'Jarius Sneed in the slot and even providing first-round rookie Mansoor Delane with two "welcome to the league" moments. He finished the first two quarters with six snags for 129 yards and a touchdown, serving as a walking nightmare for Steve Spagnuolo's defense.
That defense was downright terrible on late downs in this one; JSN was a top force in that unfolding.
It's always difficult having a nuanced dialogue about Mahomes' play. On one hand, he's held to such a high standard by many that it seems fair to point out when he doesn't meet the bar. On the other hand, he rolled into Week 7 without the aforementioned receivers and both of his starting offensive tackles.
There's room to meet in the middle. According to RBSDM , he owned an ugly mark of -0.39 EPA per play in quarters one and two. No. 15 missed plenty of throws on SNF , leaving many of them short and also putting too much mustard on one pass that got picked off. That said, constant duress made his life much more difficult.
It's impossible to consider Mahomes' shortcomings and not directly jump into the offensive line situation. In our Week 7 preview, we briefly touched on how Kansas City has typically operated a quick-game passing offense and relied on explosive rushes and play-action to help open up the occasional deep shot. With no Jaylon Moore ( and with Josh Simmons still out ), operating a functional offense seemed far more difficult than it needed to be on Sunday.
Undrafted rookie free agent Kahlil Benson whiffed on multiple occasions, and right tackle Joshua Ezeudu also had his fair share of rough moments. Sure, Reid didn't do a ton to protect his linemen and Mahomes was far from perfect, but this can't be sustained for much longer.
After he missed an extra point last week, I opened the floor for there being an active Harrison Butker problem on the Chiefs' hands. He's years removed from producing a season that lives up to his prime, and his variance from long range makes him far from the slam-dunk kicker he used to be. That trend continued into the Seahawks game.
In a vacuum, there's no shame in missing a 58-yard field goal. When Butker left his short to end the first half, though, that sent KC into the break scoreless. He redeemed himself temporarily with a 50-yard connection in the third frame, only to push a 45-yarder midway through the fourth quarter. The more the sample size grows, the worse this looks.
Speaking of the Butker miss, that opportunity was only presented due to a brilliant play on the ball by cornerback Nohl Williams on defense. He picked off quarterback Sam Darnold's pass in the end zone and returned it for 64 yards, followed by a run and timeout by the offense. Had Seattle put up seven points on that drive, it would've been far more demoralizing than facing a 10-point deficit.
With the Chiefs driving in the fourth quarter, a drop by receiver Xavier Worthy and a holding penalty on left guard Kingsley Suamataia put the offense in a second-and-20 situation. The following two plays may fade into the void over time, but rookie running back Emmett Johnson 's 12-yard catch made third down manageable. He then threw a critical block on a scramble by Mahomes for the first.
Butker wound up missing the 45-yard boot at the end of the drive, but Johnson deserves props for being a gamer when needed.
The unfortunate thing for Worthy is he just recorded seven targets and 70-plus receiving yards in back-to-back games. On the surface, he looked like he was building some significant momentum, and he even acknowledged such this week. Gifted a massive chance to be the X-factor in Week 7, however, he flopped.
It wasn't just the fourth-quarter drop, either. The former first-round pick displayed minimal or no awareness on multiple plays, including one where he ran out of bounds and another in which he failed to throw a block on a reception by running back Kenneth Walker. The latter play could've been the most explosive of the night. Unless he's getting the ball in space and given some runway, Worthy just isn't a huge impact piece.
Anyone hoping for the third-year man to blossom into a WR1 can officially call it. They can likely sell stock on him being a high-end WR2, too, even in KC.
Through five games, Walker had fully justified the Chiefs' investment in him and then some. He's been the team's best player to this point and almost singlehandedly transformed the offense from a player standpoint, leading the sport in a variety of statistics on the ground. Citing a lackluster showing in the box score is in no way an indictment on him — it's more of a praise of the home team.
Walker finished Sunday Night Football with 14 carries for a measly 36 yards, throwing him off pace and also ignoring just how hard he had to work for that output. Week 7 wasn't a talent problem for the star halfback, as just about anyone would've failed to thrive in these conditions.
At the end of the day, the Chiefs were never going to run the table, even if fully healthy. Considering the circumstances of a lack of health on offense and facing a Super Bowl-caliber team, it shouldn't be a complete and utter shock that the Seahawks looked good. It is a surprise that the Kansas City offense looked so inept.
It's this writer's view that only a handful of teams truly matter at the moment. The Chiefs are still one of them and had to face off against a member of that group on the road in prime time. The sky isn't falling in the slightest, although this is a wake-up call for many.

title: Complete Chiefs Inactives for Week 7 vs. Seahawks: Jaylon Moore & Others Sitting Out SNF
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs return to prime time in Week 7, this time for an interconference tilt on the road against the reigning Super Bowl champions. The Seattle Seahawks await on Sunday Night Football , with Mike Macdonald's 3-3 club looking to gain some ground in the NFC West standings and defend home turf.
Neither team rolls into this one fully healthy, which is to be expected at this point in a grueling season. The hosts had multiple players carrying questionable designations entering the weekend, whereas the visitors ruled out a pair of key offensive starters while also shuffling the roster quite a bit.
With that in mind, here's who's inactive for Kansas City and Seattle in Sunday's matchup.
Here are the Chiefs’ inactives for tonight’s game against the Seahawks: WR Rashee Rice OT Jaylon Moore QB Garrett Nussmeier DB Jadon Canady FB Ben VanSumeren DE Jack Pyburn
Earlier this week, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid revealed that wide receiver Rashee Rice and right tackle Jaylon Moore wouldn't be suiting up on Sunday. Rice still hasn't returned to practice since sustaining a hamstring injury in Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders, and Moore got knocked out of Week 6's win over the Los Angeles Chargers and has been in concussion protocol ever since. Joshua Ezeudu steps in for Moore at right tackle.
Cornerback L'Jarius Sneed, who didn't originally travel with the team on Saturday due to a personal issue before joining everyone on Sunday, is active. Sneed (knee) was previously questionable to play in Week 7 after being limited in practice all week.
On Saturday, the club placed second-year running back Brashard Smith on injured reserve with a hamstring issue. Undrafted rookie free agent Jadyn Ott was signed to the 53-man roster to take his spot.
At the same time, wide receiver Justin Watson was elevated from the practice squad and linebacker Cooper McDonald came off IR and is set to play for the first time since Week 1 .
Left tackle Josh Simmons doesn't appear on Sunday's inactives because he's now on IR. Earlier on Sunday, a report shed light on the day leading up to him eventually being placed on the list, including being told to leave a team meeting by Reid and quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Tonight’s @Seahawks inactives; QB Drew Lock will serve as the emergency 3rd quarterback. pic.twitter.com/OzEKzer0eH
After being non-participants in practice on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday, the Seahawks ruled linebackers Chazz Surratt (calf) and Drake Thomas (ankle) out. Five other players were questionable, with four being on the defensive side of the ball. Headlining that collective were safety Nick Emmanwori (hip) and pass rusher DeMarcus Lawrence (rest), although both stars are good to go against KC.

title: Live Game Thread & Updates for Kansas City Chiefs vs. Seattle Seahawks on SNF
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are looking to maintain their flawless record tonight in a road tilt at Lumen Field . Mike Macdonald is looking to get his Seattle Seahawks back on track after a two-game losing skid has knocked them out of the NFC playoff picture. For those who can't tune into the contest, we'll be covering the game live here at Chiefs on SI. Refresh this page periodically to keep up with all the action.
Pregame: Click here to view the Chiefs' full list of inactives. Significant players include Rashee Rice and Jaylon Moore. 14:53: Seattle wins the coin toss and defers to Kansas City. Chiefs will start the night off at their own 27-yard line. 11:57: A very Kenneth Walker-heavy drive in his return to Seattle. He had a third-down catch that would have put KC inside the 40, but Travis Kelce was flagged for an illegal shift during his pre-snap motion. Matt Araiza punted it away to the Seattle 14-yard line, where Sam Darnold will start for the Seahawks' first offensive series. 9:17: The first three plays of the night were targets to Jaxon Smith-Njigba. That about encapsulates what we should expect from Seattle's offense. The Seahawks have picked up two first downs and are near midfield after an AJ Barner tush-push moved the chains. 7:12: Mansoor Delane picks up a huge pass break-up on third down to force a punt. Chiefs will start at their own 10 after the TV timeout. 3:53: Two big catches from tight end Noah Gray this drive. He just made a diving grab on second down to enter Seattle territory. The Chiefs could soon find themselves in field-goal range. 1:48: Nothing doing on third-and-short, as Mahomes threw it away to the right sideline. It would've been a 60-yard kick if Harrison Butker to attempt a field goal, so the Chiefs punted for the second time today and pinned Seattle inside the 10. 0:00: There will be a crucial third-and-four once the TV timeout concludes. There's no score after one quarter. Chiefs and Seahawks are tied, 0-0.
13:05: Just an unbelievable diving grab by JSN on third down to keep the drive moving. The Seahawks have first-and-10 on their own 43-yard line. 8:22: Another chunk play for Smith-Njigba ignites the first scoring drive of the night. Velus Jones nearly ran it in from 20 yards out, but he stepped out of bounds and the KC defense managed a goal-line stand. Seattle kicker Jason Myers put the first points on the board with a 25-yarder. Seahawks lead, 3-0. 8:16: Nikko Remigio shortly contemplated kneeling for a touchback on the kickoff, then broke off a 43-yard return to bring the ball near midfield. Huge opportunity for the Chiefs offense here, who only need a couple of first downs to get into scoring territory. 6:44: Andy Reid gets aggressive and goes for it on fourth-and-1, an area where the running game has struggled this year. However, Walker picked up enough on an inside zone handoff to keep the drive alive. 6:00: The Seahawks pressure finally got to Mahomes. Rolling out to his left, he sailed a pass over Jalen Royals' head that wound up in the hands of Nick Emmanwori for an interception. It's the fourth pick of the season for Mahomes, and Seattle has a chance to make this a two-score game before halftime. 4:02: A catch-and-run from Emanuel Wilson has already put the Seahawks in field-goal position. With less than four minutes remaining, Seattle could look to drain as much clock as possible and keep the ball out of Mahomes' hands until the second half if the situation allows. 1:44: After an extensive review, an over-the-shoulder catch from JSN indeed crossed the pylon and resulted in the first touchdown of the day. He's up to 93 yards from scrimmage and is single-handedly tearing apart this Chiefs defense. Time for Mahomes and the offense to run a two-minute drill. Seahawks lead, 10-0. 1:16: Frustrating is mounting for the Chiefs' offensive players. Travis Kelce is visibly frustrated after Mahomes failed to connect with him over the middle of the field. It's a three-and-out and Seattle will have a little over one minute to extend its lead after a 32-yard return by Rashid Shaheed. 0:35: This has been a real wake-up call for Steve Spagnuolo's defense. They haven't faced a playmaker anywhere near Smith-Njigba's caliber, and he's making that painfully obvious tonight with 142 scrimmage yards. The Seahawks are at the two-yard line with a chance to make this a 17-point game before the half. 0:07: It was only a matter of time before Sam Darnold threw a pick. The defense turns the momentum of this game upside down with a Nohl Williams interception. He ran it back 64 yards out of the end zone, and Kansas City has one timeout to try and gain some yardage from a little past midfield before sending out the field goal unit. This could be a 10-point swing if Harrison Butker comes through. 0:00: Despite a chance to pull within a touchdown, Butker's 58-yard attempt came up multiple yards short. The Chiefs have officially been shut out in the first half for the first time this year. Seattle opens the second half with the ball. Seahawks lead at halftime, 10-0.
12:55: On third-and-medium, Darnold was able to break free and scramble for a first down to the Chiefs' 46-yard line. Seahawks offense has picked up where it left off from the first half. 11:02: Nick Bolton is down on the field with an apparent injury. Something to monitor for this Chiefs defensive unit. There's an official timeout on the field. 8:09: Another red-zone stand for the Chiefs keeps this a two-possession game at Lumen Field. Myers hit his second field goal to make this a 13-point game. Seahawks lead, 13-0. 5:44: After a couple of screen passes to Xavier Worthy and Travis Kelce, Walker took a check-down up the right sideline to set up a fourth-and-short. Mahomes found Worthy for a short hitch route to move the chains and keep the driving moving. It hasn't been pretty by any means, but the Chiefs need to muster up yards somehow. 1:42: Everyone, buy your tickets. There's a full-blown circus going on in Seattle. A swarm of players went flying after the ball when Derick Hall forced it loose on a strip sack, but the Chiefs are extremely fortunate to have come away with it. Butker redeemed his miss from the previous half with a 50-yard make to cut the deficit to 10. Seahawks lead, 13-3. 0:00: A false start by the Seahawks' offensive line makes a third-and-2 chance into a much more manageable third-and-7 for KC's defense. Big play upcoming after the TV timeout. Seahawks lead, 13-3.
14:17: The Chiefs come up with the stop they needed, forcing JSN out of bounds for a two-yard gain. Mahomes will take the ball at KC's 13-yard line to try and trim Seattle's lead. Drive of the night here for the Chiefs. 13:00: This one isn't over yet. Kelce secured a catch over the middle on third down, and he surpasses Tony Gonzalez for the most receiving yards of any tight end in NFL history with that snag. Perhaps that can be the play that gets this Chiefs offense going. 10:34: Mahomes continues to improvise on third downs. He scrambled just pass the first-down marker after facing a second-and-20 one play before. The Chiefs are now at Seattle's 34 and are starting to find an offensive rhythm. 8:33: Rather than letting the offense try to keep the drive alive on fourth-and-3, Coach Reid trotted Butker back onto the field to try one from 45 yards and make it a one-possession game. Instead, the veteran kicker hooked it wide right, and it remains a 10-point game in Seattle. That might be the nail in the coffin for the Chiefs, and it's impossible to ignore Kansas City's kicker issues right now. 6:23: AJ Barner's second tush-push of the evening gives the Seahawks another first down. They are simply playing ball-control football and milking as much of the clock as they can. At this rate, KC may not get the ball back until the two-minute warning. 3:47: That should do it, folks. The Chiefs tried playing the timeout game and preserving some clock, but Emanuel Wilson went untouched up the left sideline…

title: Chiefs vs. Seahawks: NFL Week 7 Preview, Score Predictions
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are back in prime time this weekend, taking center stage at Lumen Field in a matter of hours against a feisty Seattle Seahawks squad that's still finding its way a bit after winning the Super Bowl earlier this calendar year.
Don't let the home team's offensive struggles fool you, though, as this remains one of the premier clubs in the NFL. Head coach Mike Macdonald's group might have the game's best wide receiver in Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and the Seahawks' defense is in the conversation for being football's most elite unit once again.
Kansas City has its work cut out for it in what could be a tough road game, but one thing this year's team has shown is an abundance of grit. Will Sunday Night Football be more of the same?
How might today's game unfold? The Kansas City Chiefs On SI crew makes its predictions for Week 7 of the regular season.
Joshua Brisco: Between the Seahawks’ offensive inconsistencies and the Chiefs’ offensive injuries, this feels like a low-scoring, wire-to-wire affair between two teams with elite elements in some areas and significant questions in others. Ultimately, fitting the narrative of the week perfectly, Kenneth Walker should be the key to this game for both teams.
Jordan Foote: Going into Seattle and securing a win is easily the toughest ask of the Chiefs through the first month-and-a-half of the season. The Seahawks' defense, even while banged up, is amazing. On the other side of the ball, however, there's next to no run game. That's had a negative impact on quarterback Sam Darnold, who also isn't sniffing the production he found a season ago.
Week 7's tilt could go either way, but I'll side with the offense I believe in much more. Minus wideout Rashee Rice and right tackle Jaylon Moore , look for this one to be a statement game for one or both of quarterback Patrick Mahomes and running back Kenneth Walker III in hostile territory.
Joshua Schulman: Kenneth Walker is set to return to face the franchise he won a Super Bowl with less than nine months ago, and he'll be looking to make his former team regret letting him walk. He and Jaxon Smith-Njigba headline one of the most exciting Sunday Night Football contests in recent memory.
There's a generational quarterback in Patrick Mahomes squaring off against a generational defense that has picked up where it left off a season ago, despite the offense's inconsistencies.
Seattle's slow start has actually placed it out of the playoff picture, and a home loss before another prime-time showdown against the Bears would be disastrous. I think the Seahawks understand the importance of this matchup and will take advantage of their 10 days of rest.
Given the Chiefs' shaky kicking game and a lack of proven offensive weapons outside of Walker in what should be a low-scoring contest, I think Mike Macdonald and Co. narrowly steal one to hand Kansas City its first loss.
Tyler Brown: This one has the look of a defensive rock fight. Seattle’s passing defense ranks first in the NFL, allowing just 141 yards per game, and Kansas City’s defense has held opponents under 20 points in most of its wins. The ingredients are there for a low-scoring grind from start to finish.
That said, the Chiefs are the number one offense in the NFL for a reason. Seattle’s defense may be able to slow down Walker or Mahomes, but doing both simultaneously is a different ask entirely. If the run game gets going, the play-action attack opens up. If Mahomes starts finding his receivers, the box opens up for Walker. At some point, one of those two is going to win.
On the other side, if Sam Darnold can buy time in the pocket, Smith-Njigba is going to get loose. The Chiefs’ defense just has to make sure that happens once or twice rather than repeatedly.

title: Chiefs Stats and Milestones for Week 7 vs. Seahawks: All Eyes on Travis Kelce
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs have impressed the football world by getting out to a 5-0 start this season, and there are multiple reasons why head coach Andy Reid's crew is riding high entering a Sunday Night Football bout against the Seattle Seahawks.
On both sides of the ball, Kansas City has operated like a well-oiled machine for extended stretches, with both stars and role players alike doing their respective parts to chip in. In Week 7, it's all about the pillars of the franchise when it comes to records and leaderboards.
Let's take a look at the most intriguing stats and milestones to monitor for the Chiefs in Week 7 of the regular season, courtesy of the club's game notes.
It's been a heck of a season for one Travis Kelce thus far, as the future Hall of Fame tight end is averaging 59.6 yards per game (his most since 2023) and 15.0 yards per reception (the most of his career). The 37-year-old is posting double-digit yards per target for the first time ever, fueled by a 66.7% success rate that's the best since his second NFL season in 2014.
Kelce is turning back the clock in a big way and can continue to add to his elite resume in Week 7.
With two catches of 25 or more yards, Kelce can tie Rob Gronkowski for the most ever by a tight end. Three receptions of any kind would allow him to pass Hall of Fame receiver Marvin Harrison for the most by a player in his first 14 seasons. Finally, No. 87 is just 35 yards away from surpassing longtime Chiefs tight end Tony Gonzalez for the most by a tight end (including postseason) in a career.
Good note here from @SkylarBurg17 of the NFL: With 35 receiving yards vs. Seattle, Chiefs TE Travis Kelce can surpass Hall of Famer Tony Gonzalez (15,413 receiving yards) for the most receiving yards by a TE, including the postseason, in NFL history.
Quarterback Patrick Mahomes is great, and Reid's changes to the offense have been massive, but there's no more valuable entity to this point of the Chiefs' season than running back Kenneth Walker III. The prized free agent signing — and former Seahawk — is producing at easily the highest level of his career and is already up to 665 rushing yards and eight all-purpose scores in five games.
On Sunday night, he can take that output to a new level and contextualize it relative to his career.
A pair of touchdowns in Week 7 would give Walker a new career-high mark with 10 on the year. He'd also become the first player since 1970 (yes, over 50 years) to score multiple times in five of his team's first six games. Considering that Walker is lethal before contact, evades tackles with the best of them and can catch passes out of the backfield, nothing is off the table in this potential revenge game.
All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones hasn't had the season he or just about anyone else expected. He did manage to record his first half-sack of the campaign in Week 6, but the 32-year-old continues to show signs of slowing down relative to his peak as one of the game's most feared pass-rushing threats. With that said, it wouldn't take an insane performance for Jones to ascend the Chiefs leaderboard in Week 7.
Just 1.5 sacks versus Seattle puts Jones in a tie with former Chiefs outside linebacker Tamba Hali for the second-most in a Kansas City career (89.5). After going for five sacks in 15 games in 2024 and seven in all 17 regular-season games in 2025, it's only a matter of time before Jones adds to his current total for 2026. Sunday is a prime opening for him to do so.

title: A Wyatt Teller Trade Clearly Makes Sense for the Chargers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have spent years trying to put the right pieces around Justin Herbert. Herbert has shown he can make plays against just about any defense in the league, but even the best quarterbacks are going to have a difficult time when the pocket constantly collapses around them.
That is why a potential trade for Wyatt Teller is worth taking seriously.
The biggest reason this potential trade makes sense is pretty simple. Teller is having a clear down year with the Texans, and the Bolts have a crucial need at the offensive line position.
There is only so much a quarterback can do when he does not have enough time to operate.
The Chargers need to make sure their offensive line is capable of holding up against the best defensive fronts in football. That becomes especially important when facing teams that can generate pressure with their front four and force the quarterback to make quick decisions. Against those defenses, even a small weakness along the interior can become a major problem.
That is where Teller could potentially fit in. As a guard, he would give them another experienced option in the middle of the offensive line. His physical style of play and years of NFL experience make him a name worth evaluating. Another benefit would be the potential impact on the running game. Interior offensive linemen play a major role in creating running lanes. Which could be more of a dependable presence at guard. Establishing that balance would take some pressure off Herbert and give the offense more ways to attack opposing defenses.
Teller lost his starting position early this year after siging a two-year deal with Houston. Things have not worked the way both parties wanted it too, so a trade would make complete sense.
The Chargers also have to think about depth. Injuries are part of the game, and a team can quickly find itself in trouble when it does not have enough reliable options up front. Adding an experienced lineman could give the coaching staff more flexibility over the course of a long season. There is a financial side to consider as well. The Bolts should not give up valuable draft capital or take on an unreasonable contract just to make a move. If the Texans are willing to negotiate a deal that makes sense for both teams, however, the conversation becomes much more interesting.
They do not need to make a splash just for the sake of making one. They need to make smart decisions that improve the roster where it matters most. If Teller can help strengthen the offensive line, give Justin Herbert more time and making the offense more balanced. Bringing him aboard could be a move that makes a lot of sense.
Graziano says Wyatt Teller is a name that could be on the move ahead of the deadline. https://t.co/6A9gIaLcsh pic.twitter.com/ZhQy904uOL

title: Chargers' Post-Bye Week NFL Mock Draft, 5-Round Edition
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are emerging from their Week 7 bye with an 0-6 record and a firm grasp on the number one overall pick now that the Miami Dolphins have won a game. Miami's win leaves the Chargers as the lone winless team remaining in the NFL.
The Chargers, as an organization, have questions to answer moving forward and towards the November 10th trade deadline. Will they continue to maintain a plan of standing pat or will they decide to sell off tradeable assets and look to the future?
The Chargers and Dolphins are the favorites to land the number one overall pick. The two teams play each other late in the season in a Week 16 matchup that could easily be the deciding factor based on the current outlook of the season. Right now the Chargers have the number one pick and let's run through that scenario in a mock draft.
It’s not just the 200 yards and 4 TDs for Jeremiah Smith — it’s wild routes like these, at 6-4, 220, that make him such a special prospect pic.twitter.com/gnlWb2S5nX https://t.co/TyT6YVz5W9
This is the easiest pick that the entire NFL world would make without hesitation. The Chargers need a top receiving option to get defenses to back off the line of scrimmage and give Justin Herbert a viable option to throw to.
Smith is a 6'3 222lb monster of a wide receiver who is generating lofty comparisons. The bottom line is Smith is one of the best wide receiver prospects we have seen in years. Smith owns several Ohio State school receiving records and stands out from a school that has sent a receiver to the NFL via the first round for five consecutive years and six total.
In the event the draft order changes, this draft class has several top wide receiver prospects who could help immediately but Smith stands alone at the top of the class.
Fastest College Football Players of Week 8 2️⃣ 21.8 mph - Zabien Brown ( @zabien_brown ) CB Alabama #ReelSpeed 🔗 https://t.co/wwII6ki7cm pic.twitter.com/VPJazVtcHr
The Chargers have a thin cornerback room and could use an addition. Zabien Brown is a great blend of size, speed and instincts. He is not perfect with his technique but his talent is undeniable. If any coaching staff can get the most out of him and turn him into the lockdown outside corner he is capable of being, the Chargers defensive staff can get him to shine.
John Henry Daley 2.7 second sack time! https://t.co/ZNIKwcuT7y pic.twitter.com/bjfmMrgEqW
In all likelihood, the Chargers will be moving forward without Khalil Mack. Tuli Tuipulotu and Akheem Mesidor will be the edge anchors and Los Angeles will need another edge rusher to fill out the room with the amount of three-edge-rusher looks they use.
John Henry Daley is cut from the same cloth as Tuipulotu and Mesidor, a high effort menace who is capable of rushing from the inside but can also win quickly. Having a high pick in each round gives the Chargers a chance at players like this.
#BYU LB Cade Uluave had 3 pressures on the final drive; was a big reason why #GoIrish QB was under duress down the stretch The physical tools aren't outstanding but he checks boxes. Can rush / cover / shoot gaps vs the run. Green Dot guy. Reminds me of Henry To'o To'o at Alabama pic.twitter.com/aJHnHyMc04
The Chargers' linebacker room is incredibly thin heading into 2027 with several veterans playing out 2026 on expiring contracts. Even if the Chargers re-sign Daiyan Henley, they will need to add to the room.
BYU's Cade Uluave has been on my radar for years going back to his freshman season at Cal. Scouts from the Chargers were a consistent presence at Cal over the past few seasons and have already visited BYU games twice in 2026. It may mean nothing but the scouts will have had eyes on him for a long time as well.
Uluave is a modern linebacker who can cover, blitz and tackle. He is also highly regarded for his leadership and football character.
Texas Tech DT AJ Holmes Jr. having 5 sacks in 6.5 games at 6-3, 300 is disgusting pic.twitter.com/2Kt1MVH20K
The Chargers will be lucky if A.J Holmes Jr. is available at the top of day 3. The defensive line room has been stacking strong talent in back to back drafts and is led by veteran menace Teair Tart. Holmes is one of the top rated interior rushers in the nation and brings extra juice as a rusher.
Will be monitor #Cincinnati LG Evan Tengesdahl throughout the rest of the season. Big, physical interior lineman who has the athleticism to cut off D-linemen on perimeter runs and powerful to create displacement and stonewall pass rushers. Pocket cleaner, never gets too… pic.twitter.com/WUecXr5Ki1
I fully expect the Chargers to spend money in free agency in an attempt to solve their interior offensive line woes. However, they will also need to add more depth. Cincinnati's Evan Tengesdahl is mean and powerful interior blocker but with good movement skills. He still has some work to do as a pass protector but is a solid player with a lot to work with.

title: Chargers Bottom Out in Power Rankings…But Top NFL Draft Order
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are the worst team in the NFL . It’s a budding idea that has been whispered for a few weeks now and got confirmation while they sat on bye and morphed into the NFL’s only winless team.
With even the hapless-looking Tennessee Titans winning a game, the Chargers are now dead last in power rankings at 0-6. Any rankings without them at No. 32, frankly, aren’t worth the time of day.
Chargers fans, at least, got a win while this happened . Those fans, who probably checked out after 0-4 and turned to offseason mode already, just got to watch as the Chargers took a firm, lonely grip on the No. 1 overall pick.
So there’s that, at least. Silver linings and stuff, right?
About those power rankings.
Sporting News’ Vinnie Iyer put it best while plopping the Chargers at No. 32: “The Chargers have been hit with a bolt of poor energy under Jim Harbaugh and come out of the bye as the league's sole winless team. They need to stop playing like 53 Frankensteins who were just hit by lightning.”
Speaking of “bolts” of energy, the Chargers were hit with anything but via the arrival of Mike McDaniel. He tweaked some of Herbert’s mechanics and remolded the personnel in free agency and the draft to miserable results so far.
That makes the updated NFL draft order pretty shaky:
Shaky, because the popular idea is the Chargers going after Ohio State wideout Jeremiah Smith in the top five.
Sounds fun. The Chargers have spent too much time on first-rounder Quentin Johnston and his drop issues while names like Ladd McConkey fight injury woes and others like Tre Harris have yet to emerge.
But will it be McDaniel scheming up Smith in his offense? Will Jim Harbaugh even still be around at this point?
And knowing NFL coverage, especially in the offseason, how often will analysis call for the Chargers to take a risk on quarterback and make a big trade with Herbert?
So it goes for a team sitting 32nd in the rankings and first in the draft order. If nothing else, every day should be pretty interesting for Chargers fans…once the season ends.

title: Joe Hortiz's Trade Deadline Plan Faces a Major Bye-Week Test
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers had their bye week in Week 7. The Chargers needed a bye to regroup and hope to get some reinforcements back from injury. The reality is the Chargers are at a crossroads: they have significant injuries , their offense is still searching for an identity and they are 0-6.
The Chargers are currently in line to land the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 draft. Following the Week 7 schedule, the Chargers now are the last winless team left in the NFL with the Dolphins taking down the New York Jets for their first win of the season.
The season is essentially over for Los Angeles but questions for the future loom large. Will new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel shake up the lineup find the best offensive strategy for the available personnel or will the offense continue to be a trainwreck?
The Chargers have two games remaining before the November 10th trade deadline. If McDaniel does not get the train back on the tracks, does he survive the season? If the Chargers do not make significant changes during the bye week and show a different on-field product against the Rams in week eight, does Joe Hortiz finally cave and engage in trade talks?
The current reports indicate the Chargers are holding off trade calls and as Jeremy Fowler put it, are "still giving the impression they are standing pat."
Temperature check on a few teams entering trade deadline: -Many in league getting impression Colts will wait 1-2 weeks before determining trade course. Rallying off a few wins could change perspective. But...they need picks, too. -Bucs still in NFC South hunt, but a loss…
If the plan from the Chargers front office is to stand pat and continue to try to save the season, perhaps not for 2026 but to find some continuity heading into 2027, that plan faces a massive test against the Rams next week. The Chargers, at best, could end up 2-6 heading into the trade deadline. However, if they drop to 0-7, Joe Hortiz's phone will likely be ringing non-stop.
Currently, betting markets have the Chargers and Dolphins in a tight race for the number one overall pick. Kalshi currently has the odds at 35 percent for the Dolphins and 31 percent for the Chargers. Typically, regimes do not survive a catastrophic season that leads to landing the top pick in the draft.
The deadline math for general manager Joe Hortiz and the Chargers' front office isn't as simple as buyers vs. sellers. They have to deal with a high-stakes balancing act with little margin for error. The front office could sell off tradeable assets to build for the future and net draft capital. The risk in selling is leaving your franchise quarterback, Justin Herbert, with even less to work with.
If Los Angeles continues to stand pat and hold the line, and they essentially will be burning future capital on a lost season. But, if they decide to go full fire-sale, does that symbolic waving the white flag put everyone's job further in jeopardy. John Spanos, President of Football Operations and son of Chargers owner Dean Spanos, will likely push the decision one way or the other.
Looking back to when the Chargers fired former general manager Tom Telesco and head coach Brandon Staley, John Spanos said in the days after, "My opinion is everything starts with ownership. Ultimately, we're responsible for everything. What we've been doing has not been good enough." What direction the Chargers go at the deadline may ultimately be out of Joe Hortiz's hands. If they fall to 0-7 the plan of standing pat may collapse.

title: What It Would Cost Chargers to Trade for Quenton Nelson And Is He Worth It?
full_text:
Even with the Los Angeles Chargers being 0-6 and currently on a bye week -- a perfect storm to sell and get rid of players who deserve better -- the team has reportedly come out and told other teams that they are not ready, yet, to let go of their veterans.
This comes from Jeremy Fowler, specifically saying : "Chargers, at 0-6, still giving impression they are standing pat. But a long way till Nov. 10 deadline, and Chargers are receiving calls."
That said, does the Chargers' front office believe that they are buyers? Are they going to send assets out to make this team better? If so, who for how much?
Quenton Nelson, at age 30, is the Indianapolis Colts offensive guard, a longstanding NFL pro with accolades for a future Hall of Fame entry, even if he were to retire now. He has 3x First Team All-Pro Selections, 3x Second Team All-Pro selections and eight straight Pro Bowl selections.
This career obviously would make Nelson a very expensive addition, even if he is 30 and with a need for a likely record-setting new contract. This need for a new contract will likely make Nelson's price a bit cheaper, as the acquiring team will have to ensure their books are clear to pay for their new investment.
Once traded, expect Nelson to earn a league-high contract, likely over 25 million a year, surpassing the current league leader, Titans Peter Skoronski.
Colts Receive: 2027 Second-Round Pick (Est. Pick 33) Chargers Receive: Quenton Nelson + 2027 Fourth-Round Pick (Est. Pick 107)
It is very difficult to find any trade (dating back to 2020) that would be similar to Nelson moving on from the Colts. It is rare to find a player of that is the caliber of Nelson, but furthermore, rare to find a team willing to move on from someone of that talent.
The Joe Thuney trade comes to mind , where the Chiefs traded away the then-31-year-old to the Chicago Bears for a Bears fourth-round pick. Thuney needed a new contract when traded as well, adding that layer of similarity to this exercise with Nelson.
Trent Williams being traded to the San Francisco 49ers also draws some parallels, with Williams being 31 years old and one of the league's best players at his position. He was traded for a third-and a fifth-round pick, doing so as an offensive tackle, which is usually more costly than a guard.
All of these trade estimates show that Nelson may not cost the multiple first-round picks that fans may think. He is an aging veteran who needs a new contract, but is also one of the league's best at his position. The Chargers' 33rd overall pick is a very valuable selection, likely being enough for the Colts to say yes to the offer, while sending back a fourth-round selection to sweeten the deal for the Bolts.
While trading for a player right now feels pointless, Nelson should be the exception. Adding the Colts legend to the Chargers' offensive line to help protect Justin Herbert could be the one move made this year that can help the Chargers get back into contention...or at least hope for such in 2027.
