title: Raiders' Rookie, Sophomore Power Rankings: Up and Down We Go
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' plan all along was to depend on several rookies and second-year players they have drafted under John Spytek to be productive this season. Las Vegas loaded its roster with young, talented players at positions of need, knowing there would be growing pains.
The Raiders' Week 7 loss to the Los Angeles Rams further confirmed what the previous three losses already made clear: Las Vegas' dependence on young players would inevitably cost them games. This is normal in the type of rebuild the Raiders have embarked on under Spytek and Klint Kubiak.
Las Vegas has a long way to go to consistently compete with and beat the league's best. Below are the power rankings for the Raiders' rookies and second-year players.
The rookie quarterback's stock is through the roof right now, and he didn't even play a down on Sunday against the Rams. Las Vegas spent months evaluating every facet of Mendoza before using the No. 1 overall draft pick in this year's draft on him. Sunday's loss makes it clear his time is now.
Mendoza's skill set can help Las Vegas offset its limitations on its offensive line and at wide receiver. Still, Kubiak explained that Mendoza will see the field sometime this season, just not during their Week 8 road trip.
“Eventually Fernando [Mendoza] is going to play football. We have a plan. We don’t have a timeline for that. Kirk [Cousins] is playing really well, and we’re in the hunt. It’s really important that we keep playing really well behind him and continue to develop Fernando, but Fernando is going to play at some point. It’s not going to be this week," Kubiak said.
Sure, Las Vegas has a winnable road game against the New York Jets, followed by a tough game against the San Francisco 49ers. Starting the rookie in either game would be questionable. However, even if the Raiders split those two games, Mendoza should start after that.
The Raiders' ground game has continued to struggle. However, these issues have long existed before Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington arrived. Las Vegas has finished with the fewest rushing yards in the league in two of the past three seasons.
They finished with the third-fewest rushing yards in the third of those three seasons. Through seven games this season, the Raiders have the second-fewest rushing yards in the league. Las Vegas has swapped out multiple running backs during that time, while largely keeping the same offensive line.
Despite his ankle injury and the clear lack of the explosion that led Las Vegas to draft him No. 6 overall, he has shown his versatility by making an impact in the passing game. The Raiders have plenty to figure out, as their ground game has been largely rendered useless by their offensive line.
Overall, Las Vegas' defensive backfield struggled against Matthew Stafford and the Rams. The unit, largely composed of rookies and second-year players, was simply outmatched by a more experienced quarterback and group of Rams wide receivers.
Stafford completed 23 of his 29 passes, with the longest gain of the day being 15 yards. Although the Raiders' defensive backfield eliminated the big plays, they failed to slow down the Rams' passing attack enough to give their offense a chance to work their issues out.
Still, the unit is about where they were expected to be at the start of the season.
The Raiders started Rogers over Jackson Powers-Johnson again on Sunday. The second-year offensive guard continued to show a need for improvement, routinely missing critical blocks that led to negative plays. There were multiple plays where Rogers looked lost on the field.
Las Vegas must seriously consider adding help at offensive guard, as they don't get quality play at either guard position at a starting-caliber level. They also lack depth behind their shaky starting guards.
Rogers needs further development, as many second-year players do. However, his poor play only highlights a larger issue for the Raiders. The team may make offensive guard its top priority after the season. Las Vegas' offensive guards are holding the offense back.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo’s Raiders Report Card: The Unfiltered Truth on Team Performance
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders' (3-4) performance on Sunday was the worst of the season for the Silver and Black, and what made it worse was that it was at home against a battered team that was the unquestioned Super Bowl favorite coming into the season, whom the Raiders had a chance to knock out.
Instead, the Los Angeles Rams (3-4) leave Allegiant Stadium with not only a win, but a new breath of life for their once nearly certain Super Bowl chances.
This one hurt Raider Nation. Bad.
Each week, I offer my report on the game after watching copious amounts of film, drawing on my years of experience and sources both inside and outside the Raiders franchise, from around the world of football.
That was by far the hardest grade I will give in this report.
Raiders QB Kirk Cousins leads the NFL in passing touchdowns (16) and ranks third with nearly 1,900 yards. Kirk Cousins isn’t playing well; he is playing terrific.
Every player, including Raiders owner Tom Brady, the best QB in the history of the game, can go back to every game he ever played and find one or two plays he could have done better. The other team is full of high-priced millionaire players, too
The reality is that I predicted the Raiders would be sitting here today at 2-5 instead of 3-4, and there is no way the Raiders have the success they do without Cousins.
Of course, the elephant in the room is that the Silver and Black selected the man NFL executives ranked the best QB prospect of the last four NFL Drafts, Fernando Mendoza, waiting in the wings.
I totally understand the mindset of fans who recognize what I told you all offseason: this is not a Super Bowl team, and they want to turn the page.
Cousins is not just a man I cover, but a friend. That said, when the time comes, I also look forward to seeing the Nandoloarian, but when it comes to QB development, I trust Brady, Kubiak, and the way Cousins is executing their plan.
But the aforementioned Brady, who knew more about being a QB in the NFL long before he was an owner, talked about how sitting and watching helped him, and the franchise is sticking to the plan.
The plan is that as long as Cousins is playing well and the team is in NFL Playoff contention, Cousins is the man.
The made-up media frenzy this offseason that we told you was a farce, and the one now, isn’t reality. Kubiak pulled out a hammer and nails and put those rumors and speculation to death on Monday.
“I want to let you guys know that Kirk [Cousins] is our starting quarterback. There is no controversy there. He’s playing at a very high level, and he’s got to continue to do that for us to win. And we’ve got to keep helping all the areas around him. So, excited for him to go play here against the Jets.”
Credit Kubiak; he knows what he has on his bench, and he signed off on him. Kubiak and I agree that Mendoza looks exactly like what they wanted, but not today.
I have said since last May that the feeling I got from people in the building was probably around the Cleveland game. That changes if the team continues to overachieve, but at some point this year, I expect Mendoza to start. Kubiak talked more about the Mendoza factor and, as usual, took it head-on.
“Eventually Fernando [Mendoza] is going to play football. We have a plan. We don’t have a timeline for that. Kirk [Cousins] is playing really well, and we’re in the hunt. It’s really important that we keep playing really well behind him and continue to develop Fernando, but Fernando is going to play at some point. It’s not going to be this week.”
But despite Cousins' terrific play, the reality is that the offensive line, as a unit, is struggling and, frankly, is brutal.
The guard play on the right side has not been good all season, and on the left side has been up and down like a roller coaster at your favorite amusement park.
Watching the film and seeing input, Kolton Miller was not elite, or even top-ten at the NFL level, but did an adequate job.
Tyler Linderbaum is a star, and the Bills game was a disaster. He has had some struggles, but as one NFL executive told me about the Rams game, “There are some plays that he is getting blamed for that has more to do with the pathetic play from the guys next to him. Was he great? No, but who the hell can be great when the two guys next to him are playing like that? He has to be able to trust those guys next to him, and he can’t trust (excrement) right now.”
Delmar “DJ” Glaze, The Mule, looks like the emerging star we thought he could be. He was a problem for the Rams, who found very few along the Raiders' OL, and he played as a steady foundational piece who looks like a fan favorite and a long-term solution for a franchise with a history of elite OL play. I asked Kubiak about “The Mule” on Monday, and he didn’t hold back.
"Yeah, DJ [Glaze] was a team captain for us this week, so that tells you how highly we believe how high of a level he's playing at, how good of a teammate that he is, and how he's taking the next step in his career. And the thing about DJ is that he's not satisfied, and he's continuing to get better, which he's a very self-motivated young man."
I asked Kubiak bluntly if the poor play at guard was going to get Trey Zuhn III and Bryce Cabeldue consideration for reps this week, and without hesitation, he said, “Yes.”
They deserve the chance. They have to earn them, but players know what is going on, and Kubiak’s locker room trusts him and Rick Dennison.
Neither Dennison nor Kubiak is the problem; they are the answer, and hopefully the three young men who have been playing guard can grow into the spots, but they aren't good enough now. After Sunday's performance, Zuhn, the rookie, and Cabeldue can do no worse and deserve a chance on a team that prides itself on competition.
Ashton Jeanty continues to shine in the passing game, but rookie Mike Washington Jr., who was injured last week before the game, continues to rack up impressive plays and earn more carries.
The tight ends aren't the issue, but the wide receivers, as a unit, haven't been good. Dont’e Thornton Jr. appears to be headed out of town later this week, and Jack Bech should be back this week, but that doesn’t change the fact that Cousins has to throw quick because the pressure is on him nearly as fast as Tyler Linderbaum puts the ball in his hand.
We knew coming into the season the Raiders don’t have a WR1, and credit GM John Spytek and Kubiak for dealing with it in a rebuilding year, rather than wasting picks or money on Elmer’s Glue and Scotch tape fixes, as this franchise has relied on for the last two-plus decades.
Their discipline may infuriate some fans who don’t understand it now, but they'll thank them down the road in 2028.
I will get more into coaching later, but for now, the Raiders' defense had some players playing at a good level. Still, even with a terrific player (injured) at WR, Puka Nacua, and a future Hall of Fame QB in Matthew Stafford, they have no excuse for embarrassing themselves as they did, hindered as they were.
Missed tackles, missed assignments, and an inability in the first half should have embarrassed the men wearing the Raiders patch. They are good men, they are proud men, and many of them are better players than they looked on Sunday, but I am grading Sunday, and it was terrible.
True to his character, Kubiak didn’t hold back any punches when discussing why his team continues to struggle against the run, and teams are literally doing whatever they want to them on the ground.
"It's all team. It's all phases. It's tackling, it's at the front, it's putting them in situations to be successful as coaches, so we're all accountable."
The reality is that this defense is struggling for legitimate reasons; it is a rebuilding year. But these men are paid a lot of money, and missed tackles, especially those executed terribly, are inexcusable. These men are paid a lot of money to do a job, and Brady, Mark Davis, GM John Spytek, and Kubiak are not being unrealistic in asking…

title: The Biggest Decisions Kubiak, Raiders Got Wrong vs. Rams
full_text:
The first mistake the Raiders made on Sunday was winning the coin toss and electing to receive the ball. Las Vegas starting the game on defense has worked better for them in each game this season. Overall, they played better with their defense on the field first, even in losses.
In each of their three wins, Las Vegas' defense was on the field first. The Raiders forced a punt or a turnover on downs on the opponent's first drive in each of those three games. In those three wins, the Raiders' defense held opposing offenses to six points combined in the first quarter.
Even during their three wins, the Raiders' offense started slowly. In those three wins, Las Vegas' offense scored a total of 10 points in the first quarter. That is why electing to receive the ball against the Rams was a mistake.
In theory, getting the ball first, marching down the field, and scoring first against a reeling Rams team sounds good. However, that only works if your offense can actually execute in the first quarter. Or execute in general. Once the offense doesn't score, you're essentially behind a possession.
Not only are you down by a possession because the other team got the ball first after halftime, but you are also down by a possession to Matthew Stafford. The Raiders got the ball first, gained one yard in three plays, and punted the ball to Stafford and the Rams.
Luckily, the Raiders' defense forced a punt. Las Vegas' offense got the ball back and essentially did the same thing it did on the first drive. However, this time, a missed field goal after a 39-yard defensive pass interference call against the Rams helped the unit move downfield.
This is why electing to receive may seem insignificant, but it wasn't. The Raiders' offense took the field and quickly showed that they had nothing. They were not going to do anything that day. Their teammates on defense knew early on that they had no run support, no matter how well they played.
They made plenty of mistakes, but the attempt to gain a mental edge backfired spectacularly. After the Raiders' missed field goal, the Rams scored a touchdown on all of their next four possessions, while Las Vegas kicked two field goals. Las Vegas needs to start games on defense.
Still, the Raiders' biggest mistake was fooling themselves into thinking the game was more competitive than it was and not giving Fernando Mendoza any playing time.
"No, we made it a competitive game in the third quarter, so no, to answer your question," Kubiak said after the game when asked if he and the coaching staff considered playing the rookie in the second half.
Sure, Las Vegas' defense turned things up a notch, but the Raiders were down 28-6 heading into the fourth. The Raiders' offense scored zero points in the third quarter for the third time in four weeks. I am not sure how competitive that is.
If being down by 21 to Stafford and the Rams entering the fourth quarter, with your offense having scored only two field goals that day, is competitive, then their decision not to play Mendoza even one play makes perfect sense. However, the nearly 63,000 fans in attendance know what they saw.
Other position groups need attention, but the quarterback position is the most critical position on the field. Kubiak added that although his coaching staff did not consider making the move during the game, all options are on the table moving forward.
“I think we have to go watch the film, and I think at this point we're thinking about everything, how to fix our problems, how to fix our issues in the red zone, in the third quarter, and personnel, scheme. We've got to talk about all of it," Kubiak said.
It would be understandable if the coaching staff waited until after their matchup against the San Francisco 49ers to start Mendoza, but at the rate they were going on Sunday, he should have gotten on the field at some point. The game was already over .
Still, it is time for Las Vegas' coaching staff to begin the succession plan from Cousins to Mendoza.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Drastic Moves Raiders Must Consider After Fourth Straight Loss
full_text:
With the Los Angeles Rams entering Week 7 with a slew of injuries, the Las Vegas Raiders seemed in an opportunistic spot to end their three-game losing streak.
Instead, the Las Vegas Raiders suffered their fourth consecutive loss, falling to the Los Angeles Rams 35-21 on Sunday . The Silver and Black are suddenly below .500 after starting the season 3-0. With that in mind, here are three drastic moves the Raiders either need to make or consider after this result.
Kirk Cousins isn't the culprit behind the Raiders' struggles over the last month. Las Vegas lacks a true WR1, which allows opposing defenses to double and bracket Brock Bowers. However, the bulk of the 38-year-old quarterback's production over the last two weeks has come when the Raiders are playing catch-up or in garbage time. So, those numbers are somewhat misleading.
When a coaching staff decides to switch to a rookie quarterback, the opponent is a crucial factor in the process. Next week, the Raiders face the New York Jets, who allowed 360 total yards to the Miami Dolphins in a 28-25 loss.
While head coach Klint Kubiak and the staff have been patient with Mendoza's development, losing four consecutive games can change that train of thought. Las Vegas then faces the San Francisco 49ers in Week 9. Yes, Raheem Morris has that defense playing at a higher level than expected, but with injuries, the unit isn't overly intimidating.
Another factor to consider is the trade deadline two weeks away. It goes without saying that Cousins is near the end of his career, but that doesn't mean he wouldn't offer something to a contending team that needs a quarterback. We've already seen multiple starting quarterbacks suffer injuries this season, varying from multiple weeks to season-ending.
With two weeks until the trade deadline, if the Raiders feel that the postseason is slipping away, receiving value for Cousins isn't the worst idea.
Speaking of the trade deadline, Crosby is another asset Las Vegas can maximize before Nov. 10. If the Raiders aren't actively looking to improve the roster, then moving the two-time All-Pro pass rusher is in the organization’s best interest.
Quite frankly, as currently constructed, Las Vegas' personnel is most likely not good enough to make a deep playoff run anyway, let alone qualify for the postseason. Waving the white flag this early in the season, when the team was undefeated just a few weeks ago, comes off as reactionary. That said, the trade deadline forces teams to look at themselves through a different lens, with a more realistic perspective.
Trading Crosby will be a painful realization, but the 29-year-old pass rusher could garner substantial draft capital for a team several pieces away from comfortably contending for the playoffs.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Grading Each Raiders' Position Group Following Loss vs. Rams
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered their Week 7 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams looking to end a three-game losing streak. The Rams were looking to stop a losing streak of their own, with a long list of injured players listed ahead of the matchup.
The Rams entered the season with hopes of reaching the Super Bowl. Las Vegas entered the season looking to mark improvement over last season's dismal 3-14 campaign. Las Vegas did just that during the season's first three weeks, albeit against some of the league's worst teams.
Las Vegas' Week 7 matchup against the Rams was their fourth straight game against what was considered one of the league's best teams, despite their injuries and 2-4 record entering Sunday. Still, Los Angeles has one of the best front offices, head coaches, and quarterbacks in the league.
Even with the Rams' injuries, Sunday was always going to be a tough outing for the Raiders, as the significantly shorthanded New England Patriots thoroughly beat them. Below are the grades for each of the Raiders' position groups following Sunday's outing against the Rams.
Given how this roster is constructed, the Raiders have peaked with Kirk Cousins, and that is okay, but it is time for the future. Fernando Mendoza is as ready as he can be, without playing an actual game, and gives the Raiders their best chance to win.
This coaching staff cannot keep rolling Cousins out and telling the players in the locker room that they are putting the team in the best position to win.
The players in the locker room know the truth, even if they won't say it publicly. The coaching staff does too.
Only so many passes can be overthrown, thrown into double coverage, or not thrown at all. Yes, receivers need to get open, but passes need to get to the receivers sooner, too. Passes need more zip, and the ball needs to get out of the quarterback's hands sooner.
Maybe receivers can get open more easily with a quarterback who can extend plays and potentially even run the ball. Las Vegas' current record shows how the rest of the season will go with Cousins under center, even though this season could still be so much more.
Yes, the offensive line needs to block better, but they also need a quarterback who can run a yard or two past the line of scrimmage when things break down. It's the NFL; defenses will pressure the quarterback. He has to be able to MOVE. Geez Louise.
If the Raiders are serious about winning, it is time to take the training wheels off the 2026 No. 1 overall draft pick.
Ashton Jeanty ran the ball eight times for 15 yards. However, falling behind by multiple scores early in the game makes it hard for any offense to continue running the ball unsuccessfully. Jeanty added eight catches for 61 yards and a touchdown. He had zero dropped passes on the day.
Still, it is clear that Jeanty is missing the burst and explosion that made John Spytek use the No. 6 overall draft pick on him. He may not have been on the injury report for only the second time this season heading into Week 7, but the big eye in the sky does not lie.
Also, the fact that neither he nor Mike Washington has had much success running the ball suggests the team's struggles on the ground stem more from the offensive line than from their running backs.
It seems highly unlikely that the Raiders whiffed on drafting Jeanty and Washington; it's more likely that they still have retooling to do to their hodgepodge offensive line.
Connor Heyward caught a 13-yard pass from punter AJ Cole, converting a fake punt. There is only so much a fullback can do.
The unit needs improvement across the board.
The Raiders have two of the best tight ends in the league: Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer. They have a running back in Jeanty who has been more impactful at catching passes than running the ball because of the Raiders' offensive line.
Bowers, Mayer, and Jeanty take many targets away from the receivers. Still, Tre Tucker led all three in receiving yards with 103. Las Vegas needs more help at wide receiver, but that help is unlikely to come this season.
Las Vegas' tight ends have been one of the few bright spots over the past four weeks. That continued against the Rams.
The Raiders' interior defensive line may not be as stout as I once thought.
A defensive line that cannot get off blocks to help stop the run, nor wrap up on tackles, combined with a defensive backfield that allows completions at a high rate, makes it hard for any linebacker to be effective. Still, Las Vegas' linebackers have things they need to improve upon.
It was target practice for Matthew Stafford on Sunday against the Raiders' defensive backs.
AJ Cole averaged 56 yards per punt. He was one of the most productive players on the field against the Rams
Matt Gay made three of his four field-goal attempts, with his lone miss coming from just over 50 yards.
Dylan Laube set the Raiders' offense up with solid field position with returning two kicks for 78 yards.
Malik Benson did what he could. They may only be a tweak or two away from springing a big one.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Overreactions to Raiders' Fourth Consecutive Loss vs. Rams
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders faced the best version of the less-than-healthy Los Angeles Rams and lost their fourth consecutive game, 35-21. It was a competitive game in the second half after the Raiders went down 28-6 at halftime, putting them within 10 points of the lead.
It was another humbling experience for the Rams, who continue to show they are still maturing as a roster and overall franchise. Head coach Klint Kubiak may have them on the right track long term, but the short term feels low. With that in mind, here are some overreactions to Sunday's tough loss to the preseason Super Bowl favorites.
Whether it is the blocking execution up front or the running backs themselves, the Raiders have spiraled downward, becoming the worst rushing offense in football again. Las Vegas was held to under 50 total yards on the ground and 2.8 yards per carry on 17 attempts, with rookie Mike Washington Jr. leading the way with six carries for 27 yards, 21 of them coming from one play.
I'm not sure if there is an easy solution to the Raiders' run game issues. You can see they are trying everything, especially Kubiak and offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko. Yet these problems persist. The Raiders cannot win football games if they can't run the football, period.
For the fourth straight week, defensive coordinator Rob Leonard has allowed at least 30 or more points. 35 more were added in the Raiders' loss to the Rams, and the failures on this front point to a lack of an ample pass rush opposite Crosby and in the middle of the defensive line, and a young secondary that has been thrown in the fire and is learning the hard way.
While Las Vegas does have some good moments on defense, Leonard's unit is starting to become untrustworthy to the naked eye. The Raiders will continue to try to experiment with ways to improve, but again, this is a rebuilding season, which means Leonard will have to roll through the punches.
I applaud Tre Tucker for his performance on Sunday (five catches, 103 yards, one touchdown). He was the best receiver on the field, performance- and impact-wise, for this particular game, creating explosive plays and giving his offense a chance to score or be the one doing the scoring. I wrote earlier in the week that the Raiders should consider trading for Jacksonville Jaguars wideout Brian Thomas Jr., and Tucker silenced my take quickly (for now).
Tucker is emerging as a consistent threat in this high-powered passing offense. Tight ends Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer might be the stars of that show with Kirk Cousins, but Tucker is emerging at the right time as the Raiders head to the Meadowlands to face the New York Jets next weekend.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Winners & Losers: Brutal Truths From Raiders vs. Rams Showdown
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-4) were beat up - frankly, manhandled - by the Los Angeles Rams (3-4) last night, 35-21, and truthfully, the score wasn’t that close.
I thought the Raiders would win, and with the Rams limping in with multiple injuries, and the NFL Trade Deadline looming , the Raiders, as they have in all four straight losses, cost themselves, and ultimately beat themselves.
Each week I reflect on the game, offering winners and losers, and today will be no exception.
I love that Klint Kubiak is aggressive; when you are an underdog, you have to be. So when he came out, won the toss, and didn’t defer, I liked it. It goes against conventional wisdom, but I thought he was sending his team a message that he expected to win and was putting his offense on the field to start to prove a point.
It seemed as if the Raiders got shell-shocked early; the attacking ceased.
Field goals at the end of the first and second half seemed senseless, and when the Rams continued to punish the Raiders, who could get no pass rush, and attacked the Raiders, playing off giving a future Hall of Fame QB with nearly no mobility the ability to stand back and attack them, I was stunned.
I asked Kubiak after the game if they had considered turning up the aggression and going after Matthew Stafford, the Rams QB; he told me bluntly, “No.”
I appreciate his honesty, but I can tell you that was the Rams' biggest offensive concern coming into the game, and the Raiders, by not changing, were victims all night.
Kubiak and his DC, Rob Leonard, are good first-year young coaches. I have not given up faith at all, not one bit, but on that night, they were outcoached.
Kubiak went into more detail and didn’t pull any punches. His feet are firmly planted in reality, and he spoke the truth on that side of the ball.
"Well, no one's coming to help us. We've got to figure it out ourselves as a coaching staff with the players, and we have to complement each other as well because to we've got to start the game a lot faster offensively."
The Raiders' offensive line was as bad as their defense. But the Rams got up fast, thus making the Raiders a one-dimensional team (They threw 45 times and ran 14 called runs, and Cousins had three scrambles), and you can’t win in this league when a defense forces you to be one-dimensional. A fact Kubiak is well aware of.
"Yeah, well, you can't win in this league having to throw it as much as we're throwing it. We've got to be more competitive in the game early so that we can be balanced. But there's no balance in playing from behind."
QB Kirk Cousins elaborated on how the game changes when teams force you to go one-dimensional, and to his credit, he sugarcoated nothing.
"You certainly had to be a little bit more one-dimensional. I thought we still tried to do some things to stay varied, but yeah, when you get down three scores or whatever it was, then that's the game you got to play, and that's part of football and part of trying to get back in the game."
The Raiders' abysmal red-zone performance continued this week. The Rams were 5/5, while the Raiders were a lowly 1/5. Kubiak told the truth about it.
"Yeah, it's very disappointing, especially with the emphasis we've put on it. When it comes down to it, we have to make plays down there when we have our one-on-one opportunities. We've got to make the throws, we've got to make the catches and it didn't happen."
Matt Gay missed a 51-yard field goal that he should have made, but the truth was that special teams, led by the great Joe DeCamillis, was not good; it was great. While there are no moral victories in the NFL, truth is still truth, and he asked Kubiak about how well they played.
"Yeah, I think that's been a standard throughout the year. Coach Joe [DeCamillis] and Tim [McConnell] and Marquice [Williams] do a phenomenal job, and that's a phase that we continue to rely on."
Kirk Cousins still leads the NFL in touchdown passes, but the 15-year veteran knows the red zone is an Achilles' heel for this team.
"I think it's really a team game, and we just got to all kind of do our part. I got to hit throws when they're there and there's just any number of things that come up. I think of the throw to Cody [White] on -- It was another fourth down. But I have to go back and watch, I felt like they matched Brock [Bowers] in the flat, and maybe if you give it to Brock, it's going to be a catch tackle. But does he able to break that tackle or lean forward for a first down?”
Cousins went deeper, explaining his thought process. “Those are the things that I don't know in real time. But I thought I'll work Cody one-on-one and then wish I had given him a ball that he could have maybe just stopped and gone up for, as opposed to running underneath it. So those are some plays that I think end up looming large at the end of the game."
Ever since the Raiders selected the young man NFL executives ranked as the best NFL QB prospect in the last four years, Fernando Mendoza, questions have come up about when he will play.
That isn’t abnormal, and with the Raiders now riding a four-game losing streak, they will get louder. Cousins knew that coming in and addressed it head-on.
“It's really the same every day that it was in March or April. I mean, nothing changes in the sense that if I'm not the best option, then I don't want to be out there either. I want our football team to have the best chance to win games. And if the first OTA, if that had become apparent, I would have been the first one to say, 'Yeah, you can't play me.' So nothing changes and the organization will do what they feel is best.”
Cousins elaborated even more, “But I feel that Fernando's [Mendoza] done a great job and has a bright future ahead. I'm going to try to go out there and play as well as I possibly can, help us win, and give him a great example to learn from until he does go out there eventually."
WR Jalen Nailor is a high-priced free agent that the Raiders desperately need to break out. He addressed the Silver and Black's lack of execution in plain terms.
"At the end of the day, it's all about executing the X's and O's. We just got to find a way to do that better and complement the defense or special teams. We got to play a whole complete game as a whole team."
Ashton Jeanty may not have had a great night toting the rock, but the Rams and a poor OL performance had more to do with that than he did. Still, Cousins targeted him eight times, and he caught all eight.
Cousins is not the problem, and the sophomore RB bragged on the play of his veteran signal caller.
“He's just super detailed every single week. Obviously, he's been playing this game for a long time, but he also has the confidence in everybody who's out there, running routes, and he gives them the chance to go make plays. You see it week in and week out from him."
This is not the Raiders of old. No one is holding their head down. Nobody is quitting; this team is angry, feisty, and hungry. Superstar Maxx Crosby made that abundantly clear.
"You've got to stay close together. The world is negative in general, the world, the media, all that. That's just part of it. Negativity is what sells, and the fanbase is going to obviously be very upset, and they have every right to be, but you can't feed into that. You can't feed into the negativity. You can't lose confidence in who you are because of noise. There's always going to be noise, good or bad, but you don't let that dictate who you are. You've just got to continue improving on a daily basis."
Nakobe Dean has been a terrific signing for this team, and he held no punches back when talking about his team and how to fix the losing streak.
"Most of it is all controllable; everything is controllable. Even if you making a play, you're not making a play. You got to control it. Just got to be real. It's a performing based league, got to perform. At this point, we know what we not good at as a defense, and we got to pick that up. And like I said, it…

title: 3 Instant Observations After Raiders' Blowout Loss to Rams
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders were hoping to snap their three-game skid on Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams. Quite the opposite happened, as a dormant Raiders' offense failed to get much going against a Rams team missing several critical players.
Sunday was another forgettable outing for Las Vegas, just two weeks after a similarly disappointing Week 5 loss to the New England Patriots. The Raiders' home performance against the Rams on Sunday was confirmation that the season's first seven games were accurate.
The Raiders can beat bad teams and compete with the league's best, but they need nearly everything to go right for them to beat the league's elite. Regardless of opponents' records or injuries, Las Vegas' roster is still a work in progress.
Sunday's loss to the Rams confirmed that their 3-3, and now 3-4, record is exactly what it is. Las Vegas has a high ceiling and a low floor. They are right in between good and bad, which is still an improvement from where they were at the end of last season.
Las Vegas has reason to be cautiously optimistic about things in future seasons, but they are what they are this season. The Raiders are an improved team, but need more additions to their roster to truly compete with the league's best teams.
However, they also made enough changes during this past offseason to no longer be amongst the league's cellar dwellers. They are experiencing the expected growing pains of a team in its first season under a new head coach and a ton of new pieces on both sides of the ball.
Las Vegas is right where they are supposed to be.
Anyone who has followed the Raiders in recent seasons knows John Spytek was tasked with rebuilding one of the league's worst collections of talent. Even with all of the moves Spytek and the Raiders made this offseason, they still needed more.
In terms of roster-building, no team had a more productive offseason than Las Vegas. The rebuild they have embarked on will take multiple offseasons. Still, the Raiders entered the season with several roster holes that needed addressing, but likely cannot be addressed until after this season.
The Raiders have undoubtedly improved on both sides of the ball compared to last season. However, at some point, last season stops becoming the metric by which a team is judged. Halfway through the season is about that point.
As much as they have improved, Las Vegas still needs more pieces on both sides of the ball. The plays that work against the Raiders' defense and the unproductive play of its offense against elite teams are largely due to not having the pieces.
The season's first three games showed the improvement Las Vegas made during the offseason. Their four consecutive losses have confirmed exactly where they need more roster help. The Raiders need help along the offensive line, in their defensive backfield, and at wide receiver.
However, that is no surprise to Spytek and the Raiders' front office. A four-game losing streak is far from ideal, but at least Las Vegas now knows where to improve moving forward.
If the Raiders' entire schedule included teams like the Miami Dolphins, New Orleans Saints, and Los Angeles Chargers, Las Vegas' offense would be among the league's best. However, even serviceable defenses will give this Raiders offense trouble as they refuse to make the one change that could help.
After three games against three of the league's worst teams and three of the best, Las Vegas' Week 7 outing gave them a chance to beat a reeling Rams team. Los Angeles was the first team Las Vegas has played that fell between the bad teams and the elite teams they have faced this season.
The Rams were missing several defensive players, yet the Raiders' offense still struggled to move the ball, let alone score points. Sure, Las Vegas' defense can play better, but what does it matter if their offense scores only six points in three quarters?
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Stock Report: Biggest Risers, Fallers After Falling Flat vs. Rams
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 7 outing against the Los Angeles Rams was flat and reminiscent of their Week 5 blowout loss to the New England Patriots. Few things went the Raiders' way against the Rams.
The Raiders look like an up-and-down team that is slowly becoming inconsistent. Still, even though they are inconsistent, they are still better than they were last season.
Below are the players who are trending up and down after Sunday's loss to the Rams.
Laube had arguably the best game of any Raider on Sunday, as he averaged nearly 40 yards per kickoff return through three quarters. Unfortunately, Las Vegas' offense could not do much of anything on Sunday, even with Laube's solid returns.
Las Vegas' defensive backfield allowed Matthew Stafford to complete nine of his first 10 passes and 12 of his first 14 passes. Stafford is the league's reigning MVP and has had similar games against much better defensive backfields. Still, letting Stafford start the game on a roll is not ideal.
Along with suspect coverage, the unit often missed tackles that could have limited yards after the catch. Las Vegas' defensive backfield was the team's most significant weakness at the start of the season. However, against the Rams and the New England Patriots, the unit left a lot to be desired.
The unit played better in the second half, but Stafford completed 17 of his 19 passes in the first half.
Cousins did not necessarily do anything wrong on Sunday. However, it is undeniable that the offense, as constructed, is limited with Cousins under center. If there is any pressure at all, Cousins' chances of completing a pass attempt decline rapidly and tremendously.
The offense has several other issues overall that continue to negatively impact Cousins. Las Vegas' offensive line has kept sacks to a minimum but has also allowed many pressures this season, which has impacted the time  Cousins has in the pocket. This would negatively impact any quarterback.
However, Kubiak has been tasked with finding ways to win with the roster that he has been given. If the Raiders' offensive line is so bad that Cousins can't succeed behind it, Las Vegas' coaching staff must either change the offensive line or change the quarterback.
Las Vegas has already replaced Jackson Powers-Johnson with Caleb Rogers. They won't bench Kolton Miller or DJ Glaze. Spencer Burford is an option to replace him along the line, but they don't have a dependable replacement, other than potentially rookie offensive lineman Trey Zuhn.
The Raiders spent the offseason moving Zuhn around to different positions along the line. For them not to put him on the field more often while needing better play alog the line speaks volumes about the coaching staff's confidence in their starting lineup.
Considering there is not much more they can do to improve the offensive line this season, the Raiders need a quarterback who can move in the pocket when protection breaks down. The Raiders need a quarterback who can confidently run past the line of scrimmage when it is time to do so.
Las Vegas doesn't have many offensive linemen who can protect Cousins better. Still, they have a quarterback who is mobile enough to make plays with his legs, accurate enough to complete tough passes, and talented enough to do both. In fact, they spent the No. 1 pick in the draft on one!
If the Raiders are content to beat bad teams and either fall a few plays short or completely fall flat against better teams, they should continue to keep Cousins as the starter. If they want to actually win games against good teams and push for a playoff spot, it is time to start Fernando Mendoza.
Or, the past four weeks are exactly what this year's Raiders will be against the league's better teams. Mendoza will struggle at times, but it will be better for the Raiders' long -term future than continuing to start Cousins. Coming close is not the same as winning.
Las Vegas has upcoming games against the San Francisco 49ers, Seattle Seahawks, and the Denver Broncos. Those are all good teams. They need to decide what their goal is this season. If they want to compete, start Cousins. Mendoza gives them a better chance to actually win.
Starting Mendoza does not guarantee anything at all. He will lose games, too. However, I personally believe they have a better shot at winning with Mendoza under center. Even his struggle will help move the rebuild along. It is time.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Poup's Perspective: Why This First Dolphins Win Indeed Was a Very Big Deal
full_text:
No, the Miami Dolphins are not suddenly going to make a playoff push because they got off the schneid and got their first victory of the 2026 season Sunday.
Or let's just say it's extraordinarily unlikely because we never want to say never.
And, yes, that elusive victory did come against the New York Jets, an organization about as dysfunctional as any in the NFL, as evidenced by the fact it's got the longest playoff drought (appearance, not win because that one belongs to the Dolphins).
But, make no mistake, it was cause for celebration, not just for the players and coaches who have been working hard under difficult circumstances to become at a minimum competitive and it most definitely was cause for celebration for anybody who cares about the Miami Dolphins.
Belief. Step inside the locker room after our Week 7 win 🔊 pic.twitter.com/i20aJA405x
The video of the Dolphins' locker room celebration was something, capturing the kind of excitement you normally see when a team clinches a playoff berth or even more.
But it actually was similar for the Dolphins and not just because it was Jeff Hafley's first win as an NFL head coach.
It was the first tangible reward for the vision that Jon-Eric Sullivan and Hafley have implemented, with strong performances by quarterback Malik Willis and members of a 2026 draft class that has looked promising from the start, with Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, Caleb Douglas, Will Kacmarek, Chris Bell and Michael Taaffe all contributing to one degree or another to that 28-25 win against the New York Jets.
In that Dolphins video, we saw Hafley talk about asking his offensive linemen about going for it on that late fourth-down to clinch the victory and making the call to proceed after getting the response he wanted.
Truth is, it was the only acceptable response from the big guys up front because the second an offensive lineman suggests at that time it would be more prudent to punt and let the defense hold the lead, that's the time to replace the head coach, that offensive lineman or both.
We still like the idea of Hafley there showing he was going to trust his players to deliver after they accept a challenge, and that's a big part of what this season is for the Dolphins.
Jets or not, the Dolphins played their best game of the season Sunday and just like that any talk of an 0-17 season disappeared.
That it was there in the first place only was evidence of just how massive a rebuilding project the Dolphins undertook by dumping so many high-end players and taking on so much dead cap space in one year.
But the Dolphins, with Sullivan in charge, sure look like they've done a pretty good job of restocking the roster, to the extent that they could do it in the first year with their cap restrictions.
As we've said before, this 2026 season for the Dolphins isn't about wins and losses, it's about progress and developments and being able to identify a nice group of young players with whom the team can move forward as part of the nucleus.
At this point, it sure looks as thought the Dolphins have a decent number of those core pieces to keep watching and the hope is we'll see more performances like we saw against the Jets.
That absolutely includes Willis, who accomplished more against the Jets by actually trying to do less — if that makes sense. It probably wasn't an accident that he was more efficient than in any other previous while not going downfield nearly as much.
Look at Willis' stat line against the Jets and you'll notice an uncanny resemblance to that of his second start with the Green Bay Packers in 2024.
Against the Jets on Sunday: 14-for-21, 208 yards, 2 TD, 0 INT, 130.7 passer rating, 37 rushing yards, 1 TD
Against the Titans in 2024: 13-for-19, 202 yards, 1 TD, 0 INT, 120.9 passer rating, 73 rushing yards, 1 TD
That was just one game, of course, and the key will be for Willis to do it again and then again after that.
And if there are more games like from Willis, there will be more wins.
And then the first 2027 draft pick will get lower and lower, and the same goes for more performances like we saw from Douglas or Taaffe or Ollie Gordon II or Greg Dulcich.
And that should be the goal for the Dolphins and the hope for Dolphins fans.
If the Dolphins can go, say, 5-12 and have to settle for eighth or ninth overall pick, it would be more favorable for the future health of the franchise than going 2-15 or 1-16 and having the second or even first pick.
The difference between two picks within the top 10 isn't nearly as significant as having found a group of key pieces with whom to move forward.
The win against the Jets was big. And the hope should be there are more to come, even if they're not that frequent.
The focus needs to stay on the 2026 season, not the 2027 draft. And that's how it should have been all along.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Four Winners And Four Losers From Miami's First Win Of 2026
full_text:
Rejoice if you'd like, as the Miami Dolphins are no longer winless, taking down the New York Jets in a 28-25 thriller. If you're on the side of the room that thinks going winless would be better for "draft capital," please chill out.
No team deserves to go an entire season without winning a game. The way things are shaping up, the Dolphins are still in contention for a top pick regardless, with the only winless team remaining being the Los Angeles Chargers.
So how did Miami pull it off? The best performance of the season by their offense from the jump, alongside doing just enough on the defense to slow the Jets down. It wasn't easy, but the idea of Jeff Hafley not getting drenched in Gatorade this season has been officially put to rest.
This has to feel great for Willis, coming off a shoddy performance against Cincinnati. Instead, he shushed a lot of the doubters with a strong performance - 208 yards and two touchdowns through the air, and 37 yards and a score on the ground. Make fun of the Jets all you want, but their secondary was generally considered a tough unit.
Nothing Willis did physically stands out from what we know about his skill set. Instead, the bigger difference is what he did mentally - he was much smarter with his decision-making in this game. Whether he had to pin the ball in the right spot or escape the pocket, he made the right call more often than not.
It's a very positive sign for the Dolphins. Their quarterback looks like he has confidence again, and the big question is whether he can keep it up against tougher competition, with New England and Detroit coming to town. If he can, the idea of Miami going for a quarterback in the 2027 draft gets a bit muddled.
The offensive line played fine, but not thanks to Jackson. One mistake stands out - a missed block on third down at midfield, which led to defensive end Nate Lynn's first career sack with less than a minute to go in the third quarter. Miami looked poised to get to field goal range, but instead were forced to punt. The Jets responded with a lengthy drive, going all the way to the 1-yard line.
That was the only major negative play Jackson caused, but every play matters more when the game comes down to the wire. It's no secret that he's been a liability more often than not for the Dolphins - Pro Football Focus certainly thinks so, as he's earned a 43.7 grade. Out of all 71 eligible tackles, that's the lowest of the group.
It really seems like the future of the offensive line is bright with the consistent performances that Aaron Brewer, Jonah Savaiinaea, Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor have orchestrated this season. But Jackson hasn't proven himself worthy of being mentioned in that group, and that missed block might be bulletin-board material for the Dolphins to consider going somewhere else at right tackle.
Douglas walked into the land of questionable turf and proved he was the most explosive player on the field. He wasn't targeted much - only three times - but made the most of his opportunities with two touchdowns on two receptions.
The first score was great, creating separation from Azareye'h Thomas in the back of the end zone to give the Dolphins their first lead of the season. However, his second touchdown was stellar - a 63-yard sprint down the left side of the field, narrowly getting by Nahshon Wright while staying in bounds for the score, giving Miami the 11-point cushion they needed in the end.
Believing that the outlook of this game changed the moment it was announced that Douglas would play was justified. He's a natural difference-maker even as a rookie, and a red zone weapon that Willis and the Dolphins could rely on for years to come.
Unfortunately, it's almost obligatory at this point to include Wright in these lists, as he's just not reliable for the Dolphins. Once again, he failed to get past New York's defensive line, settling for 8 yards on six carries. Wide receiver Malik Washington somehow managed the same amount of yards in just TWO carries.
At this point, what's the excuse for not giving another running back on the roster a shot to back up Ollie Gordon II? Whether it's Kaytron Allen, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers back on October 9,  or Carlos Washington Jr., currently on their practice squad, how can it be any worse?
It feels bad to hammer Wright this much, especially because there was a small chance he wasn't able to play in this game due to a nagging foot injury. But the production at running back falls off so much when he's on the field that it's almost become a guarantee. Having two reliable running backs instead of one would do wonders for this offense.
It might not look like Taaffe had a major game just by the box score - three tackles and a pass deflection is just OK. But the major highlight on defense for Miami came at the hands of Taaffe - a clutch interception, considering the Jets were knocking on Miami's red zone in the second quarter.
Despite the achievement, it was a pretty standard play. Geno Smith targeted Mason Taylor right off the play action, never looking away, even when shuffling to the right before throwing the ball. Taaffe read it the whole way, jumping the route and denying the Jets another score for the rest of the half.
Taffee is in elite company, being one of three rookies with multiple picks this season (Hezekiah Masses and Genesis Smith). He's the first member of the Dolphins to do so in the first six games of his career, since Patrick Surtain in 1998. You can't ask for much more from the 158th overall pick.
Overall, this was a successful day for the Dolphins in terms of getting to the quarterback, especially when compared to their earlier struggles to do so this season. Geno Smith took a beating, with two sacks and six confirmed QB hits. However, these came at the hands of guys like Chop Robinson, Malik Herring, Chris Johnson, and Zach Sieler.
Phillips, in comparison, had a very quiet performance - just one solo tackle, stopping Omar Cooper Jr. in his tracks after a 3-yard gain in the fourth quarter. Of all the playmakers in the trenches, he was the most pedestrian. He didn't hurt the Dolphins in the long run, partially because of Sieler's contributions, but it was disappointing to see nonetheless.
We debuted the first coach on one of these lists in Week 5, with STC Chris Tabor being named a loser. It's only fair to flip the script this week, and Hafley gets the honor for having his team ready to play from the start all the way to the finish.
It was a near-complete game on offense, defense, and special teams. Even with a 0-5 record, Hafley made sure his team gave everything they had against a division rival, and they did just enough to get the job done. It wasn't always perfect - the Dolphins committed five penalties but had no turnovers at the same time.
His signature moment was the decision to go for it on fourth down on the Dolphins' final drive to ice the game as opposed to punting the ball, which would have been the safer choice. Hafley noted postgame that he asked the offensive line if they wanted to do it, and trusted them when they said yes. It turned out to be the right decision as it was the prior two times they went for it on fourth down in this game.
This was overall a mediocre performance by Marshall. He was the victim of a ridiculous snag by Mason Taylor (son of Dolphins legend Jason Taylor) in the end zone for New York's sole touchdown in the first half.
The coverage on the play by Marshall wasn't bad, though he made the mistake of never looking back for the ball. Taylor simply went up and made a remarkable catch on National Tight Ends Day, no less. It was a quiet performance by Marshall all around, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but he'll definitely want to have that one play back.
Jake Gibson is a writer for the Miami Dolphins on SI. He began his sports journalism career with PantherNOW, the student newspaper at his alma mater, Florida International University, where he began as a sportswriter…

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 7 Snap Counts Stories: Tight End Time, Rookie Revelations
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 28-25 victory against the New York Jets on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by veterans Jalen Tolbert and Wille Gay Jr., the latter being kept out after missing practice time this week because of illness.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Kyle McCord and tight end Justin Joly. The rookie was active for only the second time this season.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies with the return of Caleb Douglas, even though he did replace fellow rookie Chris Bell as a starter. But fullback DJ Herman was back as a starter, joining Will Kacmarek at tight end, guard Kadyn Proctor, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- While it was Kacmarek who got the start, Greg Dulcich led all tight ends in offensive snaps with 42 compared to 29 for Kacmarek and 11 for rookie Seydou Traore. Before this game, Traore had played only one snap on offense, though head coach Jeff Hafley indicated he liked the progress he had seen from the fifth-round pick.
-- In his first game since the Week 2 loss at San Francisco, Douglas ended up playing 44 of the Dolphins' 65 offensive snaps, which wasn't as much as Malik Washington's 52 snaps but still a got play count in his first game back. And he sure made the most of his time on the field with his two touchdown catches.
-- With the Dolphins controlling the ball more than in any previous game (season-high 34:36 time of possession), Herman played a career-high 29 snaps on offense, topping the 27 he had against the Kansas City Chiefs in the home opener in Week 3.
-- Ollie Gordon II had his second 100-yard rushing outing in his third start and it came on 54 offensive snaps, which actually wasn't his highest total of the season. He played 61 snaps in the loss against Kansas City when he took over as the lead back following De'Von Achane's season-ending knee injury. The good news here is that Gordon clearly didn't slow down because he did some of his best work in the fourth quarter.
-- Newcomer Jared Wayne, claimed off waivers from the Houston Texans during the bye week, got 10 offensive snaps, the same number as Kevin Coleman Jr. Wayne's superior size and physicality makes him a more ideal option to help out with run blocking.
-- The Dolphins used Caedan Wallace as a sixth offensive lineman on five snaps, with mixed results.
-- With Douglas back, Chris Bell wound up with his second-lowest percentage of offensive snaps, his lowest since Week 2. Bell was on the field on offense for 31 snaps, less than half of the team's total.
-- Four players were on the field for all the team's 59 defensive snaps — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe and CB Chris Johnson.
-- Cornerback JuJu Brents was close as well, finishing with 53 snaps, but he left the game temporarily because of an injury. Brents opened with Jason Marshall Jr. on the outside and Johnson as the nick corner, a lineup the Dolphins used on about 50 percent of their defensive snaps.
-- Safety Dante Trader Jr. also left the game temporarily with an injury (shoulder), which led to Zayne Anderson getting 14 snaps on defense after he played only two against Cincinnati in Week 5.
-- Josh Uche, who continues what quietly has been a very solid season, again led the edge defenders with 43 snaps, compared to 38 for Chop Robinson. Malik Herring was next with 14, while Rodney McGraw was limited to seven snaps in his first game since being signed to the active roster.
-- On the interior of the defensive line, it's worth noting that Kenneth Grant played only 22 snaps in his second game of the season, the lowest total in the position group. Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips were pretty even with 31 and 29 snaps, with Zach Sieler as expected leading the way with 49.
-- In his return from injured reserve, rookie safety Kyle Louis saw his only action on special teams, which pretty much was to be expected (and we predicted it Saturday).
-- Speaking of special teams, Traore again led the way with 19 snaps, followed by 15 for Louis, Jackson Woodard, Julius Wood and Shaka Heyward. With Gay out of action, Woodard also got 29 snaps on defense when the Dolphins had a three-linebacker alignment.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to the Dolphins-Jets Matchup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins grabbed their first win of the season against the New York Jets. Their 28 to 25 victory marks the first of Jeff Hafley's Miami tenure, which means it's time to overreact to this game.
After not holding a single lead over the course of their first five games, Miami never trailed against the Jets. They remained in control through an ugly second half, and started what could be one of the craziest stories in NFL history.
On a very real note, the Miami Dolphins grabbed a win that required every ounce of effort they could muster. From a stellar offensive first half closed out by some masterful clock management to a timely fourth-down conversion to seal the victory, Jeff Hafley’s unit never wavered and won several crucial momentum-swinging moments. This win adds an exclamation point to a first half of a season that has felt about as promising as 1-5 can feel.
Malik Willis played what was easily his best game as a member of the Miami Dolphins, going 14 of 21 passing for 208 yards and two touchdowns, and adding another 37 yards and a score on the ground. His decision-making was consistently positive, as he understood when to take off, when to move off of his progressions, and when to fire into some tight windows.
On Miami’s first scoring drive, Willis made multiple throws late in the progression, including the first of two touchdown passes to Caleb Douglas. Just as important, though, was what we didn’t see on the stat sheet: turnovers. Miami won the takeaway battle on Sunday, and while Geno Smith threw an early pick to Michael Taaffe, Willis kept the ball out of harm’s way.
Willis looked like a completely different player than what we saw against the Cincinnati Bengals, and if he can start to stack strong performances, his window as the Dolphins’ franchise quarterback will remain cracked open.
One of Miami’s most promising rookies made his triumphant return on Sunday, and Caleb Douglas’ impact on the health of the Dolphins’ passing game is palpable.
His two catches, both of which went for touchdowns, showcased an element Miami simply doesn’t have with any of their other weapons. In the first quarter, Douglas dusted cornerback Azareye'h Thomas, pressing into his toes and snapping off a gorgeous route to the inside. Then, when Miami’s offense struggled to remain explosive late in the game, Douglas hit Minkah Fitzpatrick with a mean stutter-step, and followed it up with a tightrope act that resulted in a 63-yard score.
Even when he wasn’t making plays, it's clear that Douglas’ size and talent put the rest of the Dolphins’ receiving weapons in a more natural spot. Greg Dulcich had one of his best games, and Malik Washington made multiple nice plays underneath. Douglas’ impact cannot be understated, and his presence was key in Miami grabbing their first win.
The Dolphins’ rookies have largely met expectations, and one who has far exceeded them is safety Michael Taaffe.
Taaffe grabbed his second interception of the season against the Jets, triggering down on a crossing route by Jeremy Ruckert. It was an excellent play, and one Taaffe continues to make this season, trusting his instincts to fly towards the football.
Even as a rookie, there are a couple of plays in each game where it seems like Taaffe knows what the offense is running before it happens. His football IQ has made an immediate impact on the back end, and in a year where the primary goal is assessing talent, the former fifth-round pick looks like a gem.
In what ended up as potentially the biggest play of the game, former Miami Dolphins kicker Jason Sanders missed a 40-yard field goal for the New York Jets, and for the first time all year, the Dolphins played what looked like a clean game in the third phase.
In the first game after Jeff Hafley not-so-subtly called out Riley Patterson for not being able to get the ball into the end zone, Patterson’s replacement, veteran Zane Gonzalez and punter Bradley Pinion took turns on kickoffs and had the distance to eliminate the Jets’ potential returns. Gonzalez also went four for four on extra points.
Pinion had a mediocre punt that was salvaged by a nice bounce, but overall, special teams wasn’t a glaring negative, and that’s the first time all season that I’ve been able to say that.

title: Miami Dolphins Week 7 Instant Takeaways: Willis, Douglas Make Sure to End Winless Foolishness
full_text:
OK, everybody can forget about this idea — farfetched as it was — that the Miami Dolphins were going to finish the 2026 season at 0-7 and we can at least hit the pause button on this idea that the Malik Willis experiment already should be deemed a failure.
The Dolphins got that elusive first victory of the Jeff Hafley era Sunday and of course it was going to come against the New York Jets, just has it had in 2007 after Miami started off 0-7.
And while there were plenty of stars on this day — welcome back, Caleb Douglas — Willis absolutely was front and center.
His final passing numbers weren't necessarily overwhelming as he finished with 208 yards on 14 completions, but he provided exactly the kind of quarterback we saw during his stints with the Green Bay Packers that convinced Hafley and Jon-Eric Sullivan to bring him over.
It was the kind of performance that would make the Dolphins look to another position with their first-round pick in the 2027 NFL draft, a pick that still figures to be pretty high, and maybe we can stop debating — at least for a little while — whether it should be Drew Mestermaker or Arch Manning or Darian Mensah.
All along, we said Willis deserved the benefit of the doubt and a longer look before making definitive judgements about his viability as a starting quarterback, but if nothing else he bought himself more time with that performance — not that we would suggest he's cemented anything, either, just off one game.
As for the win and that silly notion the Dolphins could go 0-17, did anybody really think the Dolphins wouldn't be able to improve as the season moved along.
And, as we pointed out on numerous occasions, if the 2019 Dolphins could win five games after being outscored 163-26 (basically an average of 41-7) in their four games, yeah the 2026 Dolphins pretty safely were going to win a game here and there.
-- Douglas had only two catches in his return after missing three games with an ankle injury, but they both showed why he's the most exciting player on offense (outside of Willis) with De'Von Achane on IR. His first touchdown showed off his route-running ability as he faked the Jets cornerback out of his cleats with a quick jerky movement and then there was the fabulous YAC work on what became the game-winning touchdown. And how sweet was it that the Jets player he beat to turn a short reception into a long touchdown was none other than Minkah Fitzpatrick.
-- Major hats off to the running game for being able to close out the win after the Jets cut their lead with 3:24 left. It was five straight runs that produced two first downs, starting with a 14-yarder by Ollie Gordon II and punctuated by Malik Willis' sneak on fourth-and-1 where Gordon played a big role with his push of Willis. And even though it was risky, we tweeted before the call that the Dolphins should go for the win on that fourth-and-1 instead of going the conservative route and trying to pin the Jets deep. That's the kind of aggressiveness we want to see from Hafley moving forward.
-- Since we already mentioned Gordon, he continues to shine in the absence of De'Von Achane and looks like a feature back himself.
-- A couple of changes we noticed with the offense was that there weren't as man deep shots as in previous weeks, and that led to a better completion percentage for Willis. His decision-making was better, his scrambling again was a big factor, and he showed great awareness with his slide in bounds near the end of the first half to make sure the Jets wouldn't have much time left after they scored to make it 21-7.
-- It's pretty refreshing that we won't be talking about bad special teams play this week, isn't it?
-- It's actually ironic that the Dolphins ended up winning by three and the only missed field goal came from former Miami kicker Jason Sanders.
-- The Dolphins' new kicker Zane Gonzalez did a good job of putting the ball into the end zone on kickoffs, which limited the Jets' kickoff return opportunities and we'll take the defense starting at the 35.
-- The pass defense again wasn't great, but the secondary is the youngest unit on defense, so maybe it's to be expected to a certain degree. And that was a big-time veteran play by safety Michael Taaffe on his pick when he totally read the eyes of Geno Smith as he was scrambling.
-- Another big reason for the three-point win, of course, was the goal-line stand culminated by Chop Robinson's third-down sack when he absolutely didn't bite on Smith's play fake and Zayne Anderson took away Smith's short outlet. But it was Zach Sieler who made the big first-down tackle to start the whole thing, part of a really good performance by the D-tackle.
-- Yes, we have to factor in the quality (or lack thereof) of the opposition when dissecting this first Dolphins win, but then we also have to look at the quality of the teams against which they lost. So it works both ways. The Dolphins step up again in competition next week when they play host to the New England Patriots, but we'll continue to say the Dolphins will win a game or two this season that they're not supposed to win.
-- This game again the Jets was one of those that was deemed most winnable for the Dolphins, and that's how it played out. Now we don't have to hear anymore about going 0-17, we can table the draft talk for a bit because who knows exactly how high they'll wind up picking in the first round, and maybe most importantly we can just sit back and continue watching the development of the players before making premature determinations.

title: The Five Dolphins Players in the Spotlight in Week 7
full_text:
The MIami Dolphins will be back in action against the New York Jets on Sunday, and the mission will remain the same.
The Dolphins still are looking for their first victory of the season, but more importantly want to see progress and improvement, particularly after the disappointing showing in the last outing against the Cincinnati Bengals.
The matchup against the Jets, who also are in rebuilding mode though further ahead than the Dolphins, represents a good opportunity for Miami to get its first win of the season and end all talk of a winless season.
Most importantly, the Dolphins need for their young players to get better and organically that will give them a better chance to win as the season progresses.
With that in mind, here are the five players we'll be watching closely against the Jets:
QB Malik Willis — There might come a time when this no longer applies because it will have become apparent that the Dolphins need to look elsewhere to find a quarterback for the long run, but we're not there yet — even though a lot of fans already have given up on him. It's very obvious that Willis hasn't played well enough so far in 2026, but every game is a new opportunity and at some point the entire offense (hopefully) will start jelling a bit more.
WR Caleb Douglas — It's not often that the return of a rookie third-round pick is as anticipated as Douglas being back against the Jets, but this is where we are with the Dolphins. The clear lack of playmakers on offense was exacerbated by the loss of De'Von Achane to his season-ending knee injury and Douglas' performance in the Week 1 game against Las Vegas provided cause for excitement. Having said that, it's also probably not fair to expect big numbers from Douglas right away after he missed three games with an ankle injury, but there should be some kind of impact.
RB Ollie Gordon II — Gordon has averaged 94 yards in his two games since taking over as the starter, and now he'll be facing a run defense that's had some tough outings. Gordon could become the most important player on offense before this season is over.
LB Jacob Rodriguez — The second-round pick is off to a great start in his rookie season as a tackle machine, but he'll be challenged again in the pass game because the Jets have an uber athletic rookie first-round pick at tight end with Kenyon Sadiq, whose backup is another good young pass-catching tight end, Mason Taylor (son of Dolphins legend Jason Taylor). It won't be all on Rodriguez to limit the damage from the tight ends, but he'll be involved and will need to clamp down.
EDGE Chop Robinson — Jets quarterback Geno Smith has been very good this year at avoiding turnovers, but he'll also been criticized for taking too many sacks. This is where Robinson has to come in. Some of his analytics in the pass-rushing department are very good, but they haven't translated into enough impact plays. This is where he's got to make it happen.
