title: An Oral History Of Patriots WR Kyle Dixon's 'Twisted' Collegiate Baseball Career
full_text:
Kyle Dixon , the 26-year-old wide receiver from Carlinville, Illinois, was a multi-sport athlete in high school. He was a fantastic wide receiver, a fantastic defensive back and an even better pitcher.
His journey out of Carlinville High School started on the mound. It's now taken him onto the sidelines for the New England Patriots .
How in the world did that happen?
When you ask Dixon — now on the Patriots practice squad — he still doesn't really know. He can try to explain his winding road to the NFL, but there's so many stops along the way that sometimes he forgets a few things. So here's everyone else he's crossed paths with to help fill in the puzzle.
Kyle, born in 2001 to Tim and Monica Dixon, played baseball, football and wrestled in high school. He was excellent in everything he did. His coaches rave about his athletic abilities, almost to a fault.
Don Borgini, former Carlinville baseball head coach: "He was a fierce competitor."
Monica Dixon, Kyle's mother: "He excelled in all of his sports, but was looking for ways to improve his skills. He was always looking online for new training techniques."
Kyle Dixon: "Baseball was a little bit more special for me."
Maybe it was just the athletic juices in his veins, but Kyle always lived for the moment. The homemade pitchers mound that Kyle and his grandfather made in his backyard certainly helped. Once high school rolled around, baseball is where he found his groove.
Borgini: "Every coach on Earth wants a kid that wants the ball in the moment, and Kyle is certainly that guy."
Monica Dixon: "When he did get to pitch, I had a lot of anxiety. His dad could always handle that pressure better than me."
Kyle Dixon: "It was something I really enjoyed a lot."
Borgini: "In a sectional game, he had 19 strikeouts of the 21 batters and it was a tremendous performance by him that I won't forget. ... It is the top (game) for me as far as a pitcher goes (that I've ever seen)."
Kyle Dixon: "It might have been the last game I ever played (in high school). ... We ended up losing that game."
Borgini: "He was attracting a lot of attention."
Monica Dixon: "As parents, it was nice to see his hard work pay off when he got his scholarship. He earned it."
Kyle officially committed to Southern Illinois after a coach at a local JUCO help connect the two parties. But he had committed when Ken Henderson was the head coach. Henderson was fired and the abrupt change caught Kyle — who was on his way to vacation — off guard. Still, from the first day on campus, he stood out.
Lance Rhodes, Southern Illinois baseball head coach: "He wasn't the typical high school-sized kid that was coming to college. He was very put together, just a good looking kid. He definitely looked the part."
Kyle Dixon: "You don't really know what to expect as a freshman, especially with the new staff that didn't recruit you. It was an interesting start to college."
Rhodes: "He (was) just as big as the seniors. He had a ton of ability and he threw extremely hard."
Kyle Dixon: "I was off to a pretty good start my freshman year and then we stopped. We couldn't go into our facility to train with it being COVID. We couldn't go to a lot of the gyms or anything to work out."
His freshman year was mangled by the pandemic, where he only played in eight games. He pitched in four more as a sophomore, but a 22.50 earned run average plagued him. It was a pair of trying years for Dixon. He watched pro pitchers like Max Scherzer and Aroldis Chapman to try and figure out his form.
Kyle Dixon: "I became very focused on looking at MLB pitchers' mechanics and then trying to figure out how I wanted mine to look in regards to that. ... I think I became too focused on mechanics."
Monica Dixon: "I think he started putting more pressure on himself to be perfect and it just wasn't happening. As a parent, it was hard to watch."
Rhodes: "Kyle was always one of those guys that the feel of pitching was something that he needed to develop and work on, and I really think the COVID break in action ... was probably the toughest thing for him."
Kyle Dixon: "I kept thinking if I just keep figuring out whatever mechanical thing it is, then it's gonna play, then it's gonna click. The reality, that was the problem in and of itself."
He didn't want to stick around. After his scholarship was pulled, Southern Illinois Edwardsville — who did research on him coming out of high school — came calling.
Sean Lyons, SIUE baseball head coach: "I had a local umpire stop by our baseball office, come in and tell our staff there's this really good arm pitching, high school kid, not too far from here. ... When Kyle decided to transfer from (Southern Illinois) Carbondale, we kind of had a connection."
Monica Dixon: "We just went with the flow. He would always talk to us about moving and the reasoning for it."
Kyle Dixon: "Ironically, the pitching coach there was the one who recruited me to Carbondale. I was really comfortable with him."
But that coach would later take the head coaching gig for SIUE's softball program, and so Dixon was left with another surprising staff change. Still, his stuff on the mound never left.
Lyons: "He could throw the baseball in the lower-to-mid 90s. Sometimes command and where the location of that was sometimes a mystery for him. But when it was right, man, it was really good."
Kyle Dixon: "I wouldn't say I had a good year, but it was a better year. It wasn't good, but it was progress compared to the year before."
Lyons: "He had a skillset on the mound that could have possibly given him the option ... to play professionally as a baseball player."
Kyle Dixon: "Without a doubt."
Maybe it was time to get out of Illinois. Kyle called Lyons to let him know that he would be entering the transfer portal, a decision that he think took his coach by surprise. After having some summer league teammates hype up Georgia Gwinnett, Kyle then made the trip down south to a team that would go on to make eight-straight NAIA World Series appearances, a streak still active.
Jeremy Sheetinger, former Georgia Gwinnett baseball head coach: "When you see a kid that looks like Kyle and he's built like an Adonis, you know that there's something in there. ... We just feel like sometimes Division I schools, if a kid doesn't gave it, they get pushed to the side. We could spent a little bit more time with them."
Braxton Meguiar, former Georgia Gwinnett second baseman (who played baseball with Mike Vrabel's son, Carter, at Wabash Valley Community College in 2021): "I always remember Kyle's work ethic being different. He never changed. He never wavered, even when he wasn't having success."
Like the previous two schools, it just wasn't in the cards. Kyle had the yips, most commonly associated when throwing a baseball accurately becomes a chore. He'd walk away from sports entirely at the end of the season.
Kyle Dixon: "I was still kind of holding out optimism that I was going to be able to figure it out and turn it around."
Sheetinger: "He was good for a hit an inning, a strikeout an inning and a walk an inning. ... Kyle didn't make our postseason roster."
Meguiar: "He was having some control problems."
Sheetinger: "He's a guy that didn't impact us on the field, but he impacted with the kind of kid he was."
Kyle Dixon: "I just tried to be as good as a teammate as I could and really just not let what was happening to me affect my teammates. It's never fair to them. I think I was partially being myself and then having a little awareness about how not to act."
Monica Dixon: "We were sad for him. His love for the sport had faded. He was done completely."
Sheetinger: "Our pitchers threw footballs. But more people started watching the way Kyle would go catch footballs. You could see it coming together."
Baseball was in the rearview window. Instead, Kyle moved back home and picked up a job in sales, selling marketing tools for pool companies. All the while, filming workout videos to see what could come of his extra years of…

title: 4 Postive Takeaways From Patriots' Thursday Night Loss to Bears
full_text:
After falling to the Chicago Bears (5-2) on Thursday Night Football, many are quick to pick apart what went wrong for the New England Patriots and what needs to improve. Those conversations are centered around third down defense, tackling, wide receiver play, and other scrutinies from the Patriots 30-24 let down.
However, like most games, the Patriots still put out good tape, despite the outcome. Here's what New England did well on Thursday night and what we learned about this team moving forward:
With a diminished wide receiver room, the Patriots had to rely on other skill position players to push the ball through the passing game. One of the few that stepped up on Thursday was rookie tight end Eli Raridon.
Raridon hauled in 3 catches for 56 yards, including a 30-yard touchdown reception on a seam route in the third quarter. Maye targeted Raridon earlier in the game but was intercepted in the redzone.
Raridon now has more receiving yards (168) and touchdowns (two) this season than Kyle Williams, Efton Chism III, and A.J. Brown. The third-round pick out of Notre Dame has turned out to be a great investment by the Pats, and will carry the team's pass game well after Hunter Henry retires or moves on from New England.
The Patriots are among the top teams in the NFL for players listed as inactive on reserve lists. Entering Thursday night, the Patriots had 22 players on reserve lists, with nine of those players being starters.
Most notably, the Patriots were missing four guards on Thursday, and were forced to start Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor . While the two players struggled, New England's offensive line had a decent performance, only allowing two sacks on quarterback Drake Maye.
Additionally, the Patriots had three inactive cornerbacks on Thursday, including starter Carlton Davis. Christian Gonzalez was also listed as questionable ahead of the game with an illness, but played every defensive snap.
Lastly, the Pats were limited to just four wide receievers, with Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs on the injured reserve.
With Chicago being one of the NFL's top teams, and last year's second ranked NFC team, New England's competitive showing was impressive, considering the diverse roster they were forced to use.
Similar to the last point, injuries have been a major hurdle the Patriots have had to overcome this season. Each game, the Pats leave with more diagnoses than they entered with.
Last night, the Patriots stayed relatively healthy. With depth being an issue, the health of New England's team was crucial to staying in yesterday's game.
The only significant injury was suffered by defensive linemen Christian Barmore, who appeared to sustain an upper-body injury after sacking Caleb Williams late in the game.
With 10 days until they travel to Miami, Patriots players will have plenty of time to recover from past injuries.
Running back Rhamondre Stevenson was one of the best players on the field Thursday night, and was crucial to New England's ability to stay in the game.
The sixth-year player only ran for 22 yards against the Bears defense, but carried the ball six times, which is twice the amount of his counterpart, TreVeyon Henderson.
Most notably, Stevenson impacted the game through his pass-catching. He hauled in 5 receptions for 93 yards and was New England's leading receiver. His 48-yard touchdown reception to end the first half kept the Patriots within scoring distance of the Bears for the rest of the game.
RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️ 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW
This season, Stevenson has 25 more carries than Henderson and has notched 82 more yards than the second-year player. While Henderson has dealt with an ankle injury over the past two weeks, the only action he's missed was Week 1 against Seattle.
Stevenson's production and usage points to continued increase in carries and impact plays from the veteran Patriot.

title: Drake Maye's Interception Wasn't The Reason The Patriots Lost
full_text:
CHICAGO — The New England Patriots didn't win on Thursday Night Football, and yet, their quarterback had yet another great performance.
Drake Maye threw for 300 yards for the second time in three weeks, scored 3+ total touchdowns for the fourth-straight game and used his legs to extend plenty of plays behind a banged-up offensive line.
Did he throw a bad interception in the first half that took points off the board? Yes.
Was that play the biggest reason for the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears ? Nope.
Maye was hard on himself after the game, taking the brunt of the blame for the bad interception he threw to Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson. He was trying to hit Eli Raridon for a touchdown to cut into Chicago's 13-7 lead. Instead, he didn't put enough air on the throw and it was turned over.
“It definitely was a huge point in the game. It’s those plays, I talk about all the time," Maye said. "And those plays that can swing the game, can impact the game, and that was definitely one of them right there. I wish I definitely had that one back and a lot of plays.
"But got to give credit to them. They had a good plan on a short week and they got after us. ...  I know that was a big turning point in the game and I know I let my team down."
But the Patriots had a bigger reason for the loss, and it was from the other side of the ball. The Patriots really couldn't tackle all night, and according to Pro Football Focus, they missed 16 tackles. That's the most they've had in a single game since Super Bowl LX. Marcus Jones led the Patriots with five.
Chicago controlled the ground game with D'Andre Swift (22 carries, 78 yards, 1 rushing touchdown) and beat the Patriots' zone coverages all night.
“The tackling wasn’t good enough, not against this team," head coach Mike Vrabel said. "We knew coming in, certainly against this team, whether it’s Swift, (Luther) Burden, the quarterback. It just leads to extra yards and conversions. But, we fought. I would say that we need to turn the ball over and tackle better and those are fundamental skills."
Caleb Williams hit eight passes for 20+ yards, really stressing the secondary that was down three cornerbacks coming into the game.
Ultimately, the Patriots lost the game, not because of Maye's play, but because of everything around it. There wasn't a lot of production from the ground game or the wide receivers, penalties ran rampant and the defense struggled to bring anyone down.
And yet, Maye kept them in it. He shouldn't be the one receiving the pointed finger.
"He gave us a chance. He competed and I know he’d like to have that throw back to Eli but, I thought he really competed," Vrabel said. "Whether that was running around and scrambling or finding good places to go with the football. He gave us a chance. I know he’d like to have that one back and he’ll learn from it like he always does. I’m glad he’s ours."

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: 3 Takeaways From Saints' Loss to Steelers: Same Problems, Different Country
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints traveled across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to build momentum heading into their bye week and salvage their season. Instead, they returned home with its fourth loss in five games and it just seems like another repeating nightmare for Who Dat Nation.
New Orleans fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in Paris, dropping to 2-5 through seven games under second-year coach Kellen Moore . It was the NFL's first regular-season game in France.
Despite another efficient passing performance from quarterback Tyler Shough , the Saints struggled to establish their rushing attack, failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities and couldn't get off the field defensively when it mattered most.
The loss marked New Orleans' third one-possession defeat this season, reinforcing concerns about the team's ability to execute in critical situations.
Here are three takeaways from another disappointing performance from the Saints performance.
For all the attention surrounding Shough's development, New Orleans' inability to run the football continues to undermine its offense.
Sunday's performance might have been its most concerning yet.
The Saints finished with just 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts, averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Even more alarming, Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards on three attempts. However, he is a quarterback and that is not his job.
But for Alvin Kamara (six carries for five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries for six yards) to have more carries than rushing yards is disgusting.
It shows the lack of life in a running back room without a primary option, compounded by an offensive line struggling to create leverage.
That level of production is unacceptable for any offense regardless of the level of play, especially one relying on a young quarterback to consistently move the ball.
Pittsburgh's defense shut down the run, forcing Shough to carry nearly the entire offensive load.
Although Shough completed nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans could not consistently finish drives because it lacked balance.
The problems extend beyond one disappointing performance.
New Orleans has struggled to generate consistent production on the ground throughout the season, making the offense increasingly predictable against physical defensive fronts.
Because of the rushing problems, the Saints had to rely on Shough again.
Shough did everything you could ask of him, completing 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards and a touchdown. However, one costly mistake ultimately changed the game's complexion.
Trailing 13-10 at the start of the second half, New Orleans put together a 13-play drive that moved the offense inside Pittsburgh's 10-yard line as the Saints appeared positioned to take their first lead of the afternoon.
Instead, Shough threw a pass intended for Chris Olave , which Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson intercepted at the Pittsburgh 11-yard line.
The turnover erased a scoring opportunity and let Pittsburgh respond with a field goal, extending its lead to 16-10.
The interception proved costly, but it also highlighted the impossible position Shough has found himself in because of New Orleans' offensive struggles.
Despite completing nearly 79% of his passes, the quarterback could not afford even one mistake because the Saints had virtually no rushing attack to complement him.
That is an unrealistic expectation for any quarterback, much less one still developing at the NFL level.
Shough showed he could move the football against a Pittsburgh defense, distributing the ball effectively and keeping New Orleans competitive despite a one-dimensional offensive approach.
However, his play reinforced a troubling reality: when Shough plays well, the Saints can win; when he makes one mistake, the operation unravels.
Until Moore builds a credible run game and finishes drives, Shough bears an unreasonable load and New Orleans must create an offense where its quarterback does not need to be perfect to win.
Unless the Saints give Shough a credible rushing attack and adequate protection, they risk repeating a familiar chapter in franchise history: asking a talented young quarterback to overcome problems far beyond his control, much like Archie Manning decades ago.
Daniel Carlson 's fourth missed field goal in 11 attempts this season — a 52-yarder in the fourth quarter — kept New Orleans trailing in a 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, highlighting a critical special teams weakness for the 2-5 Saints.
The missed 52-yard attempt came while the Saints trailed 16-10 in the fourth quarter, keeping Pittsburgh's lead at six points. Carlson's 63.6% success rate contrasts with Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who converted all three attempts (28, 47 and 39 yards) for nine points.
The fourth-quarter miss was especially costly as New Orleans had already squandered a promising red-zone drive earlier in the second half. Instead of entering the final minutes needing only a field goal to tie or lead, the Saints remained six points behind.
Carlson's kicking struggles add to head coach Kellen Moore's bye-week concerns. For a team hampered by offensive inefficiency, defensive lapses and turnovers, unreliable special teams further shrink a narrow margin for error.
With three one-score losses this season, New Orleans cannot afford missed points. Sunday's loss highlights that the Saints lack the margin for error to overcome recurring scoring mistakes in tight games.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

title: Saints vs. Steelers: Injury Concerns Mount Ahead of Historic Paris Showdown
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints face several injury concerns as they prepare for Sunday's historic international matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France in Paris.
Running back Alvin Kamara and starting offensive guard Cesar Ruiz headline New Orleans' injury report, while Pittsburgh is monitoring several key defensive players, including T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
According to the Saints' official Thursday injury report , 11 New Orleans players were listed Thursday, with three missing practice and three participating on a limited basis.
The Saints (2-4) are looking to build momentum following Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped a three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Pittsburgh (4-2) enters the matchup seeking its second consecutive victory.
Both teams have several injury situations worth monitoring before Friday's final practice report.
The Saints' biggest offensive concerns involve Kamara and Ruiz, who have been dealing with back and knee injuries, respectively.
Kamara was limited for the second consecutive practice Thursday, leaving his availability worth monitoring heading into Sunday's game.
The veteran running back remains an important part of Kellen Moore's offense, particularly as New Orleans attempts to establish a more consistent rushing attack.
Ruiz's situation is potentially more concerning. The veteran offensive lineman missed practice Wednesday and Thursday because of a knee injury, raising questions about his availability against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
However, Jeremiah Wright played well in his absence during New Orleans’ win over the Giants last week.
Meanwhile, linebacker Kaden Elliss (calf) and edge rusher Anfernee Jennings (knee) were limited for the second consecutive day. During today's player roundtable , Elliss was asked if he would be available to play Sunday, and he said, "Yes."
There was some encouraging news for New Orleans.
Shough, who appeared on the report with a left-hand injury, participated fully in both practices. Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (head) and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd (illness) also practiced without limitations.
Running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) improved from limited participation Wednesday to a full practice Thursday.
Kicker Daniel Carlson missed his second consecutive practice because of a personal matter unrelated to injury (he and his wife are having a baby), while defensive lineman Davon Godchaux received a rest day Thursday.
Backup quarterback Spencer Rattler was added to Thursday's report with a knee injury but participated fully.
Pittsburgh is also dealing with significant injury concerns, particularly on defense.
The most notable development Thursday was star edge rusher T.J. Watt, who was limited with a calf injury after sitting out Wednesday's practice for rest.
Watt's status matters, given the Saints' offensive line concerns. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks through six games.
Fellow pass rusher Alex Highsmith remained limited with a groin injury, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward missed his second straight practice for rest.
The Steelers also received encouraging news about star cornerback Jalen Ramsey, who returned to practice on Thursday, albeit in a limited capacity. He missed Wednesday's session with a wrist injury.

title: Saints Stock Up: 3 Heroes From New Orleans' Win Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints earned a much-needed victory over the New York Giants as they broke a three-game losing streak.
Now, the Saints are in Paris as they turn their attention to the Pittsburgh Steelers to win consecutive games for the first time this season. However, it will be a tough task: Pittsburgh still has a solid quarterback in Aaron Rodgers at 42, and the offense has plenty of weapons; on defense, they have a solid pass rush.
After fully reviewing the Saints’ win over New York and looking at which players have been trending upward, here are three players whose stock is rising.
The Saints historically produce standout special teams performers, including Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis , and Steve Gleason .
Linebacker Isaiah Stalbird has continued that tradition this year, keying special teams unit success and executing the decisive sequence of the game.
Down 10-3 late in the second quarter, New Orleans seemed poised for a halftime deficit before Stalbird made a game-altering play on coverage.
The second-year backer stripped the ball from Charlie Jones on a kickoff return, which tight end Oscar Delp recovered to set up New Orleans inside the red zone.
Shough converted the takeaway into points, finding rookie Bryce Lance for a game-tying touchdown right before the break.
That turnover shifted game momentum entirely and helped spark a 31-point unanswered run that gave New Orleans a 34-10 lead before the Giants mounted a furious fourth-quarter comeback.
Cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. posted his top outing of the year in the 34-27 victory, accumulating seven tackles, two interceptions, and four pass breakups.
His effort earned an 88.4 defensive rating and a 90.2 coverage rating from Pro Football Focus, leading all team defenders in Week 6. Emerson was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his efforts.
Emerson held opponents to four catches on 10 targeted passes while picking off throws from Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy . The performance provided valuable depth after Kool-Aid McKinstry exited due to a migraine.
Rookie guard Jeremiah Wright capitalized on unexpected playing time against New York, filling in when starter Cesar Ruiz left with a knee injury in the second quarter.
If one thing is certain, the run game started to click when Wright went into the game as he added toughness to the interior line, anchoring a run game that piled up a season-best 175 yards. If you want to know how much of an impact Wright had? When the Saints ran to the right, they averaged just over 5 yards per carry. When they ran to the left? 3.1-yards a clip.
The fourth-round selection surrendered just a single QB pressure in his most extensive action of the season.

title: Cowboys or Eagles? Giants Fans Face a Rooting Dilemma on Monday Night
full_text:
In a cruel twist, New York Giants fans face a rooting dilemma ahead of Monday Night Football that, no matter which way they lean, feels a bit like a betrayal.
With Big Blue comfortably in first place, fans could be forgiven this week if they root for one divisional opponent to beat the other, right?
That’s the dilemma Giants fans face regarding the Monday night matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles, who square off at Lincoln Financial Field.
Both teams are 2-4, behind the Giants, who sit atop the NFC East at 4-2-1 and will remain there regardless of what happens on Monday night. (The Commanders, at 1-4-1, have a bye this week.)
So who should Giants fans root for in the Monday night game? On the one hand, the answer should be the Eagles, whose roster has been significantly gutted. An Eagles win over the Cowboys would drop Dallas, widely regarded as the Giants’ biggest competition for the division crown, to 2-5 on the year.
Then there is the argument that Giants fans would be better off rooting for the Cowboys, who, if they win, would improve to 3-4 and move into second place in the division, while dropping the Eagles to 2-5.
The answer may come down to personal preference, but outside of rooting for a tie, it probably makes more sense for Big Blue faithful to root for the Cowboys.
Remember, the Giants already have a 1-0 head-to-head advantage over Dallas, which gives them a tiebreaker edge.
Meanwhile, the Giants haven’t faced the Eagles yet. That game is on tap after the bye, and it will take place at Philadelphia’s “House of Horrors,” a.k.a. Lincoln Financial Field, where the Giants have not won a game (regular season or postseason) since Oct. 27, 2013.
To put that dry spell into perspective, since that last win as led by Eli Manning, the Giants have used 12 different starting quarterbacks.
This is a new era of Giants football, and head coach John Harbaugh has the players believing they can beat anyone at any place and any time.
That was evident in how they went after a Houston Texans team that, despite entering the Week 7 game with a 2-4 record, boasted a top defense and a surging offense, neither of which did much to stop a determined Giants team.
And did we mention the Giants won that game without their starting quarterback (Jaxson Dart), their starting inside linebacker (Tremaine Edmunds), one of their starting cornerbacks (Greg Newsome II), and one of their starting safeties (Jevon Holland)?
So maybe at the end of the day, it doesn’t matter who Giants fans root for tonight, unless it’s for the Eagles and Cowboys to somehow beat up each other physically.

title: John Harbaugh Offers Update on Giants’ Kicker Plans
full_text:
Despite missing field goals in two of his last three games, New York Giants placekicker Dominic Zvada does not appear to be in danger of losing his job.
That’s the word from head coach John Harbaugh, who, when asked if there were plans to try out new kickers, said, “We’re not going to be doing that right now, no.”
Zvada, a rookie who impressed the coaches with his strong leg and long-distance accuracy, started the season going 9-of-9.
But the magic seemed to run out on him in Week 4, in a rain-soaked game at Washington, when he missed three of his five field goal attempts.
He steadied himself last week in the loss to the Saints, a game after which Harbaugh cited a technique issue with Zvada’s plant leg as the culprit behind the Washington misses.
Against the Texans, though, Zvada was off target again, missing both attempts in the win.
All of Zvada’s misses have come from 50-plus yards, where he is 5-of-8 this season. Against the Texans, after he showed signs of struggle again, the Giants decided to punt rather than attempt another long-distance field goal after reaching the Texans’ 37-yard line.
Zvada and the Giants lead the league in field goal attempts from 50 or more yards. Zvada’s 62.5% conversion rate on those long-distance field goals ranks 18th among kickers, but his overall field goal conversion rate (72.2%) ranks 27th.
"I think from a confidence standpoint, I believe you don't have to check in with him, you just got to remind him that he is damn good," assistant head coach/special teams coordiantor Chris Horton said of Zvada two weeks ago.
"That's one of the things I think when you believe in your players again, and you remind them that they're here for a reason and you trust in them. You’ve just got to remind them of those things. From a confidence standpoint, that's solely on him and him understanding that I can go out there and I can do this."
The Giants are on their bye this week. Harbaugh said the players were in on Monday for a film review session and will be in again on Tuesday for a light workout before being given Wednesday through Sunday off for the bye.
“We’ll take advantage of that as much as we can; we have five full days plus a little bit for them to rest, recover, all three phases, you know, mind, spirit, body. And then we’ll be back Monday afternoon to start on the Eagles.”

title: Giants Offensive Player Grades: McCarthy Stays in Control as Run Game Rolls
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ 27-21 overtime win against the Houston Texans was a masterclass in “slow and steady wins the race.”
Led by quarterback J.J. McCarthy, who made his first start for Big Blue, the Giants offense dominated a very good Houston Texans defense, racking up 420 yards and 22 first downs while averaging an impressive 6.5 yards per play.
The Giants running attack, challenged by head coach John Harbaugh to step up, did just that, totaling 188 yards on 34 carries (5.5 yards per carry). And all four of the Giants’ scores came on the ground.
The Giants pulled off an inspiring win, though many thought they were heading into the lion’s den without a chance; instead, they emerged with a win to improve to 4-2-1 and strengthen their hold on first place in the division.
Let’s get into this week’s grades.
After last week’s scintillating fourth-quarter performance, McCarthy came out as the team’s new starter, slinging it again, though in a much more controlled manner.
To throw the ball into so many tight places and never once put it in danger is mind-boggling, but that’s what this kid has done through five-plus quarters with the Giants.
McCarthy’s first half, while still playing in a new offense, in enemy territory, against one of the league’s best defenses, was close to spectacular. His 9-of-12 first-half throws show he wasn’t throwing it all over the ballyard; he threw it under control, with timing, accuracy, and audacity.
On his third throw of the game, he went up top to Malik Nabers for 42 yards on the throw that truly opened up the field. He then threw another 17 yards to Nabers, 49 yards to Malachi Fields, 29 yards to tight end Thomas Fidone, and another 27 yards to Nabers.
What did all this downfield throwing do? It opened up things for the running game (188 yards total on the day), and they were legit rushing yards with not a single scramble to pad the total.
Why did the Giants run the ball so well against the league’s third-ranked run defense? How did the Giants earn a 35:50-to-26:45 time-of-possession edge and a total net-yard advantage (420 to 237)?
With McCarthy attacking Houston’s vaunted corners downfield early and often, the entire defense had to back off.
The quarterback’s second half wasn’t quite as sharp, but it wasn’t needed. And when it was needed, McCarthy answered the bell.
A favorite throw by McCarthy was the 3rd-and-9 deep out, where he hit Fields in stride to beat a blitz and get the first down, right before Cam Skattebo’s touchdown run took a fourth-quarter lead.
This week wasn’t one of those crazy up-and-down passing affairs that seem to dominate the league. It was a controlled demolition by the Giants, with their quarterback managing the game smartly, making every throw that had to be made, and quarterbacking a running attack that wore down the Texans by game’s end.
When you have a quarterback who can make every throw, and isn’t afraid to try every throw, then you have a chance to open up the defense and win any way you like. McCarthy won Sunday’s game from the pocket, and that’s where we prefer to keep him.
However, he also has the mobility to run an RPO (two this week, both successful handoffs) and scramble away from pressure and hurt the defense with his legs. He truly is a quarterback for the modern game and looks like a real value for the Giants, who gave up a fifth-round pick to get him.
Contributing four successful “tush-pushes” (including a touchdown) and one nifty handoff to Cam Skattebo on another fake tush-push that went for 19 yards on a key second-half 4th-and-1 is pretty good production for the team’s backup quarterback.
Also, give credit to the coaches for keeping Winston in the offense and recognizing one thing he does quite well: short-yardage quarterbacking.
It boggled the mind that Skattebo was flagged for unnecessary roughness for lowering his head in traffic and annihilating a safety, who also lowered his head on the play. Incredibly, the officials can throw this flag and yet ignore the scores of defensive players lowering their heads into tackles.
Skattebo’s sin is that he does it so aggressively and finishes his hits with a toughness not often seen from the running back position that it doesn’t seem fair to the defense.
You know what? Too bad. Physicality is what Skattebo does best. You rarely see the NFL write rules that so clearly favor the defense, but this is one of them.
As for Skattebo’s game, it was classic ground-and-pound. He was responsible for three big yardage plays: the 19-yard fake tush-push, the 16-yard fourth-quarter rushing touchdown (his best run of the day, in which he broke and shed at least five tackles on his way into the end zone), and his 42-yard burst in overtime that set up the Giants for the winning score.
The big plays are huge, but the little plays into the teeth of the defense eventually wore the Texans down. It was power running at its purest, a style that Skattebo is built for.
He came up gimpy at the end of that overtime run after tweaking his hamstring, which hopefully will heal over the bye week.
Also in need of some bye-week R&R, Tracy was forced out of the game late in the second quarter after suffering a hamstring pull that ended his day.
Before that, Tracy made a couple of solid plays with the ball in his hands, the best one a neat cut near the goal line to avoid a tackler and get into the end zone for the team’s opening score.
Tracy’s numbers were modest: 6 carries for 15 yards and 1 catch for 2 yards. He seems to have locked down the third-down role while also serving as a rotation back.
With the other two backs suffering in-game injuries, “Mr. Reliable” had to step into the breach and calm everyone down.
Singletary caught 3 balls out of the backfield for 14 yards and had another 41 yards on the ground, the big play being his 30-yard game-winning jaunt around left end to finish things off for the big underdog visiting team.
This veteran always brings an often-needed calming presence to his many younger teammates.
With him logging his fourth straight 100-plus-yard receiving game, Nabers has become one of this team’s go-to players who always wants the ball in big situations.
We were thrilled early on when he beat single coverage deep and came down with the long ball for a 42-yard punch-in-the-mouth moment to the Texans.
Nabers never quite got deep again, but the threat opened up space for catches of 17 and 27 yards, plus a bunch of short but positive completions.
Nabers finished with 7 catches for 111 yards as he continued to take the league by storm.
He did have a rare drop over the middle on one of those J.J. McCarthy bullet throws, but Nabers’ route-running remains as clean and reliable as it gets.
Having his best game as a pro, the hard-blocking rookie (watch his take-out of two Houston defensive backs on the game-winning run) finished with 4 catches for 83 yards.
The big play was a clean down-and-out route: the quarterback got the ball to him right out of his break, with just enough time to shrug off his man.
Fields then took the ball upfield along the sideline for another north-south 20 yards after contact, refusing to go down; he never did go out of bounds. This big chunk play was the offense’s longest of the day (47 yards).
Fields also caught balls for 14 and 20 yards. Though we’re still waiting on those downfield, boundary jump balls that he allegedly specializes in, Fields continues to run clean routes and make his quarterback look good by catching everything that comes his way, including low throws.
It’s so nice to have reliable receivers who actually catch the ball. Fields is also showing some intriguing yards-after-contact running ability that wasn’t previously advertised.
Still struggling to find his way into this offense, Mooney is a player we think the coaches need to force the ball to, as his speed is undeniable.
The problem is that Mooney is so slight that he doesn’t seem able to take a hit.
He was bulldozed on his lone 4-yard catch and failed…

title: Giants Winners and Losers: Skattebo, McCarthy and Banks Find Redemption in Houston
full_text:
Redemption is the theme of the 2026 New York Giants .
Quarterback J.J. McCarthy is looking for a second chance after underwhelming with the Minnesota Vikings. Cornerback Deonte Banks wants to prove that he is, in fact, a first-round talent despite a rough few years.
John Harbaugh wants to compete for another championship after a disappointing end to his Baltimore Ravens head coaching tenure.
And Cam Skattebo aims to establish himself as a legitimate NFL lead running back after getting quasi-benched in last Sunday’s loss to the New Orleans Saints.
These individuals, and Big Blue as a whole, found redemption in a 27-21 Week 7 overtime win over the Houston Texans.
After an embarrassing outing, the Giants went to Space City and showed they could learn quickly from their mistakes. Let’s spotlight some of the players who helped bring about this turnaround, along with the few who stumbled in Houston.
The second-year running back appeared to have lost his coaching staff’s faith after getting no touches against the Saints, but he just earned a big chunk of it back.
Skattebo showed the intensity and physicality that made so many fans fall in love with him last year, and he also played with more explosiveness than most people are used to seeing.
The 24-year-old bruiser carried the ball 17 times for 124 yards and a touchdown. He refused to go down, breaking multiple tackles on his way to a go-ahead score in the fourth quarter, and then erupted for a career-high 42-yard rush in OT. Skattebo released weeks’ worth of frustration on the Texans.
He will now take the bye to recover from the apparent hamstring injury he sustained on that aforementioned clutch run. Assuming the former fourth-round draft pick is healthy enough to play, he should be New York’s No. 1 RB in Week 9.
McCarthy did not account for any of the Giants’ four touchdowns, but he was undoubtedly one of the biggest reasons they strengthened their first-place position in the NFC East. The 23-year-old quarterback is maturing before our eyes.
McCarthy got away with a couple of reckless throws against New Orleans, but he exercised superb precision and touch versus Houston. Passes that may have been incomplete a season ago are now difference-making completions.
The No. 10 overall selection in the 2024 NFL Draft completed 20-of-28 passes for 252 yards. He rushed for just a yard, but by threatening to run, McCarthy helped open up the Giants’ offense.
New York’s Dennard Wilson-led defense was truly fantastic. A seemingly surging Texans offense got thoroughly shut down. Abdul Carter did not need a sack to torment his opponent.
The impact pass rusher once again drew two offensive holding penalties and kept C.J. Stroud from getting comfortable in the pocket. He registered six total pressures , per Pro Football Focus, and now has 27 on the season.
With outstanding elusiveness, Carter will work his way through linemen and into the QB’s airspace. As we have said many times, if this disruptor keeps getting past blockers, the big sack numbers will come. Most importantly, his on-field presence is leading to winning football.
Banks has now played five games for the Giants this season, a big enough sample size to convince this writer that he has indeed revived his career under Harbaugh and Wilson.
The 2023 first-rounder looks unrecognizable from the cornerback who frequently cost New York during the Brian Daboll-Shane Bowen era.
He is playing like a genuine high-end CB. Banks smothered star wide receiver Nico Collins and allowed just three receptions for 10 yards on Sunday, with one of those receptions allowed to Collins, who gained only four yards on the play.
Banks turned his head, stayed with his guy, and recorded two passes defended. In a one-score game, an active corner is vital.
Fans hoped that the revamped Giants could light a spark in Banks. Nobody expected him to be this dominant, however.
Malik Nabers posted his fourth straight 100-yard performance and obviously deserves copious praise, but I want to give rookie WR Malachi Fields his flowers after a breakout showing.
The 6-foot-4, 222-pounder was lethal along the sidelines and did not go down easy. He notched a season-high four catches for 83 yards. Fields and McCarthy were not on the same page during a pass play that turned into an interception in Week 6, but they got along swimmingly against the Texans.
New York general manager Joe Schoen traded for the former Notre Dame pass-catcher to beef up the offense, and although he has taken some time to get settled, Fields is starting to elevate the passing game.
A standout summer performer is now struggling after another rough day. Undrafted rookie kicker Dominic Zvada missed field goals from 56 and 44 yards, and he also left John Harbaugh reluctant to attempt field goals in the second half.
The second miss came at the end of the second quarter and could have potentially cost Big Blue a win. Zvada has brought back the franchise’s kicking woes and has been a liability for much of October.
Now 13-of-18 on his FG attempts, this embattled talent may face some competition in the near future.
As long as Andrew Thomas stays on the field, good things are supposed to happen. The veteran left tackle has not competed at an elite level for most of the campaign, though he is battling a groin injury that is clearly hampering his play.
But if Thomas is active, he has to be fairly scrutinized. The 2022 second-team All-Pro allowed a Danielle Hunter sack and surrendered two pressures to a talented yet underachieving Texans defensive line. Hopefully, the week off will help.
If not, the Giants may have a season-long problem.
Dru Phillips was called for two penalties and mounted little resistance in coverage, allowing three receptions for 57 yards. He remains an effective tackler and solid blitzer, but he is sometimes exploited in the secondary.
This former third-round pick needs to improve during the bye.

title: Four Downs: Biggest Factors in Giants’ 27-21 OT Win Over Texans
full_text:
The New York Giants have fully embraced a love for gritty finishes under head coach John Harbaugh.
For the fifth straight week, the Giants’ game came down to the final minutes of the fourth quarter or overtime. It didn’t go the way Big Blue envisioned last Sunday at home against the Saints, but they flipped the script on the road with a big 27-21 overtime win over the Houston Texans to improve to 4-2-1 heading into their bye.
Against another tough team with a relentlessly aggressive defense, it certainly wasn’t easy for new starting quarterback J.J. McCarthy and the Giants to pull off the big plays that decided the game.
Still, Harbaugh’s group stayed composed under another week of late pressure, thanks to these four storylines, which authored the defining moments.
J.J. McCarthy stepped into a tough spot last Sunday with the Giants trailing big, but his first real reps under center helped him form instant connections with Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely as the trio tried to mount a comeback.
Heading into this week’s matchup with the Texans, Nabers knew he had to get open for his new starting quarterback and help him make plays. He wasted no time, hauling in a huge grab on the Giants’ first offensive possession.
On the eighth play of the drive, with McCarthy moving the huddle efficiently through Houston’s defense, the pair connected for the second time on a gorgeous 42-yard shot that Nabers brought down to the Texans’ 2-yard line before getting forced out of bounds.
Nabers, an LSU product, has been on a tear since Week 4, posting four consecutive games with over 100 receiving yards, the longest active streak in the NFL. He also tied the streak Odell Beckham Jr. posted in 2014.
He faced a tough matchup, with another Tiger product, Derek Stingley Jr., guarding him for most of the contest. Even so, he met his self-proclaimed mission early and helped McCarthy find the confidence to keep slinging it all day against a Texans defense that wasn’t laying down.
After several weeks of lackluster showings by the running game, Harbaugh challenged his running backs to step up and take the RB1 job.
They answered the bell, finishing with 180 of the team’s 188 rushing yards on the day, an average of just over 6.2 yards per carry by the running backs alone.
Cam Skattebo, who was quasi-benched last week, rewarded his head coach’s faith by recording a career-best 124 yards on 17 carries and a touchdown.
That’s a 7.3 yards per carry average for those keeping score at home, and while a long of 42 accounted for a big chunk of those yards, it was still good to see the Giants running game, which had again fallen into a rut, come out and have such a big impact on the outcome.
And how about Devin Singletary? After being banished to the inactive list for three weeks earlier in the season, Singletary delivered the winning score in overtime with a beautifully executed 30-yard touchdown run in which he showed patience and vision as a runner.
It’s probably safe to say that the man nicknamed “Motor” won’t be seeing the inactive list again this year so long as he’s healthy.
As impressive as Matt Nagy’s offense has looked with three different quarterbacks under center, the Giants hadn’t shown much creativity with trick plays until the third quarter of Sunday’s game.
One of the Giants’ smartest gambles came in the final minute of the third quarter, with the offense stuck at 3rd-and-1 at their own 29-yard line. New York ran Jameis Winston a few times to handle the short-yardage attempts and was pretty successful, thanks to his size and some extra push from the backfield.
The Texans defense sensed a trend in the Giants’ approach, which forced Nagy and company to switch things up and catch the opponent off guard. On the fourth play of the drive, Winston took the handoff as if he was going to charge forward, then quickly shifted it to Cam Skattebo behind him.
Houston crashed down expecting another quarterback sneak, but instead watched Skattebo bounce to the outside and scamper 19 yards downfield for the first down.
A stop by the Texans could have pinned the Giants deep in their own territory and likely forced them to punt back to the home team, whose offense was finding a groove.
Instead, the Giants’ run game took over the drive, and Skattebo capped it 10 plays later with a 16-yard scamper to take a 21-14 lead with just under nine minutes in regulation.
Deonte Banks had one job as he lined up in front of Texans receiver Nico Collins: shut Houston’s best weapon down and force quarterback C.J. Stroud to attack the Giants’ defense with his other pass catchers.
Collins came into Week 7 averaging 80.8 yards per game, but with the rejuvenated Banks in his way, the All-Pro receiver was nearly held to a goose egg. Banks allowed just two catches for 6 yards to Collins, one of the lowest numbers in an individual matchup this season.
Stroud certainly tried to get his veteran involved as a sparkplug for the Texans’ struggling offense, targeting him five times, the second-most among Houston’s pass catchers. Still, Collins wouldn’t secure his first catch until the 9:30 mark of the third quarter, followed by his second and final grab on the next play.
Collins’s slim effort wasn’t even enough to secure a first-down conversion on that drive, and the Texans were forced to punt in three plays and nine yards. It might have been one of the best displays of man-coverage football from a Giants defender all season.
In total, Banks finished as New York’s fourth-highest-graded defender , allowing three catches on six targets for 10 yards in all while deflecting two passes.
The Texans finished with their lowest total passing yards (153). Without a healthy running back room to try to attack the Giants’ weaker run defense and without their top target contributing chunk plays, they were largely sitting ducks as Dennard Wilson ratcheted up the pressure down the stretch.
Banks is quickly earning a new contract with his play in 2026, and it’s a great sign for a secondary marred by injuries and poor coverage metrics in recent seasons.

title: Harbaugh’s Giants Show What They’re Made Of
full_text:
In past years, a season-ending injury to the starting quarterback or key pass rusher, or a gut-punch loss to a team they were supposed to beat, might have reduced the New York Giants to a pile of rubble.
But not John Harbaugh’s Giants. They’re operating with one of the league’s worst injury situations , one that has robbed them of several key players, including starting quarterback Jaxson Dart, outside linebacker Brian Burns, and inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds, among others.
And while the team is far from a juggernaut, Harbaugh’s scrappy Giants have fought and clawed their way to last year’s win total while also padding their lead in the NFC East after a hard-fought 27-21 overtime win against the Houston Texans.
“Man, that was a players’ win in every way — blocking, tackling, special teams, covering kicks, pass game, operating, getting stops when we needed stops, fighting back from adversity,” Harbaugh said after the game.
“But just play one play at a time, as well as you can, regardless of the last play, with no thought for the next play, as hard as you can. As [OLB] Abdul Carter told the guys at halftime, ‘No matter what, empty the tank. No matter what, come back in here with nothing left,’ and that’s what they did.”
The Giants, who have now played two overtime games in three weeks, have shown resiliency, maturity, and determination. When they get punched in the mouth — and they have a couple of times this season — they don’t wave the white flag.
They take their lumps and come back ready to serve a helping of their own.
“It tells you who they are. You might have thought before the game, we’re going to find out about our guys. We’re going to find out about who they are, and we did, and you saw it. They did, they took the bull by the horns, and they got the job done,” Harbaugh said.
A look around the Giants locker room offers so many individual stories of resiliency, starting with running back Cam Skattebo. Dealt a “quasi-benching” a week ago for carelessness with the ball and his assignments, Skattebo zipped his lip, went to work, and produced a career-high 124 yards on 17 carries and one of the four rushing touchdowns the Giants had that day.
Then there is Devin “Motor” Singletary, who finished with 41 rushing yards on five carries and the game-winning touchdown, a 30-yard dash. Singletary, who took a pay cut to stay with the Giants, found himself squeezed out of the running back rotation for three straight weeks.
He didn’t complain and kept working to earn his chance. And when it came, he made the most of it.
“I can’t say enough about ‘Motor’ [RB Devin Singletary], and that’s on me. That’s on me. We were looking for the formula, and he was the odd man out for several weeks. Not because of anything he did or didn’t do; he just was the odd man out, and that’s exactly what I told him,” Harbaugh said.
“He asked me, ‘What can I do?’ I said, ‘There’s nothing you can do; you’re doing everything you can do, and your time will come.’ It was going to come. And look where it came, right there, and he came through.”
Inside linebacker Micah McFadden is another who rose to the occasion. A starter until a season-ending foot injury last year, McFadden never got the chance to reclaim his starting job once the team signed veteran Tremaine Edmunds and drafted Arvell Reese.
But McFadden, whom Harbaugh always called a starter, was right there to step into Edmunds’ role as the defense’s “quarterback” when Edmunds was lost for the rest of the season with a shoulder injury.
McFadden’s first start resulted in a 10-tackle day (all solo efforts), plus two tackles for loss and a quarterback hit, the most productive stat line of any Giants defender.
“He had a bunch of tackles. Then he made the first-down tackle when they ran that sweep play; he shows up out of nowhere and tackles it for a one-yard loss, and that set the tone. That’s really what got them off the field and gave us a chance,” Harbaugh said.
There are so many more stories of resiliency.
Quarterback J.J. McCarthy, whose career was on life support in Minnesota before he was traded to the Giants for a fifth-round draft pick a few weeks ago, has looked right at home in this offense, finishing 20 of 28 for 252 yards with no touchdowns and no interceptions.
Cornerback Deonte Banks, who many thought was on his way out the door at the end of last season, has played lights out since winning the starting cornerback job. This week, with Greg Newsome II sidelined with a concussion, Banks drew the Texans’ top receiver, Nico Collins, and limited him to one catch on four targets for just four yards.
“I probably should have given him a game ball,” Harbaugh quipped. “Maybe he’ll get defensive player of the game. But he was on it, man. He had so many tight coverages. You have to cover these guys tight, especially in breaking routes, man and zone, because his quarterback is really accurate, especially when he moves in the pocket.”
Other contributions helped make the win possible, but the common trait they all share is resiliency. And that starts with Harbaugh and his staff, who have worked to implement a support system that builds players up rather than tears them down.
“I would say just a lot of moments stacked on top of each other because they just didn’t bat an eye and they continued to work hard and fight. Every type of situation, they met the same way,” he said when asked if there was a moment when he realized the team had the mental makeup to withstand adversity the way it has.
Moving forward, Harbaugh said players who underwent season-ending surgery will be allowed to travel with the team.
“I just think it’s an ongoing type of a thing,” he said. “That’s how you build — it’s shared experiences. It’s fighting through all these things together that draws people close together, and that’s how a team is built.”
For now, Harbaugh’s scrappy, first-place Giants will go into their bye week with their effort and resiliency rewarded, and with a chance to heal up for what should be a tough second half of the schedule.
“Now, you’ve got to make something of it,” Harbaugh said. “It doesn’t mean anything if you don’t build on it, right? But it doesn’t mean we’re going to win a championship yet. It means we have an opportunity, though. We have an opportunity to get ready for the next two games starting with Philadelphia, and then a quick turnaround, so we’ll be thinking about two games as a coaching staff over the bye week.
“The two most important games of the season will be coming up after we come back from the bye, which will set the direction for the rest of the season, really. But we’re going to be in this thing until the end.”

title: J.J. McCarthy Delivers a Winning Debut as Giants Starter, Beating Texans in Overtime
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy is clearly enjoying his change of scenery.
Making his first start for New York since being acquired via trade with the Minnesota Vikings on Sept. 28, McCarthy, the 10th overall selection in the 2024 NFL Draft, led the Giants on four scoring drives en route to a 27-21 Week 7 victory in overtime against the Houston Texans at Reliant Stadium.
McCarthy completed 20 of 28 passes (71.4% completion) for 252 yards, earning a passer rating of 99.1. Across four quarters and overtime, the 23-year-old showcased his multifaceted skill set while maintaining a calm, cool, and collected demeanor.
McCarthy gave the Giants (4-2-1) exactly what they needed to topple the Texans. Despite throwing neither a touchdown pass nor an interception, the Giants’ new starter had only one number on his mind.
“Truly the only stat I care about is going 1-0,” McCarthy said from his postgame podium. “I couldn’t care less how we get it done. At the end of the day, you want to perform well. You want to execute well.”
“I’m as happy as I can be,” he added. “Whether I’m throwing the touchdowns, I’m as happy as I can be. At the end of the day, all that matters is getting that victory.”
Though he may be best suited to an offense built on zone reads, designed runs, and RPO packages, McCarthy showed his prowess in the deep passing game during the first half. The former Michigan Wolverine connected with star receiver Malik Nabers for 42 yards, wideout Malachi Fields for 47, and tight end Thomas Fidone II for a 29-yard near-touchdown.
When the Giants’ running game came to life in the second half, McCarthy adjusted his approach, using the underneath area to let the running backs find productive yardage.
All the while, McCarthy exuded the look and feel of a team leader while staying focused on his job.
“It’s the same thing that goes through my mind every time I step on the field, practice, or game,” he said. “What can I do in those six seconds to the best of my ability to help this team move the ball and help this team win?
“I just had a blast out there with these guys,” he continued. “We had a great week of practice and just executed at a really high level. To be able to go watch the tape and find ways to get better, that’s the No. 1 thing we’re focused on right now.”
McCarthy’s rise to the top of the Giants’ quarterback depth chart has been remarkable. Originally considered the third option behind then-starter Jameis Winston and scout-team quarterback Jake Haener, the ex-Viking quickly grasped the Giants’ playbook while showing comfort in coordinator Matt Nagy’s offense.
Though he was used only in select packages in the Giants’ 27-27 Week 5 tie with the Washington Commanders, McCarthy took the offensive reins with 11 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter of the team’s 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints, after Winston’s second interception of the day.
McCarthy finished the game having completed 11 of 21 passes for 243 yards and one touchdown. He logged the most passing yards in a fourth quarter by any player this season. For his efforts, coach John Harbaugh named McCarthy the Giants’ new starting quarterback.
As the Giants head into their Week 8 bye, one might assume McCarthy has extra time to rest on his laurels. However, the 6-foot-3, 219-pound quarterback understands that with his opportunity comes great responsibility. Despite the impressive stat sheet, McCarthy was sacked three times and also regretted some errant throws.
As Big Blue reconvenes to prepare for its Week 9 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles, McCarthy will be ready to lead his team toward what Giants fans hope will be their first playoff berth since 2022.
“Just the overall complementary football that was on display today was very exciting,” McCarthy declared.
“There are obviously throws that I want back, and there are plays the defense wants back and special teams. That’s exciting because there are so many other areas and other ways we can get better and keep moving forward.
“But getting the win going into the bye is an absolutely great feeling,” he added. “We just have to keep staying humble and hungry.”

title: Giants Grades: Ground Force Rules in OT Win Over Texans
full_text:
The New York Giants delivered a big overtime win against the Houston Texans, a 27-21 thriller in which the running game, challenged this week by head coach John Harbaugh, answered the call against a Texans defense that came in with the league’s third-best run defense (83.0 yards per game).
Harbaugh challenged the running backs to step up and take the bull by the horns. They produced 188 yards on 34 carries (5.5 average), with 180 of those yards on 28 carries (6.43 yards per carry) by Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr., and Devin Singletary.
Skattebo, who finished with a career-best 124 yards on 17 carries, and Singletary had the Giants’ two longest rushing plays from scrimmage this season in overtime on the game-winning drive. Skattebo went for 42 yards and Singletary for the 30-yard game-winner.
All four of the Giants’ touchdowns this week came on the ground, one each by Skattebo, Singletary, Tracy, and quarterback Jameis Winston on a tush push.
Here are a few other quick takeaways from the win.
Quarterback J.J. McCarthy, in his debut as Big Blue’s starting quarterback, had a fine afternoon, finishing 20 of 28 for 252 yards with no interceptions or touchdowns thrown (99.1 rating).
What especially stood out was McCarthy’s solid deep-ball play, completing two of his four attempts of 20-plus air yards for 69 air yards total. His two longest passes of the day went to rookie receiver Malachi Fields for 47 yards and receiver Malik Nabers for 42 yards.
Cornerback Deonte Banks’s bounce-back season continued this week as he allowed just three of six pass targets to be completed for 10 yards, only one of them after the catch.
Banks held his own against top Texans receiver Nico Collins, limiting him to one catch on four targets for four yards, one after the catch. The coaches wisely had Banks playing mostly man coverage, which is his strength, and he turned in one of his best performances of the season.
As Banks’s confidence grows each week, that can only help when the Giants return from the bye to face what should be a tougher slate of opposing receivers.
The media forgot to ask receiver Malik Nabers last week how much more he feels he has to go before he’s 100%. But if he’s not there by now after the devastating knee injury he suffered last year, then the sky truly is the limit for him this season.
Nabers recorded his fifth straight 100-yard game this season, this time catching seven of nine targets for 111 yards. He is tied with Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba for the most 100-yard receiving games this season.
This week’s Giants offense had it all, including the explosive plays it had been missing in both the passing and running games.
The offense also helped stifle league sack leader Will Anderson Jr., who was held without a sack, and credit should go to right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor, who pushed through a painful calf injury.
And how about the discipline? The Giants had only two penalties: a rather iffy unnecessary roughness flag against Skattebo and a deliberate delay of game by the punt team to give Jordan Stout more room to work with. Oh, and did anyone catch how Skattebo broke three tackles on his touchdown run?
Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson challenged his defense after last week’s lackluster showing in the loss to the Saints, and it responded. New York held the Texans to 84 yards on the ground and just 153 passing yards.
The defense also sacked Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud and covered Collins like a blanket. Tackling was better than last week, as more players ran to the ball and heeded their coach’s words to wrap up ball carriers rather than grab at them.
Kudos to Micah McFadden, who stepped in for Tremaine Edmunds and finished with a team-leading 10 tackles (all solo), two tackles for loss, and a quarterback hit.
Do the Giants have a kicking problem to worry about moving forward? After starting the season 9-of-9, Dominic Zvada has made four of his last nine field goal attempts. He missed two indoors this week, which thankfully didn’t hurt his team.
But it said a lot that in the third quarter, with the ball on the Texans’ 37-yard line, the Giants took a five-yard delay-of-game penalty and punted rather than try another field goal.
The punt coverage unit was shaky once again, allowing the Texans an average of 12.5 yards per return, with Tank Dell and Jaylin Noel having longs of 14 and 11 yards, respectively. If there’s a bright spot, it’s that the unit was better than last week.
The play calling was strong, but kudos to the coaching staff for challenging the players and to the players for answering. This was a classic example of how coaching matters, and it’s why one should never count out a team led by John Harbaugh.
From a tactical perspective, good job by offensive coordinator Matt Nagy in getting Malachi Fields more involved downfield. And what about the Giants’ version of the tush push, which faked everyone out on the last one they ran before Skattebo’s big run?
On defense, Wilson brought the heat against Stroud, who was blitzed on 44.8% of his dropbacks and faced pressure on 55.2% overall.
